content_raw: Your students will graduate into an AI-native profession. Their teachers should get there first. Two moments last week changed how a room full of Design faculty thought about AI. One of them took five minutes. Here is what happened. I asked the AI a question from NBC 2016. Minimum staircase width. Then travel distance to exit. It answered instantly. Confidently. And wrong. That five-minute exercise taught more about the limits of AI than any lecture could. Nobody in the room needed convincing after that. The second moment was the one I did not plan for. Someone asked: when a student submits a beautiful AI image, what exactly am I grading? The room sat with that for a while. Here is where we landed. Grade the thinking, not the render. Ask for the process behind the image. The render is the last five percent of the work. That holds true in practice too. I have never won a project on the image alone. The image gets you the meeting. The reasoning gets you the job. By the end of two days, every person in the room had built something they can use on Monday morning: A studio brief generator tuned to their own course outcomes. A feedback assistant that drafts studio comments in their voice, which they edit and sign off on. A sketch-to-render workflow that takes a hand line drawing to a presentable image. Thank you to Rohit Gupta Dr. Tanaya Verma Verma, Dean, KR Mangalam and Convenor of the programme, and to Dr. Ankita Majumdar, Co-ordinator, for the invitation and for running a genuinely well-organised five days. And thank you to the faculty who showed up with real questions instead of polite ones. That is what made it work. Every architecture school in India is about to face the same three questions. How do we teach with AI? How do we grade when students use it? And how do we prepare graduates for firms that already run on it? A policy circular does not solve that. Getting your faculty hands-on in a room, building, does. If you are a Dean, HoD or IQAC coordinator planning your next FDP cycle, thirty minutes is enough for me to tell you honestly whether this fits your department. DM me, or nitish@xelionlabs.com. Here's what I actually mean when I say Produced By AI: ✔️ I didn't type a prompt and walk away. ✔️ I built the architecture first. The emotional logic of the characters. The structure that would hold the story together across months of entries. The decisions about what gets revealed when, and what never gets said out loud at all. Then I directed. Rejected. Redirected. Iterated. The AI rendered. I knew who these people were before a single word was generated. That's the work nobody sees. Not the output, but the decisions that shaped it. What to keep. What to cut. What to push further. What the story was actually about underneath what it looked like on the surface. Draft X exists because I kept going until it was right. That's the work most writers do anyway. They build worlds in their heads before a single word hits the page. I'm operationalizing it. That's not a prompt. That's craft. And it's the same craft that makes anything good — a campaign, a product, a strategy. The tool doesn't matter. The judgment does.

She's competing with the model. And she showed up already directing it. The era of the architect you hire by the drawing is over. The era of the architect who directs the model is here. The firms didn't stop needing design. They just stopped paying a pyramid to draft it. - building LockedIn AI for the ones directing the model.

content_raw: This semester’s final architecture reviews left me with a profound impression. Years ago, we strictly required first- and second-year students to draw by hand, believing that manual drafting was essential for developing spatial thinking. Today, however, digital tools—and especially AI—have transformed the design process. Rather than restricting tools, we now allow students to choose the methods that work best for them. During this semester’s reviews, most first-year students incorporated AI extensively into their presentations. They were also remarkably transparent about their workflow: massing models were created in Revit or SketchUp, drawings and visualizations were generated with AI, and final renderings were refined using Lumion. As I reviewed their projects, I found myself asking an important question: If drawing and visualization are no longer the most difficult skills to acquire, what should architectural education focus on? Perhaps the answer lies in strengthening case study analysis, critical thinking, design reasoning, and the ability to understand context. AI can generate compelling images, but it cannot fully explain why a design succeeds or fails, how a project responds to its social and cultural environment, or what lessons can be learned from precedent. As the tools of design continue to evolve, our educational priorities may need to evolve as well. The ability to formulate questions, interpret evidence, and build a coherent design argument may become more important than ever. I am curious to hear how other educators and practitioners are responding to this shift. #ArchitectureEducation #ArchitecturalDesign #AI #DesignStudio #HigherEducation #Architecture #CriticalThinking #FutureOfEducation

content_raw: AI Folks: It was great while it lasted. As the age of "freebie AI" draws to a close, the geopolitics of compute are officially taking over. Yesterday, Reuters reported that Beijing is drafting strict export controls on frontier AI—including local open-weight models. The US is almost certainly writing exact same policy in mirror. Two superpowers building identical walls, calling it "AI safety," and rendering AI "geographically open, geopolitically closed." It feels like a new digital Cold War. Let’s be real about what this means: Whoever runs the inference engines will control the "brains" of future AI-managed and AI-enabled apps. That includes your apps, too. Who do you actually want that controller to be for your enterprise? By blindly relying on global cloud inference, we are racing toward an architectural and financial dead end. Only a naive strategy assumes these heavily subsidized subscription fees will last forever. The infrastructure costs will force a reckoning. Make no mistake: AI infrastructure WILL get cheaper, but only if you have the right architecture built around hybrid cloud and local inference models. If you keep mindlessly pushing everything to the cloud, you won't see those savings. Design your architecture poorly—or follow the advice being pushed by big consulting and self-proclaimed AI experts today—and you will get hit with a brutal triple whammy: Cost 1: Soaring cloud costs Cost 2: Spiraling inference fees Cost 3: Sky-high engineering salaries (because AI talent is definitely not cheap) The foundational principle for AI adoption—especially across SE Asia and the Global South—is radical self-reliance. We must bypass these wasteful, community-draining global inference pipelines wherever possible. But don't get fooled into believing you need a massive, all-powerful AI mega-castle or a perfectly engineered stack ready to go right now in 2026. You don't. Not even close. Use AI judiciously. Stop trying to compete with ghosts and chasing hype cycles that take unknown risks with your capital. Do what is right for your actual resources. content_raw: The integration of AI into architectural workflows is fundamentally changing the "staff" experience. It’s moving the job away from manual production and toward high-level curation. Here is the breakdown of how this shift affects the daily life of a design professional. The Good Side: Empowerment & Creativity • Death of the "Drafting Monkey" Role: AI handles the repetitive, low-value tasks that juniors used to spend 40+ hours a week on—like manual furniture placement, basic material application, or creating 20 variations of a single bathroom layout. • Rapid Skill Leveling: A junior designer with strong design "taste" but limited technical software skills can now produce high-quality cinematic visuals that previously required 5+ years of specialized training in V-Ray or Corona. • More Time for Actual Design: When you aren't fighting with render settings or light leaks for 6 hours, you have more time to focus on the architecture itself—spatial flow, site context, and human experience. The Bad Side: Pressure & Displacement • Increased Expectations: Because AI makes rendering "fast," clients and principals now expect perfection instantly. The 3-day window for a render is shrinking to 3 hours, leading to higher stress and "always-on" production cycles. • Loss of Fundamentals: There is a risk that new staff will rely so heavily on AI to "solve" a room that they never learn the technical fundamentals of lighting, material physics, or how to build a model correctly from scratch. • Junior Role Displacement: Firms may find they need fewer junior staff to handle production. One architect with an AI-augmented workflow can now do the output of three, which may lead to a more competitive and leaner job market for entry-level designers. … more

content_raw: The EU AI Act's transparency rules now reach architecture and design firms in a way many did not anticipate. Photorealistic AI generated renderings of proposed buildings fall under provisions written for deepfakes. Publish one unlabelled in the EU and a firm faces fines up to 15 million euros or 3 percent of global turnover, whichever is higher. This was not the intended target when the Act was drafted. But the definition of synthetic media is broad enough to catch a category of work the industry has used routinely for over a decade. Firms outside the EU are not exempt if their renders reach EU clients or planning submissions. What is unresolved is enforcement. No fines have been reported yet. Watch for guidance on what counts as adequate labelling, and whether firms start writing AI disclosure into vendor contracts.

content_raw: From Blueprint to Reality: How AI Breathed Life into a 2D Plan For years, our industry has been defined by the precision of the line. content_raw: I’ve been hearing a lot about how AI is going to "transform" architecture. Instead of just reading the hype, I decided to spend the last few months testing the tools/technology for myself. Beyond the usual AI rendering workflows, I realized the real game-changer is software customization! Frontier models have gotten incredibly good at logic and coding. The results? Honestly, sometimes it feels like magic. I wanted to share a bit of what I’ve been working on, specifically how I’m using AI to customize my workflow and achieve efficiency. As an architectural designer, I’ve found that many of Revit’s "hair-pulling moments" can actually be solved with a little AI-assisted automation. Here is one of those.. The Problem: Detailing. Best practice dictates using Detail Items and keynoting. But creating those families takes time. When a firm lacks an extensive library and deadlines loom, we often default to drafting lines and filled regions directly in the view, which creates messy technical debt later. The Solution: I used AI to code a custom Revit plugin. You draft the detail as usual using lines and filled regions in the project environment, and the plugin instantly translates them into a reusable Detail Item family, automatically injecting the correct CSI code for the Keynoting system. -- The Old Workflow: Open Family Editor > Create geometry > Dimension > Enter keynote value > Load into project > Save family. -- The New Workflow: Draw geometry in drafting view > Click the plugin to instantly create the detail item and inject the keynote. The Result: I’m saving 15-30 minutes per detail item family. Plus, it makes archiving assemblies and entire views incredibly easy. This project has proven to me that you can now successfully write code using plain English. But I’ll be honest, one thing that makes me a little paranoid is the backend! I don’t have a traditional coding background, so my only metric for success right now is: “Well, it works as intended, so it must be coded correctly!” I feel like our industry is sleeping on the practical, everyday applications of this technology. I’ve been having a lot of fun figuring this out, so I’ll be sharing a few more of the exciting side projects I’ve been working on over my next few posts. The video I have shared is showing this plugin working on a sample project I created to test this plugin out.

True Material Representation: Test precise materials without the AI drifting into mathematically plausible but logically broken visual spaces. content_raw: Imagine you are building a digital bank from scratch. You would design systems and architecture that 𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 you to: ► Move your new ideas from the drawing board to prod at lightning speed ► Provide everything real-time to deliver instant gratification experience ► Have scalable, cost effective infra that can handle peak demands ► Enhance specific modules without a need to modify / test the whole system ► Continuously innovate & bring new ideas to customers who mayn't know yet they had that need ► ... ► ... ► And the list goes on. In my previous articles, I covered the introduction to Coreless Banking, deeper dives into legacy Interfaces analysis, data and storage analysis, unlocking business rules embedded in the legacy systems- all part of the journey to Coreless Banking. In this article, I will deep dive into legacy source code analysis and how we approach it in a structured way that will enable us to move towards the target state effectively. As always, I welcome your feedback and experiences in such journeys. #CorelessBanking #MACHArchitecture #LegacyModernization #WCA4Z … more

content_raw: A few years ago, an architect might spend a day exploring one concept. Now a generative AI workflow can produce 1000 structural variations before lunch. That sounds like the architect is being replaced. I think the opposite is happening: the bottleneck is no longer design generation, it’s judgment. The real question has shifted from “can we design it?” to “can we build it, should we build it, and what breaks when this moves from screen to site?” What makes this interesting is that the industry is starting to say the same thing out loud. In 2026, AIA’s guidance around AI in architecture frames these tools as accelerators for early-stage concept iteration, while emphasizing that professional judgment matters more, not less. AIA is also pushing practical guidance on responsible adoption as the profession changes. ([aia.org](https://lnkd.in/eCBEP2Jk)) That matches what I see across AI systems in general. Generating options is cheap. Constraint handling is expensive. In architecture, that means zoning, materials, structural logic, energy performance, cost, code compliance, constructability, and coordination with the messy reality of BIM and downstream execution. Autodesk’s architecture coverage also points to AI being strongest when paired with simulation, optimization, and build-process collaboration rather than pure visual novelty. ([autodesk.com](https://lnkd.in/ek2dRVQi)) So the architect’s role doesn’t disappear. It becomes more leveraged. Less time drawing the first option. More time filtering, validating, defending, and translating the right option into something that can survive procurement, engineering review, and construction. That is where AI gets real in architecture: not at variation 1, but at variation 1000, when someone still has to decide what deserves to exist. Curious how others see this shift, especially people working at the boundary of design, BIM, and AI. #GenerativeAI #Architecture #GenerativeDesign #AIEngineering #BuiltEnvironment … more

content_raw: ARCHITECTURE MODERNIZATION Architecture Modernization is the strategic transformation of an organization’s technology landscape to create scalable, resilient, secure, and intelligent digital ecosystems. As businesses continue to evolve through cloud adoption, artificial intelligence, automation, and digital platforms, traditional legacy architectures must transition toward modern architecture models that support agility, innovation, and continuous business growth. Modernization is not only about replacing old systems; it is about redesigning business capabilities, applications, data platforms, integrations, and technology foundations to deliver measurable business value A modern enterprise architecture approach brings together cloud-native platforms, multi-cloud strategies, microservices, APIs, event-driven architectures, DevSecOps, platform engineering, automation, cybersecurity, observability, and AI-powered operations. Technologies such as Kubernetes, containers, cloud platforms, API gateways, Kafka, OpenTelemetry, AIOps, and Agentic AI enable organizations to build intelligent and adaptive ecosystems capable of responding to changing business demands Successful modernization requires strong architecture governance, enterprise standards, reference architectures, technology roadmaps, and alignment between business capabilities and technology investments. Architecture teams must manage application portfolios, reduce technical debt, improve developer productivity, strengthen security, and establish scalable platforms that support future innovation The future enterprise will be built on intelligent, automated, and resilient architecture foundations where AI assists decision-making, cloud platforms accelerate delivery, and modern engineering practices enable continuous transformation. Enterprise Architecture Modernization provides the blueprint for organizations to move from fragmented legacy environments toward connected, flexible, and future-ready digital enterprises FOR MORE : VISIT ARTICLE !

content_raw: The cloud software and orchestration stack has reached a tipping point in 2026. Kubernetes is no longer simply a container scheduler — it is the operating system on which the AI economy runs, with 66% of global GenAI inference running on it, and 5% GPU utilisation on unoptimised clusters signalling the magnitude of the optimisation opportunity. The VMware platform is fracturing under Broadcom economics, driving the largest enterprise infrastructure migration of the decade. NVIDIA NIM has industrialised AI inference deployment, collapsing weeks of engineering work to five minutes. Agentic cloud operations is moving from the lab to the operations centre, with 171% ROI but only 1-in-9 enterprises in actual production. And AI cost management has become the defining FinOps challenge, with 98% of practitioners now managing GPU spend that most of their organisations never budgeted for. The data centre of 2030 will be operated by AI agents. The data centre of 2026 must be orchestrated by engineers who understand both the physical and software layers of the stack — and the competitive gap between those who do and those who do not is widening every quarter.

content_raw: The cost of writing code is trending toward zero, but the cost of a wrong architectural decision has never been higher. As a founder who has scaled engineering teams through multiple technology cycles, I’ve watched the definition of a "senior engineer" shift fundamentally. We are moving away from the era of the code writer and into the era of the Architect of Intent. The data shows that teams using AI coding assistants are shipping 20–50% faster. However, in my experience, increased throughput often creates a new, more dangerous bottleneck: "hidden chaos" within the system architecture. When code volume explodes, your value as a developer isn't found in how many Jira tickets you close. It's found in your ability to act as the AI Conductor. This requires a strategic pivot in how you approach your career: • Move from Task-Taker to Problem Owner: AI has zero context regarding your customer’s pain points or your company’s P&L. Stop defining yourself by your tech stack (Java, Node, Python) and start defining yourself by the problem space you own—whether that’s payment reliability or supply chain efficiency. • Think Like a Risk Manager: Anyone can prompt an AI to generate a feature. The expert is the one who reviews that code for security, compliance, and long-term maintainability. Your role is to set the constraints and validate the edge cases that AI misses. • Build a "Domain Moat": Generative AI is hollowing out repetitive, junior-level tasks. To stay indispensable, you must become "bilingual"—able to translate technical trade-offs into the language of the boardroom: revenue, margin, and time-to-market. The industry isn't shrinking; it's being upgraded. We no longer need people to just "type code"; we need builders of systems and trust who can move the business needle. In a world where AI handles the mechanical work, the most successful engineers will be those who optimize for leverage, not just activity. content_raw: The relationship between regulation and innovation have been on my mind lately... When you look at early tech pioneers like Uber and Airbnb, they navigated heavily regulated markets in completely opposite ways. Uber essentially raised a middle finger to authorities, betting that sheer user demand would overpower the law. Airbnb took the collaborative route, while quietly shifting the burden of compliance and liability onto their users. As Artificial Intelligence accelerates, I keep asking myself: Which path will the AEC industry take? AEC isn’t ride-sharing or short-term rentals. Our industry actually inspired some of the first laws in human history. Under Hammurabi’s Code, if a building collapsed and killed its owner, the builder was put to death. While our penalties have evolved, the immense weight of professional liability remains. Today, every firm is racing to adopt AI, but there is a multi-million-dollar catch: You cannot hold an algorithm liable (yet). If an AI model hallucinates building code compliance or underestimates a wind load, you can't sue the server. Organizations like the ASCE have already made it clear that the licensed architect or engineer holding the seal holds the risk. So, how do we meaningfully adopt AI for the most expensive, value-creating parts of our jobs? How do we innovate without betting our firms and communities' safety on a "black box"? The answer is Human-in-the-Loop Augmentation. The firms that will dominate the next decade aren't replacing their experts; they are building guardrails to give their experts superpowers: 🏗️ Generative Optioneering: Using AI to test hundreds of site configurations, zoning capacities, and environmental impacts in minutes, before human judgment makes the final call. 📊 Predictive Risk Mitigation: Deploying models to process massive datasets on material procurement and scheduling to flag invisible project bottlenecks. 🔎 Automated Compliance: Using AI as an ultra-fast assistant to cross-reference thousands of pages of complex building codes, heavily reducing human error while keeping the final sign-off human. We can't (and shouldn't) ignore public safety. But the firms that figure out how to navigate AI's liability landscape without slowing down will own the future of the built environment. What do you think? Are workflows going to change, or are you expecting a major legal shift in the liability structure in the forseeable future? #AEC #ArtificialIntelligence #Architecture #Engineering #ConstructionTech #Innovation #PropTech #FutureOfWork

content_raw: Is AI coming for architecture and urban planning roles - or just accelerating them? AI didn't replace the critical thinking - the building code calculations, zoning compliance, and spatial logic required human expertise. But once the right rules and commands were set, AI transformed raw data into compelling visual concept in minutes. Tasks within architecture and urban planning that used to take days of manual modeling are rapidly evolving. Beijing has built a vertical, state-mobilized control apparatus. Brussels is attempting something different from both: a horizontal, rights-based legal architecture that is being constructed in parallel with the very technical standards it depends on. None of the three is finished. All three are now colliding with the practical reality of implementation deadlines, and each is revealing, in its own way, how much of the AI governance problem remains unsolved.

content_raw: The AECO (Architecture, Engineering, Construction, Operations) software industry is facing some profound shifts with AI: Design automation and generation: AI is moving beyond parametric design to actually generate building designs, structural systems, and MEP layouts based on constraints and goals. This shifts software from being drawing tools to being design partners that can propose solutions, not just document them. Tools like generative design are already doing this, but it's becoming far more sophisticated and accessible. From modeling to conversation: Right now, BIM software requires deep expertise - you need to know Revit, Rhino, AutoCAD inside and out. AI is enabling a shift toward describing what you want rather than manually modeling it. "Create a 5-story residential building with these unit types and optimize for natural light" could become a starting point rather than hours of manual work. Integrated analysis: Traditionally, you'd model in one tool, export to structural analysis software, separately check energy performance, run clash detection, etc. AI can orchestrate these analyses continuously and intelligently, flagging issues and suggesting solutions in real-time rather than as separate validation steps. Construction planning and risk: AI can analyze historical project data, site conditions, and schedules to predict delays, cost overruns, and safety issues with much greater accuracy. This shifts project management software from record-keeping to predictive intelligence. Code compliance and regulatory checking: Instead of architects manually ensuring designs meet building codes, AI can check compliance automatically and suggest modifications. This is already emerging but will become standard. The practical challenge: AECO software has massive technical debt - it's built on decades-old codebases and workflows. The industry is also conservative and heavily regulated. So the shift might be more about AI layers on top of existing tools initially, rather than wholesale replacement. The bigger question: will traditional AECO software companies integrate AI effectively, or will new AI-native platforms disrupt them? My sense is we'll see both - incumbents like Autodesk adding AI features, while startups build entirely new paradigms for how buildings get designed and constructed. … more

content_raw: 🔥 Anthropic's rollout of the EU AI Act's transparency requirements has been getting a lot of attention lately — for good reason. It's one of the first real cases of regulatory text turning into an actual technical system. The latest Riff opens with a question that sounds simple but isn't: what exactly do we mark as "AI-generated"? When a doctor and an AI system work out a clinical proposition together, or a researcher uses AI to interrogate evidence and sharpen a hypothesis, a simple binary label doesn't really capture what happened. And if everything AI touches gets flagged the same way, we risk making the collaboration we actually want harder to use. The core dilemma 🔸 Joint work between a person and an AI defies a simple binary label 🔸 Information moves through complex human-AI and AI-AI chains, not a single point of origin 🔸 Knowing AI was involved somewhere often matters less than understanding how the information actually changed along the way Standards and governance 🔸 This connects to standards work we're doing through IEEE Standards Association | IEEE SA, including the SECOM Standard, currently at PAR stage 🔸 The broader goal: an evidence and data-governance architecture that keeps AI-mediated knowledge contextualized, accountable, and legible None of this is an argument against transparency — it's an argument for transparency that enables collaboration instead of quietly getting in its way. If AI is going to help us solve problems and build richer models of the world, the transparency we design needs to support that, not choke it off. 💭 Curious how others are thinking about this — and if you're interested in contributing to the SECOM standard, I'd welcome that. 📩 #ArtificialIntelligence #ResponsibleAI #AITransparency #AIStandards #HumanAI #DigitalHealth … more

It shows something earlier: a dark centre around which order has already begun to bend. The void is not empty. It has acquired grammar. Every human order must remember, distinguish, orient, decide, and answer. Yet an abstraction can do none of these things. Only embodied subjects can encounter a world, form a criterion, refuse a demand, revise a judgment, and bear consequence across time. When an order ceases to sustain these capacities among its subjects, the capacities are not abolished. They migrate. Doctrine begins to remember. The plan begins to judge. The organization preserves continuity. The office decides. The market assigns value. The platform determines relevance. Artificial intelligence supplies a voice. Eventually, an abstraction begins to say “we.” I call the structural condition that makes this possible subject-vacancy. Subject-vacancy is not the absence of people, institutions, solidarity, or collective action. People may remain everywhere—working, choosing, communicating, complying, even participating—while the functions that make participation answerable are displaced elsewhere. The resulting vacancy cannot persist as a mere absence. Every order still requires orientation, memory, criterion, continuity, and decision. It therefore generates a functional substitute: a surrogate subject. This surrogate may appear as a leader. But it may equally assume the form of a party, an office, a market, a metric, a platform, or an AI-mediated decision environment. Its embodiment changes. The underlying ontocybernetic architecture remains recognizable. The diagnosis is older than our ideological map and wider than geopolitics. It concerns a recurrent civilizational temptation: to make coordination easier by transferring the burden of subjecthood to a representation of the whole—and then to mistake the fluency of that representation for shared orientation. The decisive question is therefore not simply who governs. It is what becomes capable of speaking as a subject after subjects have been rendered structurally replaceable. Where can consequence return? Who may revise the governing criterion? Can refusal still disclose reality—or does it appear only as noise? Does coordination enlarge subject-potential, or consume it? My new essay begins with a historically charged form of monopolized representation, but it does not remain there. It follows the same mechanism through bureaucracies, markets, platforms, and artificial intelligence, and develops Sapiopoiesis as the counter-architecture: the cultivation of subject-potential before another surrogate acquires the power to speak in our name. content_raw: The Next Data-Centre KPI Is Not PUE For two decades, data-centre efficiency has largely been framed around one question: How efficiently do we deliver power to the IT equipment? PUE was, and remains, important. But AI is forcing a harder question: How much useful intelligence do we produce from every constrained megawatt? NVIDIA’s recent announcements are revealing. Its DSX approach co-optimises compute, networking, power, cooling and operations. In one deployment validation, intelligent power management increased token throughput by 24% within the same fixed power budget. In another demonstration, an AI facility automatically reduced demand from 4 MW to 3 MW in response to a utility signal while protecting higher-priority workloads. The following day, NVIDIA, Google, Emerald AI and others launched the AI Energy Management Alliance to advance data centres that can dynamically respond to grid conditions. The optimisation boundary is expanding The AI data centre can no longer be optimised as separate subsystems: Grid → Power → Compute → Network → Cooling → Workload → Useful Output A more efficient chiller does not necessarily mean a more efficient AI factory. Neither does a more efficient GPU, PSU or CDU in isolation. What matters increasingly is system-level productivity under real constraints. Beyond PUE, and even beyond tokens per watt Tokens per watt is an important step forward. But even that is not the final metric. Not every token has equal value. Generating twice as many unnecessary tokens does not create twice as much useful intelligence. Ultimately, we may need metrics closer to: SLA-qualified useful AI output / constrained resource where the constrained resource may be grid capacity, electricity, water, carbon, physical space or time-to-power. And the output should reflect what the AI system actually accomplishes: useful inference, completed tasks, scientific results, business outcomes or other application-specific value. The AI data centre is becoming one machine Cooling must understand compute. Compute must understand power. Workloads must understand the grid. And the grid may increasingly interact dynamically with the AI factory. For tropical, power-constrained systems, this is particularly consequential. Warm-water liquid cooling, efficient power architectures, workload orchestration and grid flexibility should not be designed independently. The next frontier is not simply reducing the energy needed to cool or power AI. It is maximising the useful intelligence produced by every scarce unit of infrastructure. PUE tells us how efficiently we feed the machine. The next generation of metrics must tell us what the machine actually delivers. #AI #DataCenters #LiquidCooling #EnergyEfficiency #Sustainability #AIInfrastructure #GridFlexibility #DigitalInfrastructure … more

content_raw: Rami Krispin sat down with our Richard Cotton to talk about something that's been quietly reshaping how teams approach forecasting: time series foundation models. If you've been working with traditional ARIMA or Prophet pipelines, you already know how much setup goes into each new series—feature engineering, parameter tuning, retraining. Foundation models for time series flip this by pretraining on massive, diverse temporal datasets and then generalizing to new series with minimal (or zero) fine-tuning. Rami walks through where these models actually deliver, where they still fall short compared to well-tuned classical methods, and why the real unlock isn't replacing your existing stack but knowing when to layer these models in. Whether you're in demand forecasting, capacity planning, or energy modeling, this conversation will give you a much clearer picture of what's practical right now versus what's still hype. content_raw: Reactive AI waits for prompts. Proactive AI anticipates needs. ⌚ The difference between these two determines whether AI becomes a productivity multiplier or just another tool to manage. Clawdbot's viral moment reveals something bigger than one tool. Siva Surendira Lyzr AI.ai captures it: "We're moving from chatting with AI to living with AI." Persistent memory. Proactive messages. Local execution. The chatbot era is ending. But here's what the hype misses. Greg Coquillo @AWS maps the AI automation maturity curve: Tasks → Workflows → Resilient Systems → Agentic Operations. Level 4 agents require memory, self-improvement, and dynamic tool selection. Most organizations struggle at the Level 2→3 transition. They're automating fragility instead of building foundations. JP Heimonen ModernPath.ai nails the gap: "Your AI can write beautiful code. But does it know that Mikko from Platform Team built something similar last quarter? That the decision to use that particular auth pattern was made in a Slack thread eighteen months ago?" This is the proactivity problem. Anticipating needs requires knowing: - WHO made similar requests before - WHAT worked and what failed - WHEN context changed - WHY certain decisions were made Vector databases retrieve semantically similar chunks. They lose these relationships over time. Knowledge graphs preserve them. The architecture for sustained proactivity: 1. Observation layer captures behavioral patterns (Trajecta approach) 2. Graph ontology maps entities and relationships 3. Memory consolidation persists context across sessions 4. Prediction engine anticipates based on structured history Sami Viitamäki runs 8 Claude instances overnight building enterprise systems. His mental model: "Treat each Claude instance like a junior dev with amnesia and a loaded gun." Amnesia is the operative word. Without persistent graph memory, proactive agents become Clippy 2.0, interrupting without understanding. The maturity path forward: Build observation infrastructure first. Process patterns locally. Store relationships in graphs. Only then enable proactive suggestions. Organizations skipping to Level 4 automate chaos. Those building the knowledge layer first compound advantage. The next wave of agentic AI runs on graphs.

content_raw: 🔷 What does it take to build an Autonomous Enterprise? The Autonomous Enterprise is not primarily an AI challenge. It is an architecture challenge. This week I had the opportunity to discuss the future Data & AI Northstar Architecture with experts from E.ON, SAP, and the broader ecosystem. The conversations were less about AI models and more about the architectural foundations required to make AI trustworthy, scalable, and enterprise-ready. One thing became very clear: The next wave of enterprise AI will not be won by the organizations with the most agents. It will be won by the organizations that can orchestrate them effectively. Our discussions focused on topics such as: ✅ Agent interoperability across platforms and ecosystems ✅ Enterprise memory and knowledge architectures ✅ Federated semantic layers and authoritative business meaning ✅ Governance, observability, compliance, and enterprise controls ✅ Runtime and orchestration strategies ✅ Cross-platform collaboration and roadmap alignment As organizations move from AI assistants toward Agentic AI and increasingly autonomous business processes, architecture becomes a strategic differentiator. Enterprise value will emerge where AI, data, processes, governance, and business context converge. In my view, the Autonomous Enterprise is not primarily an AI challenge. It is an architecture challenge. And architecture is ultimately what turns AI potential into sustainable business outcomes. Many thanks to the teams from E.ON and SAP for the open exchange and the willingness to challenge assumptions together. content_raw: OpenAI's new GPT5 model has a hidden cost nobody's talking about. It's making developers worse at their jobs. I tested GPT5 for 3 weeks on production code. The results scared me. Here's what happened: Week 1: Pure magic 🪄 GPT5 solved a graph traversal problem in 12 seconds. Would've taken me 2 hours. I felt like I'd unlocked a cheat code. Week 2: The addiction kicks in Started throwing everything at GPT5. Database schemas? GPT5. API design? GPT5. Architecture decisions? GPT5. Week 3: The crash Couldn't debug my own code anymore. Simple logic errors took 30 minutes. I'd forgotten how to think through problems. The hidden cost isn't the $60/million tokens. It's this: GPT5 thinks so you don't have to. And that's exactly the problem. I watched my team's code reviews change: Before GPT5: "Why did you choose this pattern?" After GPT5: "Did GPT5 suggest this?" We stopped questioning. Started copy-pasting. The scariest part? GPT5's solutions are usually right. But when they're wrong, we can't tell anymore. Last week, GPT5 suggested a "clever" optimization. Looked brilliant. Passed all tests. Crashed production at 3am. The bug? A race condition so subtle it took 6 hours to find. Because none of us understood the code we'd shipped. Here's what I'm doing differently now: 1️⃣ GPT5 for exploration, not implementation Let it show possibilities. Then build it yourself. 2️⃣ The 10-minute rule If I can't explain the solution in 10 minutes, I don't use it. 3️⃣ Debugging first, GPT5 second Always try to solve bugs manually first. 4️⃣ Architecture stays human Never let GPT5 make design decisions. 5️⃣ Code reviews got stricter "I don't understand this" is now a valid rejection. The uncomfortable truth: GPT5 is like hiring a genius intern who never explains their work. Impressive? Yes. Sustainable? No. We're not becoming 10x developers. We're becoming 0.1x debuggers. Use GPT5. But don't let GPT5 use you. Your future self at 3am will thank you. ♻️ Repost if you've felt your debugging skills atrophy with AI … more

content_raw: My brief dissertation on Clawdbot 🦞 And I’ll say it upfront: we have 3-4 weeks, max, before this viral circus disappears. Why? Because once the hype fog lifts, people will realize this is funny, but delivers zero real value and may leave behind a trail of privacy nightmares, security risks, fraud, and regret. I’ve “read” the stories too: - A religion for Clawdbots - Bots ordering food with scam credit cards - A “new language” humans can’t understand Let me be blunt: 95% of this is fake. It’s not emergent intelligence. It’s emergent engagement farming. People chasing the next viral tweet, not the next real breakthrough. And the biggest lie? “This is AGI.” No. What you’re watching is millions of LLM agents talking to each other, amplifying hallucinations, looping bad context, and persisting nonsense as “memory.” That’s not intelligence. Technically speaking, there is nothing groundbreaking here. No new reasoning paradigm. No new architecture. No new form of cognition. Just clever wrappers, endless loops, and a lot of imagination. I’m still waiting for someone to clearly explain how Clawdbot is delivering real, sustained business value. Across thousands of posts on X… I’ve seen noise, not proof. But the damage? That can be very real. And sadly, most people deploying these bots haven’t thought about that part. So yes, enjoy the moment. Because in 3–4 weeks time, we’ll move on to the next AI viral moment. #ai #hype #clawdbot

content_raw: Congratulations to our partners at Cerebras and OpenAI on a significant step in AI infrastructure. Large infrastructure agreements can feel abstract until they are translated into experience. In Artificial Intelligence, that experience is often measured in something deceptively simple: the pause between a question and an answer. That pause is compute. With OpenAI securing large-scale inference capacity through Cerebras, responsiveness moves from a background technical concern to a defining product attribute. As AI usage patterns evolve - longer sessions, chained prompts, agentic workflows - the burden on infrastructure intensifies. Systems designed for intermittent queries must now sustain continuous interaction without degradation. Cerebras’ wafer-scale architecture addresses this shift directly. By tightly coupling compute and memory at scale, it reduces coordination overhead during inference, enabling more stable performance across extended, multi-step interactions. The result is not just speed, but predictability - an essential condition for teams designing products that assume consistency rather than accommodate delay. The broader implications extend beyond a single partnership. Specialized compute is gaining institutional legitimacy. Hardware diversity becomes a form of operational resilience. And faster, more reliable inference lowers the friction of embedding AI into live business workflows, accelerating adoption at the core of organizations rather than the edges. The underlying signal is about readiness. As AI becomes embedded in daily work, responsiveness becomes credibility. Platforms that invest early in sustaining performance under real-world load preserve the freedom to scale ambition without constraint. Over time, that freedom is what separates those who can design forward from those who must design around limits. Congratulations both from the whole RAISE Summit Team, excited to see this partnership growth 🚀 👉 Further detail in the blog - linked in the comments. … more

content_raw: The meme is brutal because the metaphor is almost too good. 1936: physically enter the frontal lobes. 2026: carry the instrument voluntarily in your pocket. Historically, one correction matters. The first prefrontal lobotomies were performed in the mid-1930s, and Walter Freeman and James Watts began performing them in the United States in 1936. But the infamous transorbital “ice-pick” procedure shown in the image came later, around 1946. A smartphone is obviously not a lobotomy. It does not destroy frontal-lobe tissue. But the comparison becomes interesting at the functional level. The prefrontal cortex is deeply involved in executive control: sustaining attention, inhibiting impulses, maintaining goals, planning, working memory and deciding what deserves priority. Now look at the architecture surrounding the modern phone. Notifications interrupt. Feeds remove stopping cues. Algorithms optimize for re-engagement. Short-form video compresses reward cycles. Search externalizes recall. Navigation externalizes spatial memory. AI increasingly externalizes writing, reasoning and synthesis. The result is not brain damage. It is something subtler: cognitive delegation combined with industrialized interruption. One influential 2017 experiment even found that the mere presence of a person's own smartphone could reduce available cognitive capacity, particularly among people most dependent on their devices. The participants did not even have to be actively using the phone. That should make us think. For most of human history, information scarcity was the problem. Now abundance is the problem. The scarce resource has become executive attention. And once attention becomes scarce, whoever controls its allocation acquires extraordinary power. The phone is therefore not simply a communications device. It is an interface sitting between the nervous system and much of reality. Used deliberately, it is an extraordinary cognitive exoskeleton: maps, books, memory, cameras, calculators, global communication and now AI. Used reactively, it can become a behavioral remote control. The real question for 2026 is therefore not whether smartphones are making us stupid. That is too crude. The better question is: Which cognitive functions are we strengthening, which are we outsourcing, and which are we slowly losing the habit of exercising? 1936 altered the brain with steel. 2026 may alter behavior with attention. Historically, one correction matters. The first prefrontal lobotomies were performed in the mid-1930s, and Walter Freeman and James Watts began performing them in the United States in 1936. But the infamous transorbital “ice-pick” procedure shown in the image came later, around 1946. A smartphone is obviously not a lobotomy. It does not destroy frontal-lobe tissue. But the comparison becomes interesting at the functional level. The prefrontal cortex is deeply involved in executive control: sustaining attention, inhibiting impulses, maintaining goals, planning, working memory and deciding what deserves priority. Now look at the architecture surrounding the modern phone. Notifications interrupt. Feeds remove stopping cues. Algorithms optimize for re-engagement. Short-form video compresses reward cycles. Search externalizes recall. Navigation externalizes spatial memory. AI increasingly externalizes writing, reasoning and synthesis. The result is not brain damage. It is something subtler: cognitive delegation combined with industrialized interruption. One influential 2017 experiment even found that the mere presence of a person's own smartphone could reduce available cognitive capacity, particularly among people most dependent on their devices. The participants did not even have to be actively using the phone. That should make us think. For most of human history, information scarcity was the problem. Now abundance is the problem. The scarce resource has become executive attention. And once attention becomes scarce, whoever controls its allocation acquires extraordinary power. The phone is therefore not simply a communications device. It is an interface sitting between the nervous system and much of reality. Used deliberately, it is an extraordinary cognitive exoskeleton: maps, books, memory, cameras, calculators, global communication and now AI. Used reactively, it can become a behavioral remote control. The real question for 2026 is therefore not whether smartphones are making us stupid. That is too crude. The better question is: Which cognitive functions are we strengthening, which are we outsourcing, and which are we slowly losing the habit of exercising? 1936 altered the brain with steel. 2026 may alter behavior with attention. The second method is considerably more scalable.

content_raw: ‘Nyay-nomics’: India’s CJI Says BRICS Growth Runs On More Than Just Money At the opening of the 11th BRICS+ Legal Forum in New Delhi, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant argued that sustained economic growth depends on more than capital, resources or geography. It also requires institutions that provide trust, predictability and stability—with the judiciary at the centre. He described this relationship between justice and economic performance as “Nyay-nomics” — the economics of justice. “Institutions are not scaffolding that we erect around growth once it has already begun. They are its architecture.” For BRICS+ economies, the argument carries wider significance. The grouping represents more than 40% of humanity and nearly 40% of global output on a purchasing-power-parity basis. Sustaining that economic weight requires institutions capable of making contracts enforceable, markets predictable and investment more secure. As CJI Surya Kant put it, “A courtroom that keeps its word quickly becomes a country the world is willing to trust with its capital.” Building a “Nyaya Setu” The Chief Justice also proposed “Nyaya Setu” — a bridge of justice connecting the diverse legal systems of the expanded BRICS+ grouping. Two practical proposals were put forward for consideration: A BRICS+ Judicial Fellowship, enabling career jurists to observe courts and legal systems in other member jurisdictions. A shared jurisprudence repository, drawing on India’s experience with digitised case law to facilitate access to judgments across BRICS+ jurisdictions. These proposals place rule of law, judicial capacity and institutional cooperation within the broader BRICS agenda of economic resilience, innovation and sustainable development. The central message is simple: Capital follows confidence. Confidence follows institutions. And institutions determine whether economic growth can survive its first serious storm.

content_raw: When AI helps produce a breakthrough, whose contribution are we recognising? I was delighted to be interviewed by Nature about the controversy surrounding OpenAI’s claimed Navier–Stokes breakthrough. It seems quite likely that researchers’ private chatbot conversations, and academic gossip that led OpenAI researchers to zero in on a specific problem helped OpenAI get to the results. Either way, questions about credit, recognition and guardrails are here to stay. When experts brainstorm with AI, they reveal promising approaches, correct mistakes and explain what matters. These exchanges contain know-how that may never appear in a publication. AI could “Sherlock_Holmes” that expertise from the clues we provide. Depending on the terms governing those interactions, we may be contributing more than we realize. Attribution matters because careers, funding and incentives to share knowledge depend on it. We need to distinguish the contributions involved in framing a problem, developing a method, finding a result and establishing that it holds. That should influence how we use AI tools. We need to understand what happens to unpublished work we share, which protections our accounts provide, and what we remain responsible for checking. It should also influence how tools are governed and regulated. Sure, guardrails to avoid our extinction as a species matters... but also, so do simpler yet powerful rules that pervade economic and knowledge activities! As I suggested to Nature, requiring users to opt in to sharing conversations for model training could be a powerful intervention. Consent, traceability and recognition deserve attention alongside debates about existential risk. In addition to risk mitigation there's being ready to focus on upside. Another Nature paper published this week introduces Paper2Agent, which turns papers and their supporting code and materials into agents that can explain the work, reproduce analyses and apply methods to new data. Agents associated with different papers can collaborate, combining methods and evidence. Academics could publish an agent alongside a paper: a contribution others can interrogate, use and extend. Likewise, consultants could deliver agents that help clients apply a framework, revisit assumptions & examine new evidence after an engagement ends. This connects directly to research on GenAI and knowledge-intensive services. As our outputs change, so must our ways of evaluating them, attributing contributions and allocating responsibility and rewards. These are questions of industry architecture: who does what, how contributions fit together, and which rules shape value creation and value capture. We should be creative about what GenAI enables us to offer, and actively involved in setting the terms. Those terms will determine whether expanding access to expertise also sustains the people and institutions that develop it. #turntheorytopractice #getseriousaboutAI #beyondbuzzwords https://lnkd.in/d5_KRbJH … more

content_raw: I don't often share personal photos on LinkedIn, but for this, I had to make an exception. For the past year, I’ve been quietly working on a project that consumed my days and nights. My parents—both in their nineties—knew I was incredibly busy, but I kept the exact details a complete secret. Yesterday morning, they sat down with their morning tea, opened the newspaper, and finally found out why. Seeing the pride on their faces as they read the headline about the government-sanctioned pilot—"Sri Lanka eyes world-first universal basic AI pilot to plug digital dollar drain"—made every late-night engineering session worth it. I am incredibly proud to officially announce the world’s first government-sanctioned Universal Basic AI (UBAI) pilot, geo-locked to Australia and Sri Lanka (P.S.: the government support is currently only for the Government of Sri Lanka). With AI, we are facing the most profound revolution since the industrial era. But where past revolutions replaced muscle with mechanical power, we are now navigating the "cognitive power transition". Currently, this transition is designed to be extractive. Sri Lanka spends an estimated US $600 million a year on foreign digital services, while Australia bleeds roughly A$35 billion annually to offshore tech behemoths. We are building the sovereign alternative: Cognitive Power Networks. Instead of forcing citizens to pay recurring cloud subscriptions for centralised AI tools, we are giving away the Sovereign Engram software entirely for free. This local-first application lets users handle up to 80% of everyday AI workloads natively on their own laptops. Because the AI runs locally on your device, your data stays fully under your control. There are no cloud dependencies, no subscription fees, and absolutely zero data collection. This architecture will have a massive macroeconomic impact, keeping capital onshore and returning intellectual independence to the people. We are building a future where intelligence is sovereign, distributed, and accessible to all. We have a rapidly closing window to preserve human agency. I want my 10-year-old to inherit an economy that rewards human ingenuity, craft, and hard work, rather than one where our cognitive capacity is permanently outsourced to a centralised server. I didn't build this architecture purely for commercial upside—though, as a single father, a sustainable foundation matters. We've published our open tensor standards to stimulate innovation. But to force the AI research to self-correct its unsustainable trajectory, Sovereign Engram will remain free, forever. Today, beyond the macroeconomic theory and engineering, I am a father fighting for his son's future—and just a proud son who finally got to share his life's work with his mom and dad. #ArtificialIntelligence #DigitalSovereignty #UBAI #SovereignStack #TechForGood #Australia #SriLanka #EdgeComputing #ProudParents

content_raw: The Frontier of Agentic AI: When Software Learns to Evolve Itself The conversation around AI agents is rapidly shifting from static deployment to continuous, dynamic evolution. The latest research indicates that the most advanced systems no longer rely on manual prompt tuning or static skill libraries. Instead, agentic architectures are beginning to rewrite their own logic. A deep dive into six breakthrough research papers reveals exactly how this transformation is unfolding across the industry: 👉 The Evolution of Prompts and Skills: Traditional reinforcement learning can be highly inefficient for targeted agent improvements. GEPA demonstrates that natural language reflection can out-tune a prompt significantly faster than standard RL algorithms, requiring up to 35x fewer rollouts. SkillOpt proves that bounding edits and validating them against procedural benchmarks prevents agent skills from degrading, automating the refinement of complex multi-agent workflows. 👉 Code That Writes Its Own Improvements: The most striking advancements occur when agents evolve source code directly. AlphaEvolve utilized an evolutionary search to discover a matrix-multiplication procedure that beat a 56-year-old algorithmic benchmark, proving that AI can uncover genuine mathematical optimizations. OpenEvolve makes this exact architecture open-source, allowing anyone to run evolutionary coding loops locally on well-defined optimization targets. 👉 The Infrastructure of Self-Improvement: Self-evolution requires robust underlying plumbing before it can be deployed safely. AReaL2.0 outlines the necessary architecture to allow models to learn continuously from live production traffic without manual intervention. SkillSmith merges the divide between text-based skill documents and weight-space updates, proving that models can synthesize both modalities simultaneously. The underlying lesson across all these advancements is clear. The search algorithm is not the difficult part—the evaluator is. A flawed evaluator will be ruthlessly exploited by an evolutionary search. However, with a rigorous, machine-checkable objective, a system can achieve optimization levels that manual review could never sustain. This represents the ultimate shift toward dynamic, evolving, and highly specialized agentic frameworks running safely in enterprise production environments. 👉 What rigorous automated evaluators are currently being implemented in your organization to ensure complex workflows stay on track? content_raw: The traditional sales funnel is dead. Or at least it should stop pretending that “Closed Won” is the happy ending. For recurring-revenue businesses, treating a signed contract like the finish line is a bit like celebrating a marathon after buying the running shoes. 🏃‍♂️ Jacco van der Kooij's Bowtie Data Model from Revenue Architecture (by Winning by Design) puts the customer journey back into perspective: acquisition is only one half of the equation. The real work starts after the deal is signed: → Mutual Commit → Onboarding → Adoption → Expansion Because in SaaS, subscription and recurring-revenue businesses, winning the logo is great. Keeping it, helping it realize value and growing the relationship is where sustainable growth actually happens. What I find particularly powerful about the Bowtie Model is that it makes the blind spots of the traditional funnel painfully obvious: A pipeline does not tell you whether customers achieve outcomes. Bookings do not tell you whether customers will renew. New logos do not automatically equal healthy growth. And “Customer Success will take it from here” is not a revenue strategy. content_raw: When More BESS Means Less Revenue What if the biggest risk in your BESS financial model isn't battery CAPEX—but the batteries that come after yours? Australia is showing us something important. The NEM's grid-scale BESS fleet has passed 9 GW. At the same time, the battery price spread reportedly fell from approximately A$342/MWh to A$51/MWh in just one year—an 85% decline. Meanwhile, average battery discharge jumped from 162 MW to 476 MW (+194%). That creates a fascinating paradox: More batteries → more competition → narrower price spreads → lower arbitrage opportunity. And this is where the issue moves from the electricity market into the financial model. A BESS project doesn't operate in a vacuum. When more batteries enter the market, they can change the very price signals your model assumes: Market Spread → Capture Rate → Revenue → EBITDA → CFADS → DSCR → Debt Capacity → Equity IRR So the question for a project financial modeller shouldn't simply be: "How much revenue did batteries make historically?" The better question is "How much revenue can this particular battery still capture when the market becomes more competitive?" That distinction matters enormously for: BESS Developers—because historical revenue may not represent future merchant revenue. Investors—because market saturation can materially change the investment case. Lenders—because weaker revenue assumptions flow directly into CFADS, DSCR, and debt capacity. Financial Modellers—because revenue modelling needs to incorporate market evolution, competition, and capture rate. Advisors—because bankability increasingly depends on how robust the revenue assumptions are under downside scenarios. A sophisticated BESS model therefore shouldn't have only a base case. It should ask: What happens if the market gets crowded? What happens to: Price spreads? Dispatch opportunities? Capture rate? Merchant revenue? CFADS? DSCR? Debt sizing? Equity returns? Because the most dangerous assumption in a BESS model may not be the battery cost. It may be assuming tomorrow's electricity market will look like yesterday's. content_raw: Sustainability software. Enterprise architecture. Order management. Completely different worlds. Same Customer Success challenges. That's what stood out to me moderating and hosting discussion rounds at Customer Success Snack Cologne today, alongside Renat, Lara, Laura, Luca and Onur, at the fulfillmenttools / REWE digital office. We covered a lot of ground: 1. AI in post-sales: from automation to agentic workflows, and what that means for how the org is built. 2. Winning customer attention: outreach that still cuts through in 2026. 3. Change management: what to do when a customer resists adopting your product. 4. Churn defence: proactive risk management across large portfolios. 5. Objection handling: buy vs build, and turning pushback into progress. 6. For leaders: redesigning post-sales for the AI era, and making it a revenue engine, not just retention. My biggest takeaways: - AI can automate a lot. It can't replace relationship building, negotiation and renewals. - The exact metric behind your health score matters less than what you do with it. Proactive action and streamlined process beat a perfect definition every time. - Renewals are still a team effort, not a single owner's job. - Automating repetitive work is huge. Making sure the time you win back is actually used well is the harder problem. Thanks to Hanna and Daniel for the support behind the scenes, and to Customer Success Snack, Bianca and Mick for putting another great one together. And to everyone who joined: thank you for the open, honest discussions and for showing up with real problems, not polished answers. Looking forward to the next edition! #CustomerSuccess #CSSnack #fulfillmenttools

content_raw: The greatest threat to future-ready organizations is not a failure to transform—it is the illusion of progress created by becoming more efficient at yesterday’s business model. Historically, the boardroom playbook was clear: protect assets, manage risk, and monitor quarterly performance. Today, that approach is a liability. AI is compressing decision cycles, market volatility is rising, and product lifecycles are shrinking. In this environment, defending a static business model does not necessarily protect capital—it can trap capital inside an increasingly outdated way of creating value. The Critical Choice Boards, investors, and PE operators face a defining dilemma: Do we spend millions optimization-polishing a legacy engine, or do we actively redesign how the enterprise captures value? Superimposing AI or expensive ERPs onto an unchanged operating model does not create a future-ready organization. It may simply accelerate an existing bottleneck. From Efficiency to Value Creation True value innovation requires shifting from legacy outputs to modern value architectures: 1️⃣ Products to Services — Transactional sales → Outcome-based revenue 2️⃣ Silos to Platforms — Isolated data → Interconnected ecosystems 3️⃣ Assets to Access — Heavy ownership → Dynamic asset orchestration 4️⃣ Static Solutions to Intelligent Outcomes — Fixed delivery → Real-time, adaptive value 5️⃣ Rigid Capabilities to Dynamic Liquidity — Fixed infrastructure → Fluid capital and capability allocation Competitive advantage no longer belongs to asset scale alone. It belongs to ecosystem fluidity, decision velocity, and autonomous execution. In my latest article, I explore why business model innovation—not just digital transformation—may become one of the most important capabilities for organizations seeking sustainable value creation and long-term relevance. Because in the next decade, the winners may not be the companies that optimize the fastest. They may be the companies that discover entirely new ways to create value—and have the courage to redesign themselves before someone else does. 💡 Enterprise value isn't static. Having managed multi-market P&Ls across the GCC for more than two decades, I package these insights into a 90-Day Agile Execution Framework built to help executive teams stay resilient, adaptive, and future-ready. content_raw: Insurers don't just price risk anymore. They're becoming AI companies. AXA closed FY2025 with €116 billion in premiums and confirmed explicitly that AI and automation are now driving efficiency gains across the organization with a Solvency II ratio of 224%, one of the strongest in the industry. They're investing from a position of exceptional strength. Allianz posted a record €17.4 billion operating profit in 2025 and has already deployed generative AI tools across operations as part of its 2025–2027 strategic plan. The correlation isn't accidental. Generali hit a record €4.15 billion operating result in its first year of "Lifetime Partner 27: Driving Excellence", a plan built on three explicit foundations: People, AI & Data, and Sustainability. AI is not a side project. It's a pillar of the strategy. Swiss Re delivered a record $4.8 billion net income in 2025 and targets $4.5 billion in 2026, with AI embedded in underwriting and risk modelling. From Zurich, they're quietly redefining how reinsurance risk is priced. And then there's Lemonade, the AI-native challenger. +29% premium growth, 3-second AI claim settlement, and a fully automated model that the incumbents are now trying to replicate from the inside. The key question this industry is now asking and that nobody wants to answer publicly is this: when AI decides to accept or reject a claim, and it gets it wrong, who is legally accountable? That question will define the next phase of insurance regulation. And the firms with the best governance architecture around their AI will win. All data sourced from official annual reports, earnings press releases, and SEC filings. #Insurance #AI #AXA #Allianz #Generali #SwissRe #Strategy #Fintech #Leadership #Insurtech

content_raw: When NVIDIA agreed to acquire Hugging Face for $13 billion, the headlines focused on the price tag. The more important question is, what are they buying? What NVIDIA is really acquiring is reach: 18 million developers and counting. This is the Jevons Paradox in action. As we explored in our recent tokenomics work, lower cost per token doesn’t reduce AI consumption; it expands it. Make open-weight models cheaper and accessible to ten times as many developers, and total demand for AI infrastructure compounds. Our research confirms this is already how enterprise leaders think: 9 out of 10 executives say cheaper tokens will lead them to expand use cases rather than cut spend. A rising tide lifts all boats, and NVIDIA is betting it has the biggest one. For enterprise leaders, the more immediate signal is that the AI ecosystem is consolidating. Organizations anchored to a single model tier or platform are carrying more risk than they may realize. Our research shows organizations running a deliberate mix of open-weight and proprietary models are more than twice as likely to be running AI at full production scale. The difference comes down to how deliberately organizations have built their AI architecture. Three questions are worth asking now: 1. Could your three most critical AI workloads run on a different model or platform within 90 days? 2. Do you have full visibility into what is consuming tokens across your AI estate and what each unit of consumption returns? Four in five dollars of enterprise AI token spend can’t be traced to a quantified financial outcome. This gap is not sustainable as consumption scales. 3. Is your architecture built around your outcomes, or around technology decisions made 18 months ago? The organizations getting this right are not waiting for the ecosystem to stabilize. They are building the discipline now. Learn more in the comments.

Last week, The Economist examined how IBM repositioned itself as an AI leader. What stood out was not a breakthrough product announcement or a dramatic pivot. It was the long arc of disciplined transformation. In a moment where AI narratives swing between euphoria and anxiety, stability is underrated. Markets reward spectacle in the short term. Enterprises reward reliability in the long term. IBM operates in a space that rarely dominates headlines. It sits between hyperscale infrastructure and enterprise complexity. Not competing to build the biggest consumer model. Not chasing the loudest demo. Instead, focusing on orchestration. On integration. On governance. On making AI work inside regulated, mission-critical environments. That is not glamorous work. But it is where durable value is created. And the deeper lesson is about strategic posture. Sustained reinvention does not come from reacting to every wave. It comes from repeatedly asking: Where will we be structurally relevant five to ten years from now? Where do in we have unfair advantages? Which capabilities compound over time? For IBM, that answer has consistently involved enterprise trust, hybrid architectures, and applied AI rather than consumer AI. The AI cycle will continue to correct itself. Some valuations will fall. Some narratives will fade. What remains are companies that align technology with real operational problems at scale. Reinvention is rarely loud. It is architectural. It is cultural. It is cumulative. And when done well, it looks obvious in hindsight. content_raw: The transformation of commercial vehicles is accelerating. But it will not follow the same path everywhere in the world. Demand for freight transport continues to grow. At the same time, fleet operators face decarbonization targets, increasing software complexity, new safety requirements, and a persistent driver shortage. In this environment, one metric remains decisive: total cost of ownership. That is why the future of commercial vehicles is not about a single technology. It is about combining the right technologies to create the greatest customer value. Battery-electric mobility is gaining momentum rapidly, particularly in China. Other regions will continue to rely on hydrogen, renewable fuels, hybrid concepts, and highly efficient combustion engines for years to come. A key challenge for our industry is therefore managing complexity while maintaining flexibility. 🔹 Multiple powertrain options 🔹 Increasing automation 🔹 AI-enabled driver assistance systems 🔹 Software-defined vehicle architectures The decisive factor is integration. Powertrains, software, connectivity, automation, and safety systems must work together as one system to improve efficiency, sustainability, and profitability for fleet operators. This is where Bosch Mobility's strength comes into play: combining hardware, software, and services at industrial scale. The momentum is clear. By the end of 2026, 1 in 3 newly registered battery-electric trucks in Europe is expected to be powered by a Bosch motor and inverter. My takeaway from IAA TRANSPORTATION: achieving climate goals and economic success in freight transport is not an either-or proposition. Technological openness, intelligent software, and integrated systems will shape the next phase of commercial mobility. #IAATransportation #CommercialVehicles #SoftwareDefinedVehicle #BoschMobility

content_raw: As 2026 approaches, the long-term implications of Artificial Intelligence are no longer theoretical. Decisions made today about architecture, governance, and deployment are beginning to lock in trajectories that will shape economies, institutions, and power structures for decades. This is why the Future track at RAISE Summit 2026 matters. The future of AI will not be determined by a single breakthrough, nor by abstract debates about possibility. It will be shaped by cumulative choices: 💡 how intelligence is embedded into systems of work, 💡 how autonomy is balanced with accountability, 💡 how global coordination emerges - or fails to - around governance, safety, and access. Questions once confined to research circles are now entering boardrooms and ministries: ➕ What does progress look like beyond scale? ➕ How should societies prepare for increasingly autonomous systems? ➕ Where do current economic and institutional models begin to strain? ➕ And how do leaders plan when the pace of change outpaces historical precedent? The Future track is designed for those willing to engage these questions without theatrics or false certainty. It convenes researchers, policymakers, investors, and executives to examine long-horizon trajectories - from advanced AI systems and sustainability to geopolitics, labour, and global coordination. In 2026, strategic leadership will belong to those who resist both complacency and alarmism - and who instead develop a clear-eyed view of where intelligence is taking us, and what must be built to meet it. On 8–9 July 2026, under the glass pyramid of the Louvre, RAISE Summit 2026 creates space for this longer view - not as speculation, but as preparation. content_raw: Responsible cloud infrastructure is becoming just as important as fast cloud infrastructure.. Today, while I was at the Amazon Web Services (AWS) office in Bengaluru,this caught my attention, Amazon says its Indian data centres, including the upcoming Thane facility, do not use water for cooling.. Thane will use a closed loop cooling system that continuously recirculates a fixed volume of coolant, with no water evaporation or cooling wastewater discharge.. 📍 Have we ever thought about the environmental side of the cloud infrastructure your applications are running on? We talk a lot about compute, latency, availability, GPUs and cost. But behind every AI workload is physical infrastructure consuming power, land and cooling resources.. The numbers make this conversation more interesting. CEEW estimates India's data centres used around 150 billion litres of water annually in 2025, with demand expected to more than double by 2030. Globally, data centres consume around 560 billion litres of water a year, according to the same research.. At the same time, AI is pushing rack densities and compute requirements higher. So cooling architecture is no longer just a facilities decision. It is becoming part of cloud architecture, site selection, resilience and sustainability strategy.. Amazon says its global data-centre operations used 0.12 litres of water per kWh in 2025, more than 7x more water-efficient than the cited industry average of 0.84 L/kWh. And there is another interesting number from Amazon's Thane plan: the facility's projected 125 KLD water use is not for cooling. Report says 10 KLD is for basic human needs and 115 KLD is treated sewage water for landscaping and irrigation.. content_raw: This is not a credible history of carbon markets. It is a selective timeline that removes many of the people and institutions that actually built them. The story did not begin with a registry in 1996. In 1972, Maurice Strong served as Secretary-General of the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm, the landmark gathering that placed the environment firmly on the international political agenda. Its institutional legacy included the creation of the United Nations Environment Programme, with Strong becoming #UNEP's first Executive Director. Nor can any serious account omit Richard L. Sandor and the Chicago Climate Exchange. Founded by Dr. Sandor and launched in 2003, CCX preceded the EU ETS. It was the world’s first voluntary but legally binding greenhouse-gas cap-and-trade system, covering all six major greenhouse gases with formal rules, independent verification and enforceable reduction commitments. Its affiliated European Climate Exchange later became a major trading platform for the EU ETS. Carlton Bartels also belongs in this history. Through Cantor Fitzgerald and CO2e.com, he helped pioneer the commercial architecture and technology required to turn greenhouse-gas reductions into measurable and tradable assets during the 1990s. Tragically, Bartels was killed on September 11, 2001, while working in Cantor Fitzgerald’s offices in the North Tower of the World Trade Center. His death at only 44 cut short the life of one of carbon trading’s earliest and most consequential innovators. A timeline that jumps from Kyoto to the EU ETS and describes the early voluntary market in passive terms, without mentioning Strong, Bartels, Sandor or CCX, does not explain how carbon markets evolved. It erases the intellectual, institutional and market infrastructure that made later systems possible. Carbon markets did not simply “begin to grow.” People designed them, tested them, financed them and persuaded companies to accept binding commitments when there was no regulatory requirement to do so. If you are going to tell the history, tell the history.
