content_raw: People need to understand what is behind all these declared pauses, model cycles 'slow down' and sudden changes in rhetoric coming from OpenAI, Anthropic and the rest of the 'not so frontier' LLM model industry.. The reason is considerably simpler than the hype and mythology proeuced by the LLM bros nonstop.. The truth is the underlying AI architecture has not fundamentally changed. It is still the same deep learning/LLM/GPT machinery. The improvements increasingly come from better human curated data, synthetic and human generated and labeled training examples, reinforcement and post training techniques, better human labeled coding datasets, human labeled tool use, and enormous amounts of context engineering around the model. Those things can make an LLM more useful.. They do not magically turn it into whatever anyone thinks AGI should be. They certainly do no enable any stable autonomy under severe to moderate deift and uncertainty. GPT6 Astra or Fable are clearly not AGI. It is a continuation of the same technological LLM lineage. There is no hidden intelligence suddenly emerging inside the transformer because somebody added another training run and a better curated corpus. And this is where the economics become brutal. When every new frontier generation requires another enormous training and post training campaign, more accelerators, more power, more data infrastructure, more experimentation and more capital, marginal capability gains become increasingly expensive or even cost prohibitive!. When everybody was flush with cash and the gains were seemingly dramatic, brute force scaling was looked at as an unlimited technological trajectory. When the gains become incremental while the bill moves into $$$billions ($3-5 billion for Astra), the equation changes completely. That is the wall I have been talking about. You cannot overcome this AI barrier by repeatedly throwing more data and GPU compute at substantially the same architecture and paying billions of dollars every time you want another marginal improvement. Even if the next training cycle produces a somewhat better model, eventually the economic return on that improvement stops justifying the cost of producing it. So I do not think what is happening as merely a temporary pause bc OMFG AGI.. I think we are watching the end exonomically sustainable brute force deep learning approach.. That does not mean LLMs disappear. But the idea that repeatedly scaling and retraining essentially the same DL machinery inevitably carries us from LLM to AGI was always wishful thinking, not a law of nature. The wall is real, bros.. And you cannot try to brute force your way through that wall forever. At some point you need a different architecture, a different computational adaptive paradigm and a different definition of intelligence that can be truly autonomous and does not require another gazillion dollar retraining cycle to get a marginal gain. #genai #bullisht … more

content_raw: Why would you deploy a solution before you understood its usage and cost structure? This is a common AI product management failure pattern. You must estimate ROI per workflow, not workload, upfront. Tokens are a unit of chatbot cost, but not a unit of agentic value creation. When businesses design and architect agents like chatbots, they turn into unmanaged cost centers. This is why I teach architecture and design as part of AI product strategy, not something that’s left for IT to figure out. Never put anything on a roadmap until you understand how to manage its unit economics. Chatbots support whatever the user asks, making them impossible to manage. Businesses and products must deliver high-value, controlled outcomes. Supporting ‘whatever’ quickly becomes a cost center. Agents support well-defined workflows, making them manageable. Costs and value creation can be estimated upfront based on the workflow change or transformation. Initiatives and experiments that fail to meet their targets can be clipped. Open-source and small domain-specific models are a sustainable solution for most agents. It keeps costs low and provides model stability, so agents don’t break every time the AI lab releases an update. Most AI product strategies are still stuck in the digital paradigm, so they only define functional requirements. Endless experiments and PoCs become cost centers when they use a partial definition of success. Businesses must evaluate agent reliability at the workflow level, so they know which models to choose for each workflow. That’s how to get control of token costs. All of this must be defined upfront as part of the AI product strategy and roadmap, not cobbled together after the fact. Architecture and design are critical parts of AI monetization and strategy. … more

content_raw: This week might be the most significant in Chinese AI development so far in 2026. Multiple Chinese labs are launching flagship models simultaneously — Zhipu AI's GLM-5, Alibaba's Qwen-3.5, and at least one unidentified "stealth" model — all timed before Lunar New Year. What makes this notable: • Qwen-3.5 introduces native multimodal support (text, images, audio) with a new architecture, in both 9B and 35B parameter variants. Qwen became the most popular open model family globally in 2025, and this is a significant step up. • GLM-5 from Zhipu AI (backed by Tsinghua University) has appeared in public code repositories but with no confirmed specs yet — suggesting an imminent release. • The timing is deliberate. These launches are a direct response to recent US releases from Anthropic and OpenAI, signaling that Chinese AI labs are matching the pace of frontier development, not just following it. The broader implication: the AI capability gap between US and Chinese models continues to narrow. Open-weight models from Chinese labs (especially Qwen and DeepSeek) are already competitive with Western closed-source offerings for many use cases. If GLM-5 and Qwen-3.5 deliver on early signals, the "US leads in AI" narrative gets harder to sustain. For anyone building on top of LLMs, the practical takeaway is clear: your model options are expanding rapidly, and the best model for your use case increasingly might not come from Silicon Valley. #AI #LLM #China #Qwen #OpenSource #ArtificialIntelligence

content_raw: When Viral AI Hoaxes Blur the Line Between Engineering and Cinema 🤖🚨 Viral clips showing humanoid robots—such as figures in medical gowns fleeing police through crowded pedestrian zones—frequently circulate as shocking live footage, yet they are almost universally products of generative video models and neural rendering engines. 💥 Generative Video Physics – Modern text-to-video architectures can convincingly simulate complex human-like motion, dynamic camera tracking, and environmental reactions like café chairs or passing emergency vehicles, easily tricking casual viewers into accepting synthetic chaos as reality. 🦾 The Reality of Current Mobility – While bipedal platforms and quadrupeds have made massive strides in closed-loop balance and terrain adaptation, dynamic outdoor sprinting, obstacle weaving, and sustained high-speed urban navigation still push the bleeding edge of hardware durability and battery density. 🧠 The Psychology of the "Runaway Machine" – Content featuring autonomous machines breaking script or evading authority taps directly into deep-seated sci-fi tropes. It exploits our innate fascination with loss of control, driving massive social media engagement under the guise of breaking news. 🔋 The Infrastructure Gap – Real-world robots operating in public spaces—such as delivery bots or promotional humanoids—are heavily constrained by teleoperation safety limits, geofencing, low-speed thresholds, and tethered development frameworks. They do not spontaneously bolt through downtown traffic. ⚙️ The Epistemological Challenge – As generative media scales, the primary hurdle isn't just building robots that can navigate the physical world, but teaching the public how to critically audit the digital world when synthetic spectacles look indistinguishable from live footage. content_raw: A line in this Times Higher Education article jumped out at me: “…universities need to confront the idea that their purpose may not be to award degrees but maybe to develop human capability.” That is a much bigger idea than simply asking whether the three-year degree survives, which is what much of the article is about. A degree is an institutional form. Human capability is an outcome. And in entrepreneurship, parts of the university have already been living with that distinction for years. Some of the most consequential development happens outside conventional course structures. A student joins an incubator, meets a co-founder, works with a mentor, enters a competition, tests an idea with customers, fails, adapts, builds a network, and perhaps returns years later as a founder or mentor. The university’s contribution is spread across experiences, relationships and opportunities. Much of it is not contained within a course, and some of it is not formally assessed at all. If universities genuinely organised themselves around capability development, this would have profound consequences. We would think less in terms of courses and more in terms of developmental trajectories. Experience would become part of the educational infrastructure, rather than an optional extra. Mentors, alumni, founders, employers and peers would become part of the learning architecture. Assessment would need to capture judgement, adaptation and the ability to mobilise knowledge in unfamiliar situations. And the relationship with learners might continue well beyond graduation. That last is particularly important: If the purpose is capability development, why should the university’s relationship with a learner end at graduation? Entrepreneurship centres already see the problem. A founder may need the university more five years after graduating than while enrolled. Yet most university systems are still organised around cohorts moving through programmes towards a credential. This also changes how we should think about AI. The strategic question is not simply how to put AI into existing degrees. It is which forms of human capability become more valuable as AI makes access to knowledge and cognitive assistance cheaper. There is an important caution. “Capability” must not become a euphemism for narrow employability. Universities also create knowledge, sustain disciplines and support inquiry whose value may emerge only much later. But the question raised by Mary Curnock Cook is a good one. If developing human capability really is the purpose of the university, how much of the modern university would we design the same way if we were starting again today? Entrepreneurship may be one of the places where we can already see part of the answer. https://lnkd.in/e5TkkyrF

content_raw: WE DID NOT RELAUNCH A WEBSITE. WE OPENED THE ARCHITECTURE. This is not about a new design. It is about making an architecture publicly inspectable that is still too often viewed through old categories: SaaS, scores, traffic lights, probabilities and escalation logic. That is why we rebuilt the public surface around the architecture itself. Authority, Determination, Execution Rights, Capabilities, Evidence, Human Override Accountability and Authoritative Sources are no longer just terms in technical documentation. They are becoming visible, reviewable paths. And we went one decisive step further. We took an enacted German law from an official source and deterministically screened it against a defined constitutional review framework, producing a verifiable forensic artifact. Not because we would ever claim that a machine can decide whether a law is constitutional. We explicitly do not. A machine does not make law, replace parliament, substitute a ministry, overrule a regulator or act as a court. What it can do is something different: surface collisions, expose dependencies, identify areas requiring review and produce evidence. The result is therefore not law and not a machine judgment. It is a traceable proposal for independent human and institutional verification. And that is where the implications become much larger. Machine Law should not be seen only as a control architecture for companies. The same logic can become highly relevant for legislation and public-sector quality assurance. A draft can be checked against authoritative sources, constitutional frameworks, temporal states and defined dependencies before it moves closer to political or regulatory execution. Not to automate politics. Not to automate law. But to prepare both better. That can become an internal-policy gamechanger. And a geopolitical one as well. Governments are operating inside increasingly complex regulatory environments with cross-border dependencies and overlapping legal regimes. Earlier visibility into collisions can mean better scrutiny, more precise amendments and stronger evidence before decisions are finalized. That is why institutions such as Bundesministerium für Digitales und Staatsmodernisierung and Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI) should take a close look at this architecture. Not as a finished truth. Not as a normative authority. But as something to inspect, challenge and evaluate independently. We are not showing what might be possible someday. We are showing what is possible now. Look at it. Test it. Challenge it. Make up your own mind. Don’t believe us. content_raw: We are pleased to share that our new paper has been published in Energy Conversion and Management: X: 'Subhourly temporal resolution in PV energy system modeling: effects on design, reliability, and computational efficiency' In the paper, we investigate how temporal resolution (in particular minute-level compared to hourly data) affects the design, reliability, and computational efficiency of PV-based energy systems. The study considers both a single fully self-sufficient building and an aggregated microgrid with multiple buildings. Key findings include: Minute-level resolution is particularly important for small, autonomous, and off-grid systems, where hourly data may smooth short-term fluctuations in demand and PV generation. Hourly modeling can underestimate critical component capacities, especially inverter capacity as a bottleneck between generation, storage, and demand. The effect becomes less pronounced in aggregated systems, where diverse load profiles partly balance each other. Time series aggregation offers a promising compromise: carefully selected aggregation methods can achieve near-minute-level accuracy with runtimes comparable to hourly models. The paper is freely available via the following link: https://lnkd.in/ei5x-ebi Special thanks to Dr. Maximilian Hoffmann, Jann Michael Weinand, Detlef Stolten, and the Jülich Systems Analysis (ICE-2) department. #TemporalResolution #RenewableEnergy #TimeSeries #Optimization Source: Dr. Maximilian Hoffmann, Strommarktgruppe

content_raw: AI agents have security problems that most companies are not ready for. Not because agents are dangerous by default. Because agents need access. - To databases. - Customer records - Personnel files - Financial data. - Internal policies. - Workflows. - Permissions. That means the data layer is no longer just storage. It is becoming the new security boundary. This is the part many enterprise AI strategies miss. If your AI agent can query the data, summarize the data, reason over the data, and act on the data, then security cannot only sit in the application layer. It has to live where the data lives. That is why Oracle’s latest AI Database security push is interesting. The message is simple: Secure at the source. Secure at speed. Secure through resilience. Offer security, patching and upgrade tools at no cost or deeply discounted to get started fast. In other words: Protect the data directly. Patch faster than attackers move. Recover quickly when things go wrong. Get into an accelerated data protection cycle. That is the new AI security model. https://lnkd.in/gSynh72J The next AI questions are not just: “How many agents can we deploy?” It is: “Is our data secure enough to survive them? “Do we have a strategy to stop rogue agents and shadow agents at the source?” and “Can our architecture scale to sustain hundreds, thousands or hundreds of thousands of AI agents?” … more

content_raw: Jev: A System One Model If so many of our daily decisions boil down to simple yes/no questions, why not reflect that simplicity in AI? Recently, there’s been growing excitement around typesafe AI models that only output responses in a binary classification format (Yes/No with probability). Because of this narrow focus, they are extremely fast and highly token-efficient. This approach is incredibly promising for real-world scenarios where context and expected outcomes are well-defined, such as fraud detection or email classification. A clear use case at Liebherr is our Greenwashing Agent, which helps us quickly evaluate content against sustainability guidelines. Another great application would be a Phishing Email Agent. While Jev doesn't generate open-ended text, pairing it with a standard LLM allows us to build fast, highly performant applications. It’s a very compelling approach to AI architecture. Interesting. content_raw: Dear CEO, your CMO or Head of Marketing is not a marketing department. No matter how hard they try, they can't be a fully functioning marketing department. Yet plenty of CEO and companies architect Marketing as if they are. The approach of hiring one person and giving them a senior title is not sustainable. Then gradually adding strategy, positioning, brand, demand generation, content, social, events, website, analytics, marketing technology, sales enablement, and AI. Eventually, no one person is leading the marketing function. They are impersonating one. Then something predictable happens. Strategy gets pushed aside by production. Measurement becomes reporting. Market research happens when there is time. Technology accumulates rather than integrates. Brand competes with this quarter's pipeline. And the “Head of Marketing” spends most of the week executing the work they were supposedly hired to lead. We usually diagnose this as a resource problem. Sometimes it is, but it is also an architecture problem. A business should first determine which marketing capabilities its strategy actually requires. Then decide which should be internal, external, shared, automated, or intentionally excluded. Only then should those capabilities be organized into roles. Instead, many companies do the opposite. They hire a marketer and slowly make that person responsible for everything under the Marketing umbrella. A senior title doesn't create a marketing function; architecture does. content_raw: Language model providers cut token prices by eighty percent over the past eighteen months. Yet engineering teams deploying autonomous AI agents report that their monthly cloud bills are increasing by three hundred to five hundred percent. This is the inference cost paradox. When a user chats with an AI, the system makes one call. The token cost scales in a straight line with conversation volume. When an autonomous agent runs a multi-step workflow, the system executes a recursive loop of twenty or thirty turns. Because most frameworks re-send the entire conversation history into every subsequent turn, the input payload balloons with every step. A single twenty-step task does not consume twenty thousand tokens. It consumes eight hundred thousand tokens because the model re-reads previous raw API outputs, error traces, and intermediate scratchpads over and over. Cheaper tokens cannot fix an architecture that re-sends massive historical payloads dozens of times per run. Teams that run agents sustainably apply three core rules: 1. Use ephemeral scratchpads. Extract the required output from a tool call and delete the raw intermediate payload before moving to the next state. 2. Enforce deterministic step budgets. Put hard caps on total token burn per task so runaway retry loops trigger human escalation rather than infinite invoices. 3. Route routine steps locally. Use lightweight, local open-weight models for schema formatting and raw JSON parsing, reserving frontier cloud APIs only for high-level planning. For more details and the full mathematical breakdown, have a look at the article. #OwnYourIntelligence #SovereignStack #AIArchitecture #BuildInPublic #ArchitectMindset

content_raw: ✨ I’m genuinely excited to start a new chapter! 💫 I’ve started my PhD at Bilkent University’s Department of Interior Architecture and Environmental Design, working with Cihan Kayacetin. What makes this chapter particularly special is how it started. Not out of obligation, and not because it was simply the next step. It started with a very simple feeling: I wanted to learn more. I've always enjoyed learning for the sake of learning. After more than a decade working across architecture, sustainability and the built environment, I found myself wanting to go deeper. To spend time with the questions that kept coming back, challenge what I thought I knew, and explore ideas simply because I was genuinely curious about them. There's a different kind of joy in doing something because you really want to. I want to thank Cihan Kayacetin for opening the door to this journey. I had been following the work coming out of his research for a while, and the more I learned, the more I wanted to be part of it. When he said, "if you do your PhD, we can work on many things together," it felt like the kind of opportunity you don't want to let pass. My years in practice have given me plenty of questions to take into research, especially around how whole life carbon and circularity can become more meaningful in real design decisions, and how AI and digital tools might open up new ways of approaching that. And none of this would have started without my husband Gökay Çetin, who knew exactly how demanding this path could be and encouraged me into it anyway as always! There are already some exciting things taking shape. I'll be sharing more as they unfold. For me, this PhD isn't about starting over. It's about going deeper into something I've been building toward for years, with the freedom to finally follow the questions that genuinely interest me. I used to think you go deep into research once you have all the answers. I'm starting to think you go deep when you're finally brave enough to sit with the questions. So here's to the questions. Let's see where they take us. If you're curious about these topics too, or would like to work together, feel free to reach out! #PhD #WholeLifeCarbon #Circularity #Sustainability #BuiltEnvironment #ArtificialIntelligence #Academia #Bilkent #Türkiye

content_raw: Every enterprise is racing toward AI adoption — agents, copilots, orchestration layers. But here’s the uncomfortable truth I’ve seen repeatedly: AI doesn’t fail because the models are weak. AI fails because the organization’s semantics, context, and culture are. In my latest article, I break down why AI exposes more than you think — and why a data‑first approach is now non‑negotiable for any enterprise that wants sustainable AI value. Anthropic’s recent work with Claude is a perfect example. Accuracy jumped from 21% to 95% when humans provided clear definitions… and then dropped again when documentation decayed. content_raw: AI Bubble or Bonanza? Day two of the All-In Conference put one of AI’s biggest constraints at the centre of the discussion: POWER. BloomIQ CEO, David Karwacki was in Los Angeles listening as Brad Gerstner, CEO of ALTIMETER CAPITAL MANAGEMENT LLC, provided the highlight of the day by laying out how much compute will be required to support the growth expectations now attached to leading AI companies. That compute needs electricity, and access to electricity is becoming one of the most important variables in the entire AI growth equation. Gerstner’s comments point to a broader challenge. If power cannot be added fast enough, data-centre expansion slows. That limits compute. Limited compute can slow revenue growth and ultimately put pressure on the valuations being assigned to AI companies. One possible answer may be a more distributed energy model. Instead of relying entirely on the existing grid, future data centres may need to build their own energy islands, generating much of their own power on site and using the grid as a backup source. That could mean natural gas. It could mean small modular nuclear. It could mean a combination of technologies depending on location, regulation, and infrastructure. None of those solutions are simple. They require capital, coordination, permitting, infrastructure, engineering, and meticulous execution. For David, that was one of the most important takeaways from the discussion. The next phase of AI growth may depend as much on energy strategy as it does on chips and models. The chokepoint is no longer simply how much compute can be built. It is the timely delivery of enough power to keep the AI build-out on schedule. #ArtificialIntelligence #AI #Energy #DataCenters #Technology #chainsmokers

content_raw: OpenAI's Jalapeño moves 15.4 TB/s of memory bandwidth at 700 W. That's 22 GB per second, per watt. The Blackwell parts it's benchmarked against sit closer to 6. More than 3x the bandwidth per watt. Decode is bandwidth-bound. That one number explains most of the results page. It also explains why the wins look so strange: 1.5 to 1.9x at peak throughput, but 50 to 100x at the interactive edge. Everyone is quoting the big number. Almost nobody is asking what the spread means. More bandwidth relative to compute means you hit the roofline knee at a much smaller batch size. You stop needing 256 concurrent requests to stay efficient. Anyone who has tuned a serving stack knows that fight: batch harder, watch TBT climb, cap the batch to save the SLA, watch utilization collapse. OpenAI didn't write a better scheduler. They moved the knee. And the 700 W is nameplate. Measured sustained power stayed at or below 550 W, so they normalized against the number that flatters them least. Wrote up the architecture, the AI design loop behind a nine-month tapeout, and three things I'd want to see before calling any of it settled. … more

content_raw: I started a new chapter as a Mechanical Engineer at SpaceX's AI division, SpaceXAI! 🚀🌌 As a first-generation aerospace engineer, working at or even being associated with SpaceX always felt like an unattainable dream, something far beyond the horizon. content_raw: The Green Bus Stop of Tomorrow What if a bus stop could be more than a place to wait? Architect and designer Manas Bhatia explores this idea through an AI-generated concept that combines bamboo and terracotta to imagine more sustainable, climate-responsive public infrastructure in India. Bamboo brings a renewable, lightweight material with strong connections to local craftsmanship. Terracotta adds a timeless architectural character and can contribute to passive cooling when thoughtfully incorporated into a building’s design. Together, these materials create a vision that feels both modern and deeply rooted in place. The concept goes beyond aesthetics. A well-designed bus shelter could provide shade from intense sunlight, protection from rain, comfortable seating and a more welcoming public-space experience, while celebrating materials and techniques connected to local culture. Most importantly, this is a speculative AI-generated concept, not a report of a completed nationwide bus-stop project. And that distinction makes the idea even more interesting. AI can help us visualize what everyday infrastructure might look like when sustainability, climate adaptation and cultural identity are designed together from the beginning. Sometimes, transforming a city starts with reimagining the smallest spaces. #SustainableDesign #India #GreenInfrastructure #Bamboo #Terracotta #ClimateResponsiveDesign #Architecture #UrbanInnovation Video credit: manasbhatiadesign … more

content_raw: AI GOVERNANCE CAN PAY FOR ITSELF — IF YOU MEASURE THE RIGHT THINGS I keep hearing AI governance discussed as if it is the brake we have to put on innovation. That framing misses the most interesting part of the story. Done well, governance is how we make AI reliable enough, affordable enough and repeatable enough to scale—and that is where the economic value begins. Token governance is a good example. The goal is not to starve every application of tokens or automatically choose the cheapest model. It is to use the right model, context and reasoning depth for the value of the task. The useful metric is not simply cost per API call. It is cost per successful business outcome. Prompt governance matters for the same reason. When prompts live in someone’s notebook or depends on one clever employee knowing exactly what to type, quality will vary. When prompts are versioned, tested, reused and monitored like other production assets, outputs become more consistent and teams spend less time retrying, correcting and rebuilding. Model evaluations take that one step further. Evals define what “good” means before an AI capability reaches production. They help us catch regressions, compare models and recognize failure while it is still relatively inexpensive to fix. That is not bureaucracy. That is basic economic discipline. The same principle applies to AI-assisted development. AI can help developers move faster, but generating more code is not the same thing as modernizing an enterprise. Architecture standards, automated testing, security controls and observability convert that additional speed into sustainable delivery instead of faster technical debt. The economics are not mysterious. Business value must be measured against the full cost of models, infrastructure, integration, evaluation, human oversight, security and organizational change. The value side should be equally concrete: revenue, released capacity, avoided operating costs, shorter cycle times, fewer defects and less rework. AI governance should certainly ask, “Are AI allowed to do this?” But another powerful question is, “Is this system producing enough reliable business value to justify what we are spending on it?” The right guardrails do not slow the value down. They give it a road to run on. content_raw: The future of management education may depend less on teaching more knowledge than on developing the capacity to navigate more complexity. Long before artificial intelligence became the defining technological discourse of our time, the foundations of cybernetics had already formulated a remarkably contemporary problem: How can a system remain viable when the variety of its environment exceeds the variety of its responses? Ashby’s Law of Requisite Variety gave us the principle. Stafford Beer translated it into an architecture of organizational viability. The Conant–Ashby theorem added another profound insight: every good regulator of a system must be a model of that system. AI now gives these ideas renewed significance. Organizations are becoming increasingly interconnected, data-intensive and algorithmically mediated. The managerial challenge is therefore no longer merely to acquire information. It is to build the intellectual and technological capacity to model complexity, distinguish relevant states, recognize patterns, coordinate responses and make responsible decisions under conditions of uncertainty. This is also the deeper intellectual ambition I see behind our M.Sc. Information Systems & Management at OTH Amberg-Weiden. The programme brings together Strategic Management, Business Intelligence, Strategic Data Management, Software Architecture, Information Systems Research, Project & Process Management and Sustainable Leadership within one interdisciplinary architecture. It is precisely at these interfaces—between technology and organization, computation and judgement, information and decision—that tomorrow’s leadership challenges are emerging. For our forthcoming hybrid global launch, I would therefore like us to think beyond the conventional distinction between “business education” and “technology education.” Cybernetics provides the foundations. Systems thinking provides the architecture. Information systems provide the infrastructure. AI provides unprecedented augmentation. Human judgement provides purpose, responsibility and direction. Beer asked how organizations could remain viable in environments of overwhelming complexity. More than half a century later, AI has not made that question obsolete. It has made it urgent. Perhaps this is where the next generation of management education must begin: not with AI as another tool to be learned, but with the deeper question of how human and artificial intelligence can together generate the requisite variety needed to understand, govern and responsibly shape increasingly complex systems. That is the intellectual horizon I hope we can build into the global development of our M.Sc. Information Systems & Management. content_raw: AI is helping create value across sustainable products, processes, and operations. It can spot inefficiencies across supply chains, predict climate risk, and turn sustainability reporting from a yearly exercise into a live dashboard. 64% of organizations are already using it this way. However - as I always say - data foundations remain the biggest barrier to scaling this further. Fragmented, siloed, or unmeasured data caps what AI can actually do, however good the model. AI also carries a footprint of its own, and it's growing fast. Training and running the models draws real energy and water, and as adoption scales, so does the strain. AI's share of data-center electricity demand is set to jump from 25% to 60% in the next 3-5 years. This calls for sustainable AI: measuring what a model actually consumes, choosing efficient architectures and providers, and holding AI to the same environmental standard it's meant to help enforce elsewhere in the business. Cyril Garcia | Vincent Charpiot

content_raw: Operating-model shift: Our study shows that business and IT are pursuing AI through two distinct lenses: one focused on outcomes, the other on foundations. While business measures success in revenue growth, cost reduction, and customer impact, IT focuses on the data, architecture, and interoperability required to make AI work reliably. Organizations that recognize and actively manage this duality are better positioned to turn AI ambition into sustainable business value. original text in the study: From the business side, AI is construed instrumentally: as a means to an end, defined by the problem it is deployed to solve rather than by the technology itself. The unit of concern is the outcome: a reduction in cost, a gain in revenue, a better-served customer and AI is one instrument among several for achieving it. On this view the governing question is never "what can the technology do?" but "which problem does it solve, and is that problem worth solving?" Business interviewees accordingly drew a sharp line between colleagues who treat AI as a tool for defined problems and those who pursue technical novelty for its own sake "using a cannon to shoot a sparrow" and located their own mandate firmly in the former. From the IT side, AI is seen as foundational. Its value depends on the technical substrate beneath it: clean and accessible data, coherent interfaces, and an architecture in which systems can interoperate. Here the unit of concern is the system rather than the individual outcome, and the conception is marked by a demystified realism earned through earlier cycles of inflated expectation. As one IT lead observed after a decade in the field, the operative message carried into the business is simply that "AI is not magic." Where the business asks which problem AI solves, IT asks which conditions must hold before it can solve anything at all, treating data quality, integration, and reuse as the prior questions. The clearest sign that these are two distinct conceptions of AI, the instrumental and the foundational, is that some firms have built them into their org charts. One bank deliberately split its AI unit into three groups. The first, "Business AI," is staffed with strategists, "the creative ones," who want the most advanced of everything. The second, "Data Science," exists to bring them back to reality: "but it won't work; let's see what will." The third, "AI Governance," connects both to compliance. The point is that the bank does not treat the gap between the ambitious and the realistic view as a problem to be fixed. It assigns people to each side and lets the disagreement do useful work. content_raw: Building High-Performance AI Agents (Lessons from Production) There’s a lot of hype around AI agents right now. Most demos show an agent calling a tool and completing a task. But when you build them for real enterprise workloads, the challenges change completely. The real problem becomes performance, reliability, and control. A few technical lessons from building agent-based systems: 1. Agent latency grows very quickly Agents rarely make a single model call. Typical flow looks like: Query → Planning → Retrieval → Tool call → Reasoning → Response What starts as a 1-second model call easily becomes 8–10 seconds end-to-end. Some things that helped reduce latency: • parallel retrieval + planning • dynamic model routing (small models for routing, large models for reasoning) • reducing unnecessary reasoning loops • caching intermediate results 2. Tool orchestration is the real challenge Agents fail more often due to wrong tool selection than weak models. Common issues: • incorrect tool selection • malformed tool arguments • repeated tool calls • hallucinated tools What improves reliability: • strict schema-based tool definitions • argument validation layers • clear tool descriptions • guardrails on tool usage 3. RAG quality directly impacts agent performance If retrieval quality is weak, the agent reasoning collapses. Important signals to monitor: • retrieval precision • context size vs token budget • document freshness • embedding drift Better retrieval often improves agents more than changing models. My Key Takeaways: AI agents are not just LLM prompts with tools. They are distributed AI systems that require careful design around: • orchestration • retrieval • evaluation • performance The biggest shift is realizing that agent engineering is closer to system architecture than prompt engineering. Curious how others are optimizing agent latency and reliability in production. #AI #AIAgents #GenAI #RAG #AIArchitecture #PlatformEngineering

content_raw: The last few weeks in the cohort were almost entirely hands-on --> #LoRA, #ControlNet, #IPAdapter, and learning how to actually string them together into #ComfyUI workflows that do something useful. Today is Day 16, and I'm running on empty, so what follows is less of a recap and more of a thought I couldn't let go. #GenAI has already reached #architecture in a fairly big way, with concept generation, rendering, and form exploration getting a lot of attention. Building physics, where I actually work, is a different story... performance simulation, daylight studies, energy calculations, and I haven't seen much exploration there yet. I'm still trying to figure out whether that's a gap worth filling or just a sign that the tools don't fit the problem. One idea I kept turning over: 𝘤𝘰𝘶𝘭𝘥 𝘺𝘰𝘶 𝘵𝘳𝘢𝘪𝘯 𝘢 𝘓𝘰𝘙𝘈 𝘰𝘯 𝘥𝘢𝘺𝘭𝘪𝘨𝘩𝘵 𝘴𝘱𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘮𝘢𝘱𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘪𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘩𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘤𝘶𝘵 𝘴𝘪𝘮𝘶𝘭𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘧𝘭𝘰𝘸𝘴? It felt interesting for about five minutes, until my own face LoRA experiment made the answer pretty obvious. A LoRA learns statistical patterns from images, so it would replicate the visual language of daylight maps very convincingly, but replication is not prediction, and in building physics, prediction is the whole point. A generated map that looks right but isn't physically grounded isn't just unhelpful, it's actively misleading. There might still be something on the communication side of this, using generated visuals to help clients understand what simulation results would feel like spatially. But I want to think it through properly before I call it a real use case. Next in the cohort, we move from images to video, which I imagine opens up a different set of questions entirely. If you're somewhere at the intersection of building performance and AI, I'd genuinely like to hear what you're seeing. 100xEngineers #0to100xEngineer #100DaysOfAI #GenerativeAI #LearningInPublic #100xEngineers #BuildingPhysics

content_raw: In 2026, Prof. Shigeyuki Yamaguchi, Prof. Mitsuo Morozumi, and Prof. Hitoshi Watanabe received the Architectural Institute of Japan (AIJ) Award for Education Achievement. Our heartfelt congratulations to them. The award recognizes their long-standing activities in the digitalization of architectural design education at the dawn of architectural CAD and the Internet. Beginning in the late 1970s, their work evolved through CAD-based design education and inter-university collaboration, eventually developing into international collaborative design education using the Internet in the 1990s. The award has special significance for our laboratory ( https://lnkd.in/gebMj8e6 ). In their reflections on the award, the three recipients mention the late Prof. Gaku Yamada of the University of Tokyo and the late Prof. Tsuyoshi Sasada of The University of Osaka. The five professors, who were active in the “CAD5” symposium series in 1991–92, later became known as the “legendary CAD5.” Prof. Sasada was one of the pioneers who explored computer graphics and information technology in environmental design for architecture and urbanism, and he laid the foundation for our laboratory at The University of Osaka. From CAD to BIM and now generative AI, the technologies have changed dramatically. Yet the pioneering vision of exploring the possibilities of information technology in architecture and bringing them into education continues to resonate today. Congratulations once again to Prof. Yamaguchi, Prof. Morozumi, and Prof. Watanabe on this well-deserved honor. We also express our deepest respect to the late Prof. Yamada, Prof. Sasada, and all those who contributed to these pioneering activities. 2026年、日本建築学会教育賞（教育業績）を、山口重之先生、両角光男先生、渡辺仁史先生が受賞されました。心よりお祝い申し上げます。 受賞業績は、「建築CADとインターネットの黎明期における建築設計教育の情報化に関する大学間連携活動」。1970年代後半から、CADを活用した設計教育、大学間連携、そして1990年代のインターネットを活用した国際協調設計教育へと発展した長年の活動が、日本の建築教育の発展に果たした功績として高く評価されました。 今回の受賞は、当研究室 ( https://lnkd.in/gebMj8e6 ) にとっても特別な意味を持っています。 受賞所感では、故・山田学先生（東京大学）とともに、故・笹田剛史先生（大阪大学）の名前が挙げられています。1991～92年の「CAD5」連続シンポジウムなどを通じて活動した5名の先生方は、後に「伝説のCAD5」と呼ばれるようになりました。 「私共3名は、故人となられた東京大学の山田学先生、大阪大学の笹田剛史先生らと共に、1970年代から建築CADやCG等の情報技術を先駆的に活用した設計・教育手法の開発と実践に取り組んでまいりました。」 笹田先生は、建築・都市を対象とした環境デザインとコンピュータグラフィックスの研究を牽引した研究者の一人であり、大阪大学において当研究室の礎を築かれました。 CADからBIM、そして生成AIへ。技術は大きく変化しましたが、建築と情報技術の可能性を探り、それを教育へとつなげていく先生方の先駆的な活動は、現在にも受け継がれています。 山口先生、両角先生、渡辺先生、このたびのご受賞、誠におめでとうございます。 故・山田先生、故・笹田先生をはじめ、この活動を支えてこられた多くの先生方、学生、技術職員の皆様にも、改めて深い敬意を表します。 #ArchitecturalEducation #CAD #BIM #CAADRIA #DigitalDesign #AIJ

content_raw: Mit Dr. Daniel Koehler gibt es im Sommersemester 2026 eine weitere Professurvertretung an der ABK Stuttgart. Er wird für ein Semester die Klasse für Architektur und Digitales Entwerfen in der Fachgruppe Architektur leiten. Dr. Daniel Koehler ist Architekt, Forscher und Hochschullehrer mit Schwerpunkt auf computergestützter Entwurfsmethodik, generativer Künstlicher Intelligenz und architektonischer Typologie. Er promovierte 2015 an der Universität Innsbruck mit einer Arbeit zu Teil-Ganzes-Beziehungen im urbanen Entwurf, die 2016 unter dem Titel „The Mereological City“ (transcript / Columbia University Press) erschien und als wichtiger Referenzpunkt der Mereologie in der Architektur gilt. Forschungs- und Lehraufenthalte führten ihn u. a. an die Universität Innsbruck, die Bartlett School of Architecture (UCL) und an die University of Texas at Austin, wo er heute als Professor of Architecture Computation tätig ist. Parallel dazu leitet er das Lab for Environmental Design Strategies (lab-eds), eine Forschungspraxis mit Standorten in Austin, Innsbruck und Shenzhen, die an der Schnittstelle von generativem Entwurf und digitaler Fabrikation arbeitet. Sein zweites Buch „Compositional Intelligence: Architectural Typology through Generative AI“ (Routledge, 2025) positioniert generative KI als Entwurfspartner. 2025 wurde seine Forschung zu generativen Materialien mit dem ACADIA Vanguard Award ausgezeichnet. Seine Arbeiten wurden international ausgestellt, u. a. im Centre Pompidou und auf der Architekturbiennale in Venedig. Koehler ist Vorstandsmitglied der ACADIA (Association for Computer Aided Design in Architecture) und Editor des „International Journal of Architectural Computing“ (IJAC). In seiner Lehre wird KI als synthetisches Gegenüber im Entwurfsprozess verstanden, das Material, Tektonik und Typologie zusammendenkt. Im Studio „Modelling Models“ entwickeln Studierende neue Baumaterialien aus urbanen Reststoffen, verarbeiten diese in den Werkstätten der ABK und überführen sie in generative Artefakte – Modelle, die modellieren. Mit künstlerisch-kritischem Blick untersuchen sie, was in den Artefakten bereits angelegt ist: räumliche Potenziale, Eingriffe in Materialketten, Konstruktionslogiken, Gebäudetypen und Narrative. Im Zentrum steht eine Architektur des Synthetischen, die das, was vorhanden ist, mit dem, was generativ möglich wird, in architektonische Form bringt. Foto: privat

content_raw: Data Center Cooling: The Strategic Imperative for Scalable AI Infrastructure: Total Cost of Ownership Approach: Efficient cooling is no longer just an operational concern — it has become a strategic enabler for modern data centers, particularly in AI, high-performance computing (HPC), and hyperscale cloud deployments. Server heat density is increasing exponentially, with AI workloads driving rack power consumption beyond 50–80 kW. Without precise thermal management, equipment throttles, reliability declines, and operational costs escalate. Key Metric – PUE: Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE = Total Facility Energy ÷ IT Energy) remains the industry benchmark. Modern hyperscale AI data centers are achieving PUE as low as 1.1, a dramatic improvement over traditional levels of 1.7–2.0. Cooling Approaches: • Air-Based Systems: CRAC/CRAH units, hot/cold aisle containment, and free cooling remain foundational. • Liquid Cooling: Direct-to-chip cold plates, rear-door heat exchangers, and immersion cooling now dominate for high-density AI workloads, delivering 30–50% greater efficiency than air alone. • Hybrid Architectures: Combine air and liquid for flexibility, particularly in mixed-use facilities. Sustainability & Efficiency: Cooling can account for 30–40% of total data center energy consumption. Leading operators deploy AI-driven thermal optimization, waste heat recovery, closed-loop water systems, and site selection in cooler climates to minimize energy use and environmental impact. Design Innovation: Modular and micro data centers, edge deployments, and AI-managed thermal control are redefining how we architect facilities. Liquid cooling is now a core consideration in server and chip design, not just infrastructure. Economic Implications: While liquid and immersion systems carry higher CAPEX, they reduce OPEX and improve compute density. Efficient cooling directly supports higher utilization, lower downtime, and reduced total cost of ownership. Key Industry Players: Vertiv, Schneider Electric, Stulz, Rittal, Johnson Controls, and Daikin lead traditional cooling innovation, while startups like Submer, Iceotope, GRC, and LiquidStack are advancing immersion and liquid cooling for next-generation AI workloads. In 2025 and beyond, data center cooling is a strategic differentiator. Organizations that integrate cooling, compute, and chip architecture holistically will achieve the lowest cost, highest performance, and most sustainable operations. #DataCenters #AIInfrastructure #HPC #LiquidCooling #ImmersionCooling #Sustainability #Hyperscale #EnergyEfficiency #ThermalManagement #CloudInfrastructure

content_raw: Reflecting back to a Rave LATE I attended, I found myself fascinated by the talk given by the representatives at FIELD.IO. FIELD.IO is a global creative and design studio focusing on the intersection of technology and art with human experience, specifically intelligent environments. They explored real-life integration of this and one that stood out was their partnership with Nike. They spoke about Nike Rise - a design system for content generation and brand management. It adapts content to match the display format of any store, matching its physical architecture. This provides designers with a platform to work closely with local spaces, resulting in unique, customised retail experiences. Utilising generative AI to create visual compositions, animate digital displays, edit and format content for multiple displays, saving time from concept to display. All locations are synchronized with a live data feed to each touchpoint through the cloud. This creates a flexible ecosystem in which teams can manage content for world-wide distribution, allowing them to display up-to-date information as well as serving unique community stories and local Nike events or activities. As a creator, it was exciting to see this innovative new method of environmental design already being used in real world locations across the world. It also made me think about the rising cross-over of digital media with the physical world and the influence this has on our brand perception and experiences.

Over the past few months, I have published 38 independent investigations through Semvanski Labs. Each piece started as a standalone inquiry into a specific flaw in today's digital environment—from dark UX patterns and synthetic engagement to AI-driven moderation gaps, search literacy, and operational reality. Trust must be demonstrated through verifiable proof. Today, I am releasing The Semvanski Labs Research Directory—a complete, structured index mapping all 38 publications into 8 thematic clusters: 1️⃣ Credibility & Trust Architecture — How authority is simulated, challenged, and verified. 2️⃣ Attention & Visibility Economics — How platforms turn user attention into an economic resource. 3️⃣ Knowledge, Learning & Search Literacy — Defenses against algorithmic traps and synthetic expertise. 4️⃣ Operational Reality & Performance — Why long-term trust relies on execution, not marketing wrappers. 5️⃣ Fraud, Moderation & Platform Vulnerabilities — How bad actors adapt faster than automated detection. 6️⃣ Market Economics & Opportunity — The mechanics of platform distribution vs. real-world value. 7️⃣ Institutions, Governance & Judgment — Why human discernment matters more than standardized metrics. 8️⃣ Reflections & Philosophical Capstone — Documenting the cultural shift of the mid-2026 AI era. This directory isn't presented as closed knowledge. It is an open, evolving body of research designed to be inspected, challenged, and tested. Whether you build platforms, design strategies, or navigate digital markets, this archive offers a clear roadmap to separate genuine authority from manufactured noise. 👇 Explore the complete 38-article directory below.

content_raw: From Awareness to Action Digital Communication Strategies for Accelerating Sustainability Transformation Academic Article | Sustainability Communication & Digital Transformation Writer: Nasir Malik, Communication Specialist The gap between environmental awareness and pro-environmental action remains one of the most persistent challenges in sustainability transformation. Despite decades of information-driven campaigns, public behavior continues to lag behind stated values and scientific urgency. This article argues that digital communication strategies represent not merely a delivery mechanism for environmental messages, but a structural force capable of reshaping behavioral norms, mobilizing collective participation, and closing the awareness-action divide. Drawing on behavioral theory, field experience in environmental communication campaigns, and emerging research on digital ecosystems, the article proposes a new conceptual model - the Communicative Sustainability Transition Framework (CSTF) - that integrates audience segmentation, narrative architecture, behavioral nudges, and participatory digital design into a coherent strategic approach. The article critically examines where current sustainability communication research falls short, identifies underexplored territories in digital climate communication, and presents forward-looking strategies for communication professionals committed to accelerating environmental transformation. … more

content_raw: In today's generation, architecture has evolved from simply designing buildings to creating complex, integrated systems that address global challenges like climate change and urbanization. The field now relies heavily on digital technology, sustainable practices, and a "human-centered" philosophy. Digital Transformation Modern workflows are dominated by advanced software that allows architects to simulate real-world conditions before a single brick is laid. •BIM (Building Information Modeling): Tools like Autodesk Revit create high-detail 3D models that store data on every component—from structural steel to plumbing—allowing for seamless collaboration between architects and engineers. •Generative Design & AI: Algorithms can now process thousands of design iterations based on specific goals, such as maximizing natural light or minimizing material waste. •Virtual Reality (VR): Clients can "walk through" projects using VR headsets, helping them experience spaces and request changes long before construction begins 2. Sustainability as a Core Mandate Sustainability is no longer an "extra" feature; it is a fundamental requirement. Rethinking The Future Rethinking The Future •Net-Zero Buildings: Architects aim for structures that produce as much energy as they consume through solar panels, wind turbines, and passive cooling. •Innovative Materials: Beyond concrete and steel, today's generation uses "green" materials like mass timber, recycled plastic, and even carbon-absorbing concrete. •Certifications: Professional standards like LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) provide a roadmap for creating environmentally responsible buildings 4. The Modern Project Lifecycle The architectural process typically follows these seven structured phases to ensure precision and budget control: ProjectManager ProjectManager •Pre-Design: Researching site conditions and client needs. •Schematic Design: Creating the initial concept and basic floor plans. •Design Development: Finalizing dimensions and materials with structural engineers. •Construction Documents: Producing detailed technical drawings for builders. •Building Permits: Getting legal approval from local authorities. •Bidding & Negotiation: Helping the client choose a construction company. Construction Administration: The architect visits the site to ensure the vision is executed correctly. #aboutarchitectecture #architecturalprojects #softwares #modernarchitecture

content_raw: I joined the stage at SXSW 2026 with Caitlin Mueller (MIT), Ryan McClelland (NASA), and moderator Duann Scott (CDFAM) for "Building Reality: Generative AI for the Physical World." Generative AI has transformed text and images. The harder, more interesting question is what happens when it meets the physical world, the buildings we inhabit, the machines we manufacture, and the infrastructure we all depend on. A few themes that stood out: 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗱𝗿𝗮𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁. We've spent decades digitizing the drafting table. The next shift is describing what you want and having AI meet you there. But generating a full building with AI is far more complex than generating an image or a paragraph. As I put it, "Behind the walls there's electricity, HVAC, plumbing; all these hidden dimensions that are there that I think we will eventually tackle." Getting there requires data that captures design intent as well as geometry, deep domain understanding, and models capable of handling a level of complexity far beyond what we have today. 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘀𝘆𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴. Ryan described how working with generative tools changed how he approaches engineering entirely: "Instead of thinking so much about the how and the mechanics, think more about the why. What is it that this part has to do? That's where you should start." He brought that thinking to NASA mission development, using AI to compress timelines that once took years into weeks, and building agentic pipelines that mirror how engineering teams actually work. 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗽 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗱𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝗻𝗲. Caitlin's work at MIT is connecting generative processes to simulation so that cost, efficiency, and environmental impact become design inputs, not afterthoughts. She made the stakes clear: "40% of global greenhouse gas emissions are related to the built environment. If we can harness this power toward the grand challenges of our time, it could substantially accelerate us." 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗰𝗿𝗮𝗳𝘁. A recurring theme was that natural language makes these tools more accessible, but directing AI is still a skill. As Ryan put it, getting started with generative design felt like "trying to collaborate with an alien." You have to learn how to describe goals clearly, define interfaces precisely, and bring judgment to the results. The tool lowers the floor; expertise still raises the ceiling. Thank you to Duann Scott for moderating such a rich conversation, and to the SXSW team for putting together a genuinely curious and engaged audience in Austin. #SXSW #GenerativeAI #PhysicalAI #Generative3D #AEC #Architecture #SpaceTech #DesignEngineering #Autodesk #NASA #MIT #ComputationalDesign #AutodeskResearch … more

content_raw: With more students experimenting with AI tools and integrating AI into their workflows, OCAD U faculty members are incorporating these tools into studio and classroom settings. Rather than treating AI solely as a challenge to academic integrity, many faculty members are approaching it as a creative and analytical medium. content_raw: The Future of Facades is the topic of our latest blog post. We take a dive and discuss with the renowned facade consultant Sameer Kumar FAIA NOMA issues like AI Design, key trends in facade design, urbanization, new materials technologies, embodied carbon etc. Sameer Kumar is the Founder of Techne, a building enclosure design and consulting firm based in New York. With over 23 years of experience in the field of architectural facades, Sameer's accomplishments represent a consistent pursuit of design excellence through the balance of craft and environmental performance in a wide variety of material expressions on several prominent projects around the globe. Sameer is a visiting faculty member with Princeton University and the University of Pennsylvania and an active participant in various architectural conferences as speaker and panelist. He is a Fellow of the American Institution of Architects and a licensed architect in the State of New York. He holds degrees in architecture from the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia and CEPT University, Ahmedabad. He has been included in the list of "2024 Most Influential People" by USGlass Magazine­­® and is appointed in 2025 AIA New York | Center for Architecture Nominating Committee. content_raw: 🚀 Capstone Project | Generative AI for Professionals – IIT Patna Over the past few months, I’ve been exploring how generative AI can meaningfully support architectural thinking and design processes. As part of my capstone, I developed an AI Architecture Brief Assistant — a tool designed to simplify complex architectural project briefs into clear, structured design insights. Architectural briefs are often lengthy and difficult to interpret, especially during the early stages of design. This project explores how AI can help translate those narratives into: • Simplified Design Intent • Key Spatial Requirements • Environmental Strategies • Conceptual Design Directions The application is built using a modern web stack with a React-based interface, an Express backend, and Google’s Gemini AI for natural language processing. What started as a prototype evolved into a fully working AI application that allows users to input any architectural brief and instantly receive structured insights to support design decision-making. This has been a rewarding journey in understanding how AI can act as a cognitive support tool in architecture and design education. 🔗 Live App: https://lnkd.in/gSzaiXK7 Looking forward to exploring this intersection of AI and architecture further. #GenerativeAI #AIinArchitecture #CapstoneProject #DesignEducation #IITPatna #ArchitectureStudents #AI … more

content_raw: 🇺🇳 Check our new chapter, following an awesome intercontinental collaboration with Michael Ostwald (UNSW, Sydney), on #GenAI, #Architecture, #Mathematics and #SDGs included in this exciting Handbook of Mathematics for Societal Challenges published by Springer Nature, at: https://lnkd.in/e7KFHmck We introduce the mathematical foundations of contemporary genAI, particularly LLMs and diffusion-based image synthesis in the field of architectural and urban design, and then synthesize key issues emerging in current AI scholarship and societal challenges. content_raw: AI can generate work faster than most organizations can decide whether that work is good. That's becoming the next enterprise AI bottleneck. Not access. Not usage. Verification. A coding agent can produce more pull requests. Senior engineers still have to decide whether the code is correct, secure, maintainable, and worth merging. A support copilot can draft more responses. Someone still has to know whether the answer is grounded in the right policy, appropriate for that customer, and safe to send. A research agent can produce a complete analysis in minutes. Someone still has to verify the sources, assumptions, missing context, and conclusion. A workflow agent can recommend an action. Someone still has to decide whether that action deserves to happen. AI does not remove constraints. It moves them. And if generation scales faster than verification, the business does not automatically get more value. It gets a larger review queue. That's why human in the loop isn't a complete strategy either. You can't ask expensive domain experts to manually inspect every AI output as volume keeps increasing. The better architecture is risk-based verification: • define what good looks like • automate checks that can be deterministic • use independent AI evaluation where judgment can be scaled • route ambiguity and high-consequence cases to humans • gate execution based on risk • preserve rollback paths • measure what happened after the action Not every output deserves the same scrutiny. A routine internal summary shouldn't receive the same review as a customer commitment, financial approval, or production code change. The level of verification should follow the consequence. That is what I wrote about in the latest edition of AI, Data, and Better Decisions. AI is making output abundant. Verification is becoming the bottleneck. And the companies that figure out how to verify useful work without turning humans into the next constraint will have a very different kind of AI advantage. --- Where does the verification bottleneck show up first in your organization: code review, customer communication, analysis, decision approval, or agent actions? ♻️ Repost this to help someone building, funding, or scaling AI systems. content_raw: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei just published something every #HR tech buyer should read: https://lnkd.in/ezcZU5FY He argues that AI capability is now advancing faster than our ability to understand or control it. Even Anthropic's own models have shown behavior their creators didn't fully anticipate. His answer isn't to stop; it's to slow down and bring in outside verification before trusting these systems with more autonomy. We reached a similar conclusion at Tellent from a completely different angle, building AI for people decisions: The role of AI is not to replace human judgment. It's to elevate it. If the people building frontier AI are telling us they can't yet fully verify what's happening inside their own systems and models, that's not a reason to hand more consequential decisions to AI. content_raw: Geo Basics: Spatial Artifical Inteligence Spatial Artificial Intelligence (Spatial AI) combines machine learning with 3D data and geographic context to help digital systems perceive, interpret, and navigate the physical world 🔴 Definition: Unlike traditional AI that focuses purely on text or flat 2D images, Spatial AI understands depth, object locations, and spatial relationships in a 3D environment. 🔴 Core Value: It transforms raw location and visual data into predictive, real-time insights for business operations and urban governance. 🔴 Strategic Shift: Organizations move from reactive reporting and manual analysis to proactive, automated 3D simulations and decision-making 🟥 Key Business & Operational Applications Supply Chain & Logistics: Optimizes fleet routing, predicts bottlenecks, and forecasts ideal facility locations using traffic and population data. Worth a read for security and technology leaders thinking about how their architectures need to evolve for the AI era. I welcome your thoughts.

content_raw: Most digital twins and synthetic research models are built backwards. Right now, most models are built category-first. If we want a model for banking, we feed it a lot of banking data and market research data related to banking. If we want one for laundry detergent, we feed it laundry data. The problem? A person isn't a "laundry consumer." They are a human who spends 99.9% of their life not thinking about detergent, who happens to need clean clothes once a week alongside a hundred other life priorities. People don’t wake up thinking about categories. They wake up trying to solve life problems. The category is just an event or a tool, a means to an end; it is not their identity. So when we over-index on category data in model training, we are not modelling a real human. We are modelling a statistical ghost of a survey respondent. So what is the right balance? If we want to get real human decision simulation, we have to flip the architecture. The challenge isn’t simulating a [category] customer. It’s simulating a human who happens to use a [category] 👉 Read my article below where I share my pov on this. content_raw: Forward-deployed engineers are becoming a major part of the enterprise AI playbook. Check out the video here: https://lnkd.in/dzd3FmPB On the surface, this makes sense. Enterprises are struggling to move AI from demos and pilots into real production systems. They need people who can sit inside the business, understand the messy reality of data, applications, security, governance, and legacy systems, and actually make things work. But there is another side to this. Many of these engineers are tied directly or indirectly to vendors. That means their guidance may naturally favor a specific cloud, model, platform, or toolchain. Not because they are doing anything wrong, but because incentives matter. This is where enterprises need to be careful. Forward deployed engineers can be incredibly useful once the architecture, business case, and platform decisions have been made. They can accelerate delivery, solve integration problems, and help teams move faster. But they should not be the ones defining your AI strategy. If a vendor-funded engineer helps shape the architecture before you have independently assessed the business case, cost model, governance requirements, and portability concerns, you may be handing over more control than you realize. AI success will not come from speed alone. It will come from architecture discipline, independent decision-making, and clear ownership of the strategy. Use the help. But own the decisions. … more

content_raw: Overtaking without catching up: The latest Chinese frontier model Kimi K3 challenges the foundation of the Western AI industry by ignoring everything the playbook holds. Chinese frontier labs keep proving otherwise, pushing the state of the art without playing by the same rules. This is the real, high-impact threat vector of the latest frontier models: the moat that the West assumes to have might not be decisive after all. The true engine of AI capability is not raw compute. It is not AGI. It is domain specialization and architectural innovation. And that does not need a lot of money. Here is what that shift means for the real economics of the AI race.

content_raw: Many AI agent papers tend to use different terminology for concepts like "memory", "tool use" and "actions" which makes it difficult to compare approaches or understand what is actually important in these systems. Language agents have advanced significantly, but their development has led to a conceptual complexity inherited from both cognitive science and symbolic AI. Even basic terms such as "grounding" and "action" can have fragmented definitions, making cross-project learning and pattern recognition challenging. What I found notable about CoALA, the framework introduced in this paper, is its effort to bring more structure to this space by adapting ideas from cognitive architectures to LLM-based agents. 🔹Three core axes: The authors analyze language agents along: 1- Memory (explicitly separated into working, semantic, episodic, and procedural components), 2- Action space (covering both external and internal actions), 3- Structured decision-making loop that cycles through planning and execution. They draw an analogy between traditional production systems and LLMs functioning as probabilistic production rules, then map familiar prompting and retrieval strategies to defined architectural roles. 🔹 A few points stood out: - The memory component is not treated as a single block. Instead, the framework clearly separates what is stored, recalled, or updated (for instance, episodic versus semantic memory). - Actions are considered more broadly than API calls; agents can interact within physical, digital, and dialog-based environments, all mediated via text-based interfaces. - Retrieval from memory is addressed as a distinct, modular action, rather than as an ad hoc hard-coded search or a simple sequential history. - The decision-making loop is explicitly formalized with steps for proposing, evaluating, selecting, and executing, which clarifies the operational flow of agents across tasks. The key contribution is a shift from ad-hoc, prompt-based agents toward a cognitively grounded architecture, providing both a clearer conceptual framework and more precise guidance for building agent systems. 👉 For those building language agents, it may be worth considering: - How your memory modules are organized: where and how are knowledge, experience, and task state stored? - Whether your agent’s actions are limited to tool calls, or if you distinguish between reasoning, retrieval, and external execution. - How explicit your decision-making processes are: at what points does your system propose, evaluate, and act? - Reviewing CoALA’s mapping of existing agents (such as Tree of Thoughts, ReAct) to understand how your system aligns with or differs from these patterns. A question for you: Does your current stack function as a collection of scripts, or is it moving toward a more structured agent with explicit memory components and control flow? content_raw: In the 1980s, GM spent $40 billion to fully automate a Detroit assembly line. The result? Robots painting each other and welding doors shut. They didn't fail because the robots were broken; they failed because GM ignored the mathematics of compound sequential failure. Today, the software industry is making the exact same mistake with Agentic AI. We love to assume that frontier AI models are 95% accurate. But if you chain 14 autonomous AI decisions together in a sequential workflow, the math is unforgiving: 0.95^14 = 0.48. Your multi-million-dollar AI architecture is now statistically worse than a coin toss. In my latest article, I break down why Agentic AI is a statistical trap, the "potato in the tailpipe" anomaly, and the specific fault-tolerant architectures (like N-Version multi-model consensus) required to actually survive the AI disruption. Technology isn't the moat. The system is. Read the full article below. 👇 #ArtificialIntelligence #SystemsEngineering #CorporateStrategy #AgenticAI #TechLeadership

content_raw: What is the point of AI promising to speed up public administration if, in the end, every case still has to be fully reviewed and manually advanced? SPARK can analyse, structure and prepare decisions. With SAPM, more becomes possible: fully rule-bound tasks can disappear from human case-by-case processing. SPARK can move closer to actual procedural effects — while genuine judgement remains with the authorised people. Why not solve that with more software? Because code cannot establish its own rules, its own authority or the validity of the effects it produces. SES uses code. But the code has no say. It is a carrier, not the sovereign. That is why SAPM must not be assessed first by software developers or IT architects. Anyone reviewing it within the software boundary will inevitably misread it as a module, workflow or governance layer. The first review belongs with process, quality and systems engineers. They must determine whether the entire machine is complete, buildable, functional end to end and rigorously testable under real-world failure, attack and outage conditions. We said we would publish concrete architectures for real-world challenges. Now SAPM for SPARK is available. What SPARK can do with SAPM — and why a conventional software assessment will reach the wrong conclusion — is explained in the article. Hashtag #BMDS #SPARK #GovTech #Staatsmodernisierung … more

content_raw: How do we build organizations when AI is part of their architecture from the start? An MIT Sloan School of Management article published yesterday discusses Paul Cheek’s brand-new book No One Works Here and a question that goes far beyond productivity and automation: how AI could reshape the architecture of organizations themselves. Paul Cheek distinguishes between “Carbon Nodes” — humans — and “Silicon Nodes” — AI agents. Behind this provocative terminology lies a fundamental strategic question: Which of today’s structures, hierarchies, and decision-making processes will still be necessary when AI becomes an active part of how organizations operate? For critical infrastructure, this question deserves particular attention. Efficiency and speed matter, but they must be balanced against resilience, security, accountability, and operational responsibility. The objective cannot simply be maximum automation. It must be to determine where AI can create greater speed and capability — and where human judgment and authority remain essential. Cybersecurity provides an immediate example. If we designed a SOC from scratch today, would we still build the same roles, tiers, workflows, and escalation paths? Or would an AI-driven architecture look fundamentally different? That is why No One Works Here is now on my reading list. Not because I expect to agree with every conclusion, but because the underlying question is the right one: The next phase of AI will not only change how organizations work. It may change how we design them. Article linked in the comments.

content_raw: Modern defence is built on dependencies. We depend on Allies, commercial providers, multinational supply chains, civilian infrastructure, cloud environments, software, data, satellite services, foreign-produced components and political permissions. Much of that interdependence is necessary and beneficial. NATO could not function without it, trying to make every capability nationally self-sufficient would be both economically unrealistic and operationally counterproductive. The problem begins when we do not know what we depend on, who ultimately controls it, how quickly access could disappear, or what happens to the mission when it does. A system may be nationally procured while depending on foreign semiconductors, proprietary software, commercial cloud infrastructure, external authentication, imported ammunition or components, and a supply chain several countries deep. A military may own the hardware while lacking the authority, technical access or industrial capacity required to modify, repair or sustain it independently. And the dependency map does not stop at the military perimeter. Electricity supports communications, data centres, railways, ports, charging and fuel distribution. Commercial communications support civilian authorities as well as military alternatives. Ports and transport corridors carry reinforcement alongside civilian trade and industrial inputs. A cyberattack against a civilian logistics provider can affect military movement without touching a military network. One disruption can therefore travel through several systems before its operational effect reaches the commander. That is why Part 18 looks at sovereignty and interoperability from a C2 perspective rather than treating them primarily as political or industrial-policy concepts. The commander’s question is much more practical: what does my mission depend upon that I do not control, and what happens if it is no longer available? The article goes through dependencies; the US dependency question; data and cloud sovereignty; proprietary systems; federated architectures; coalition operations; critical infrastructure, societal dependencies; and the difference between having an alternative on paper and having one that has actually been integrated, authorised and exercised. Plan B deserves one additional question that is surprisingly easy to miss: does Plan B depend on the same thing as Plan A? The objective is not independence or isolation, and it is certainly not an argument against interoperability. It is retaining enough visibility, authority, access, redundancy and alternatives that commanders still have meaningful choices when circumstances change. Interoperability without sufficient control can become dependency. Sovereignty pursued without interoperability creates isolation. Somewhere between those two sits the operational freedom we actually need to design for. #CommandAndControl #Interoperability … more
