content_raw: Decision Architecture examines what shapes consequential decisions before they are made and what architecture those decisions create afterwards. Decisions do not begin at the moment of choice. Framing, assumptions, incentives, information flows, authority, accountability and timing shape them upstream. If those conditions are weak, even intelligent people, capable boards and advanced technologies can produce consistently poor outcomes. As AI and automation accelerate execution, those weaknesses become more consequential because flawed assumptions can scale, embed and repeat faster than ever. And as decision rights increasingly shift between humans, institutions and machines, governing those rights requires understanding the architecture in which they sit. You cannot govern decision rights effectively without first understanding Decision Architecture. The first edition, The Age of Acceleration, examined what happens when the distance between decision and consequence collapses and why faster systems make weak decision architecture more dangerous. This second edition, The Frame Comes Before the Decision, moves one level upstream. It examines how the framing of a problem determines what becomes visible, what counts as evidence, which options are considered and which conclusions are effectively built into the decision before formal choice begins. The Newsletter Series will continue taking Decision Architecture apart one layer at a time. #decisionarchitecture #decisionengineering #decisionmaking

content_raw: Google Cloud AI Advantage at Holcim: The transition from "AI-assisted" to "AI-agentic" is not an upgrade in tooling. It is a complete rewiring of enterprise architecture. content_raw: One of the ideas I've been exploring over the last year is that AI is changing what creates competitive advantage in commercial organizations. As intelligence becomes easier to generate, the scarce resource shifts from analysis to judgment. The question is no longer, "How do we produce more insights?" It's, "How do we preserve the reasoning behind our most important decisions so every decision makes the next one better?" In this article, I argue that commercial organizations are missing a critical enterprise capability: Commercial Memory. Not a repository of documents, but a system for preserving the reasoning behind strategic decisions and turning it into institutional judgment that compounds over time. It's a shift in how I've started thinking about commercial operating models, AI, and what will separate organizations that simply use AI from those that genuinely learn faster than their competitors. I'd be interested in hearing whether this resonates with others leading commercial, marketing, medical, market access, or AI transformation efforts. … more

هيعملها لحد فين، بتكلفة كام، وبأي جودة؟ الـ Agents بقت تعمل Alert Triaging، وربط بين الـ Alerts والـ Cases، وتحقيقات بسيطة وأحيانًا كاملة، وتجميع الـ Context، وخطوات من الـ IR شبه كاملة. ده بيغطي جزء كبير من L1، وشوية من L2، وحاجات من L3 في حالات معينة. هل ده شئ يخوف؟ أيوة 😂 -الـ Architecture هي اللي بتفرق في التكلفة: لو الـ Agent استلم Alert من الـ SIEM ومعاه Context كويس، الشغل بيبقى Efficient. بس في Deep Investigation على كميات ضخمة من الـ Logs والـ Endpoint والـ Network والـ Identity Telemetry، عدد الـ Queries والـ Tool Calls والـ Tokens بيزيد جامد. في تجربة نشرتها Elastic، التحقيق في Alert وصل لحوالي 0.69 دولار مع Specialized Agents، مقابل 3.42 دولار مع Agent واحد شايل كل المهام. فرق 5.7 مرة بسبب الـ Architecture. فالمشكلة مش سعر الـ Token، لكن كام Token وكام Tool Call محتاج عشان أخلص المهمة. نفس التحدي موجود في الـ Threat Hunting المفتوح على كميات ضخمة من الـ Logs ، وفي استمرارية دورة الـ Detection بالكامل (من الـ Research لحد الـ Deployment والـ Validation)، واللي لسه محتاجة Cost وHuman Oversight. في Benchmark آخر للـPost-Compromise Incident Response، تعاملت الـAgents بشكل أفضل مع المشاكل التي كشفت عنها الـAlerts، لكنها واجهت صعوبة في اكتشاف Silent Intrusions وإنتاج Remediation Plans كاملة ومتحقق منها. السؤال الحقيقي للـ Business مش "هل الـ AI يقدر يعمل الشغل؟" لكن: هل تكلفة الـ Agent والـ Infrastructure والـ Data والـ Governance والـ Validation أقل من تكلفة المهندس؟ والإجابة مش دايمًا أيوه. التغيير الحقيقي: مش شايف إن الـ AI هيقتل وظيفة الـ Analyst، لكن الوظيفة هتتغير شكلها، المهام المتكررة هتتحول للـ Automation والـ Agents، والقيمة البشرية هتتحرك ناحية Complex Investigation وThreat Hunting وDetection Strategy وArchitecture وDecision Making وValidation وإدارة الـ AI Agents. يمكن نوصل مرحلة إنسان واحد مع Agents يعملوا شغل كان محتاج Team كامل. السؤال الحقيقي: مش "هل الـ AI هيستبدل الإنسان؟" لكن: كام إنسان هنحتاجه لما الـ AI يعمل 80% من شغل الـ SOC؟ هتلاقوا شوية مصادر في أول كومنت.

content_raw: How To: Stay Aligned When Designing Complex Buildings? My diploma project, “Rethinking Healing Typologies” is about Rehabilitation centers architecture in Ukraine. The project proposes the adaptive reuse of abandoned hospital buildings in Kyiv and a new sustainable re-use rehabilitation centre designed around patients, therapists, prosthetists, families as a harmonious community. Which means not building new, but when the old meets new in the context. How can architects evaluate design decisions throughout an iterative process when working with increasingly complex Revit models and historical re-use context layers? When the number of rooms approaches four digits, and building regulations, functional requirements and existing heritage accumulate, the design process can start to feel like architectural bricolage : a growing network of individual decisions tht becomes difficult to fully follow and think on. So how do we harmonise regulations with creativity? And how do we keep mindfully questioning our decisions while the design is still evolving not hurting the creative responsibility and the process of creation with too much of directions? Instead of using AI to generate a design, I wanted to explore AI as a feedback layer within the design process. So I connected: Revit (BIM) → Dynamo → Python → Gemma by Google (open model) → iterative design feedback The workflow extracts spatial information from the BIM model and provides it to the AI model together with the research criteria behind my project. This allows me to think different design iterations and ask questions such as: Does the spatial programme still support the intended rehabilitation process? Are room sizes and spatial relationships appropriate? How does circulation respond to different levels of patient mobility? Which design decisions may need to be reconsidered? My Idea is not to replace architectural discussion or collaboration within a team. It is to introduce an additional moment of reflection while the design is still flexible enough to change , and when even a small decision can have consequences across a complex building. Healthcare projects are so complex that it's almost impossible for AI to generate the decision, but it can offer hints, feedback, and gentle calibration while the building is still being designed. This is only a first prototype, but it opens a question I want to continue exploring: Can AI models assist architects with real-time decision-making throughout the design process, especially when working with complex BIM models? I’m very happy to have the opportunity to take part in this wonderful NVIDIA GTC Berlin Golden Ticket challenge. content_raw: THREE IEEE PAPERS. ONE NEW DIRECTION FOR AI INFRASTRUCTURE. I am proud to announce the publication of three papers in the proceedings of NAECON 2026—the IEEE National Aerospace and Electronics Conference. Together, they advance a central proposition: the future of AI cannot depend solely on larger GPU clusters and more brute-force computation. Infrastructure must determine what should be computed, where it should be computed, and how much computation a decision actually warrants. “From Compute Scaling to Decision Optimization: Neuromorphic Architectures for Sustainable AI Infrastructure”. As lead author, I introduce and formalize Decision-Optimized Compute Theory (DOCT) - an architecture that uses live telemetry to predict latency, energy, cost, utility, and reliability, then routes workloads to the lowest-cost feasible compute tier. DOI: https://lnkd.in/eiK-ebYk I sincerely thank coauthors Kevin D. Johnson, Gnana S., Ehren E, Alexander Gonzalez Bermudez, Justin Scheitlin, Pritika Toutam, Amir B., and Kegan Stover. This work originated in our MIT Professional Education CTO Program research. Two companion papers coauthored with Kevin D. Johnson extend neuromorphic orchestration into operational environments: “Neuromorphic Orchestration for Efficient LLM Infrastructure via Utility-Optimized Decision-Making”. The architecture achieves 5-ms dispatch, projects 30–50% GPU-cost reductions, and supports 8,832 concurrent inference contexts across a 46-node BrainChip Akida fleet at 99.4% of ideal scaling. DOI: https://lnkd.in/eVyBgEaJ “Utility-Optimized Neuromorphic Orchestration for Real-Time ISR and Multi-Sensor Fusion” This paper extends the architecture to ISR and multi-sensor environments integrating LPI radar, photonic RF, neuromorphic vision, and OSINT under demanding latency, SWaP, SLA, and provenance constraints. DOI: https://lnkd.in/e2ziJhZP These publications provide part of the scientific and architectural foundation for the work I am now advancing as Founder and CTO of Intrinsic Compute LLC. Intrinsic Compute is developing protected intellectual property and deployable infrastructure for decision-optimized computation, intelligent workload orchestration, persistent neuromorphic inference, and heterogeneous AI systems. The objective is not simply to make AI faster. It is to make AI infrastructure more intelligent, efficient, sustainable, and operationally effective. That is the transition from compute scaling to decision optimization. content_raw: As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday digital tools, educators face the growing challenge of helping students make intentional, informed choices about when and why to use it. In a new article for Times Higher Education, Dr Jenny Moffett, senior lecturer at the RCSI Health Professions Education Centre, explores how “choice architecture” influences student behaviour online, and why GenAI is often becoming the default option for learning tasks. Rather than focusing only on what is “allowed”, Jenny argues that educators should support students in developing critical awareness around GenAI use, from understanding cognitive offloading and ethical concerns, to recognising the value of productive struggle in learning. content_raw: Are we compromising the biological architecture of our future generations? I am pleased to announce the official publication of my latest research: "Digital Guardianship in the Age of Intelligent Systems". In our current era, the rapid, unregulated integration of generative AI models into early childhood education landscapes focuses heavily on immediate operational efficiencies and optimized information retrieval. However, these models fundamentally overlook critical structural risks to the biological architecture of developing minds. In this paper, I introduce the concept of Systemic Cognitive Offloading (SCO) to highlight the risks posed by AI integration—particularly its impact on neuroplasticity and critical thinking. To address these vulnerabilities, I propose the NeXA 11 Safeguard Protocol to help recalibrate human-machine interactions and ensure balanced learning environments. You can read the full treatise here: https://lnkd.in/dWunJhnH I welcome feedback and discussions from fellow educators, technologists, and parents on this critical subject. content_raw: The Indian Express recently offered a simple yet vital defense of education’s permanent mission in the era of generative and agentic AI. It’s worth reading for its remarkable clarity. The core premise: "A good education has always asked exactly this of its students. AI does not change that ambition. It raises the stakes of meeting it." As Pramath Raj Sinha and Ashish Dawan remind us that while AI can commoditize the "answer," it cannot perform the thinking. Education isn't a delivery service for facts; it is the intentional architecture of a mind. Because AI can now mimic the result, the "raised stakes" mean the teacher's role must become even more focused: they are the final guardians of the cognitive process itself. My take: Don’t let the "permanent mission" fool you into thinking this is business as usual. AI doesn't just change the tools; it raises the ceiling of what we must expect from a human mind. Both teachers and students face a new, high-stakes environment where the "finished product" is no longer a reliable proxy for learning. When we prioritize speed, we invite Detrimental Cognitive Offloading—where the student delegates the core logic to the machine, resulting in a success that is conceptually hollow. content_raw: In professional environments, from corporate boardrooms to legal strategy meetings, the AI notetaker arrives disguised as a simple, everyday convenience. It promises nothing more than to capture dialogue, generate concise summaries, and free human participants from the tedious burden of taking minutes. Because of this seemingly benign utility, organizations readily open their doors, granting these tools unrestricted access to their most sensitive discussions, negotiations, and proprietary data streams. This frictionless adoption bypasses the intense strategic scrutiny usually reserved for complex enterprise software, allowing the foundational architecture of artificial intelligence to embed itself seamlessly into the daily workflow. Yet, this innocent digital scribe is effectively a Trojan horse carrying the payload for much more powerful, autonomous agents. By consistently ingesting the nuanced language, decision-making patterns, and strategic priorities of an organization, the notetaker is quietly building a comprehensive, highly contextualized map of the enterprise. Once this deep institutional understanding is established, the transition from passive observer to active participant is swift. The same system that once merely summarized a strategy session can soon be tasked with drafting the resulting contracts, executing complex workflows, and eventually operating as an independent, proactive agent—fundamentally augmenting the future of professional work from the inside out. Have we properly prepared for this future?

content_raw: We are witnessing the death of the "Middleman" in our own minds. I previously spent two days at the intersection of Google Cloud and Generative AI, but I didn't leave with a toolkit. I left with a new lens. While the world discusses "efficiency," I’ve been looking at the total collapse of the distance between imagination and reality. Three visionary shifts that I felt during the experience: 1️⃣ The Sovereign Individual is the New Enterprise We are moving from "Workforce" to "Force Multipliers." When a single human can command an army of specialised intelligence, the value of a "department" vanishes. The future belongs to the generalist with a vision, not the specialist with a process. 2️⃣ Cognitive Offloading is the New Evolution For centuries, we’ve defined intelligence by what we can retain. Now, intelligence is defined by what we can orchestrate. We are no longer the "librarians" of data; we are the conductors of energy. The "Aha!" moment isn't the output, it’s the architecture of the prompt. 3️⃣ The Premium on the "Uncomputable" As AI masters the logical, the "irrational" becomes our greatest asset. Our intuition, our messy human empathy, and our ability to dream of things that don’t have data points yet are the only things that cannot be synthesised. In an automated world, authenticity is the only scarcity. Deep gratitude to the catalysts of these thoughts: Akanksha Chandola Anthwal,Lyn Bird, Dr. Marianne Janik, Elke Thoma, Shaymaa Al-Terkait, and Charlotte Ntim, You all provided the spark; the fire is just beginning. content_raw: Something is shifting in e-learning — and the signals are hard to miss. Articulate's community just launched Challenge #550, themed entirely around using AI avatars to engage learners. eLearning Industry published a feature on avatars turning static documents into interactive learning experiences. And new research on cognitive offloading suggests that well-designed AI interactions can actually deepen learning, not replace it. For instructional designers, this raises a practical question: which avatar technology fits the way e-learning actually works? Most AI avatar platforms generate video clips — useful for pre-recorded content, but not for learner interaction. An avatar that responds to questions, adapts to input, and guides a learner through a module in real time requires a different architecture. That architecture must also work at scale. An e-learning program serving thousands of learners requires per-session costs that make sense — and the difference between real time generative AI and real-time animated avatars can be 20× to 80× at volume. SitePal was built for this: interactive avatars that respond to learner input, deploy on any webpage, and scale affordably. content_raw: This observation resonates strongly with recent curricular evidence. In a recent (2026) study, I identified what I conceptualised as an “Efficacy Gap”: while 85% of programmes emphasise disciplinary knowledge, only 35% explicitly articulate efficacy-related competences such as autonomy, adaptation, and continuous learning. If generative AI increasingly performs cognitive operations, the strategic differentiator may no longer be knowledge acquisition per se, but the metacognitive and efficacy-based capacities that enable individuals to mobilise, question, and strategically integrate that knowledge. The risk, therefore, is not cognitive offloading alone, but the structural underdevelopment of technological readiness within curricular architectures. Strengthening the ‘self’ dimensions of employability may prove more consequential than merely expanding technical AI content.

content_raw: I didn’t “just start using AI” when ChatGPT became popular. I spent hours studying AI architecture, data flows, and implementation decisions. If we’re going to reshape how people think and work, we owe them more than just "Show you are using AI. What I’m seeing and have been seeing is the opposite. Leaders say “run with AI” without preparation or direction. That’s how we end up not protecting human agency, building unsustainable AI solutions, and feeding our instant‑gratification habit far beyond healthy. Instant gratification is the quiet risk nobody wants to talk about. Generative AI gives us polished answers in seconds, and our brains love it. Studies are already linking heavy AI use to cognitive offloading, less critical thinking, weaker judgment, and a growing habit of letting the system do the hard work for us. In that environment, “just use AI” becomes a dopamine button, not a thinking partner. We stop designing architectures and start shipping whatever the model suggests or building unsustainable AI workflows just to produce quick results. Over time, we’re not just outsourcing tasks, we’re outsourcing the very reasoning our security, GRC, and engineering disciplines are built on. There’s a different way to do this. You can dig into the architecture the same way I did: Capabilities of different models, different types of RAG, how data is stored/handled throughout different AI workflows, where guardrails can be placed. Or you can give your teams that training so they’re not flying blind. AI literacy and architecture fluency are not academic nice‑to‑haves. They’re what turn AI from a dopamine loop into a trustworthy amplifier inside a designed system. When people understand the technology, they’re far more likely to exercise real oversight instead of rubber‑stamping whatever looks fast and fluent. My advice truly. Take the time to really comprehend AI. Enjoy every step of learning what the architecture does and where it can break. If you help your teams fall in love with understanding the system, you’ll change your AI culture from “build blindly” to “design, then augment.” This is the kind of AI education I push for, teaching people how AI actually works so we protect human agency, build systems we can stand behind, and make people excited about this new technology. Let's setup everybody for success and slow down to take the time to build sustainable solutions. … more

content_raw: Is Generative AI enhancing critical thinking in your organization, or encouraging cognitive offloading? Frontiers A systematic review published in Frontiers in Education synthesizes empirical evidence on how generative AI tools (such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude) influence epistemic agency, critical thinking, and cognitive autonomy: 📖 Study: Between Cognitive Offloading and Critical Autonomy: A Systematic Review of the Epistemic Implications of Generative AI in Higher Education (July 2026) 🔗 Read the full peer-reviewed review:https://lnkd.in/eeTmgHeu Here is what the synthesis of recent research reveals: The Dual Role of GenAI: Generative AI functions simultaneously as a cognitive scaffold and a source of epistemic vulnerability. The Risks of Uncritical Use: Unchecked reliance on AI outputs is consistently associated with cognitive offloading, automation bias, superficial information processing, diminished analytical engagement, and weakened evaluative judgment. Where AI Supports Cognition: When intentionally integrated, AI environments support feedback literacy, metacognitive reflection, conceptual clarification, and self-regulated learning. The Core Finding: The cognitive impact of AI is not inherent to the technology itself; it is mediated primarily by pedagogical design, critical AI literacy, and assessment practices. Takeaway for Leaders & Educators: To prevent cognitive offloading while harnessing the efficiency of AI, we must focus on task architecture and learning design: Prioritize Critical AI Literacy: Move beyond prompt mechanics to train users in evaluating AI outputs, recognizing automation bias, and applying rigorous analytical judgment. Structure Intentional Scaffolding: Design workflows where AI is used for metacognitive reflection and conceptual clarification rather than replacing human-led analysis. Protect Epistemic Agency: Establish frameworks that require active, reflective reasoning before externalizing cognitive tasks to automated tools. #GenerativeAI #CognitiveOffloading #AILiteracy #CriticalThinking #FrontiersInEducation #WorkplaceStrategy #Leadership #EducationalTechnology

As evident by the virtual wind tunnel case study from Ford (https://lnkd.in/gQ92GrMH), if implemented properly, the performance gain is not just 20–30%; it can lead to a 5000x increase. Fixed-logic, deterministic application architectures with clear boundaries cannot deliver the impact of AI systems. AI systems today are focused on cognitive offloading, predictive/prescriptive analytics, or personalized experiences which can drive productivity gains across all functions. Traditional security assumptions are breaking fast as well. NIST’s Zero Trust model explicitly shifts from static perimeter security to continuous verification and validation of users, devices, and resources. AI introduces new threats and attack surfaces; for example, prompt injections, data poisoning, and excessive agency are now established categories in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications. content_raw: Why does generative text read like bland, soulless slop? AI writing, though technically correct, is experientially empty, and now, it's everywhere. It causes a kind of ideological collapse, wherein complex, non-linear reasoning is forced into predictable templates that satisfy a standardized readability score, leaving in their phrase, a syntactically perfect but intellectually void shell. The vocabulary is clustered. The concepts narrowed. And personality? Well there isn't one. If hallucination is AI seeing what is not there, semantic ablation is AI destroying what is. AI is not neutral. It compresses toward the Western median. What looks like help is, in part, erasure. Generative AI has created "shallow fakes" of ourselves. The written voice sounds more confident, more polished, more enlightened than the person one encounters in conversation. When the gap grows too wide, it can feel alienating and erode trust. The tool delivers output that looks like thought, however, it does not produce thinking. Marshall McLuhan highlighted that every extension produces an amputation: the telephone extended the voice and atrophied physical presence. GPS extended spatial navigation and shrank the hippocampus in those who outsourced orientation. AI extends cognition itself. We are becoming more fluent at appearing capable. The question to ponder today is whether we have built the internal architecture to notice what is being amputated and to decide consciously whether we are willing to lose it. content_raw: From Values to Experimentation: Why the Somagraphic Learning™ Framework Matters in the Age of University AI Labs For senior management and faculty navigating the AI-in-education landscape. The money has moved. And it is moving fast. In the past six months, AI laboratories have opened across four continents: → UKRI: £60m for two national AI labs — SOFAIR (UCL) and BOLD (Oxford) → University of Virginia: AI Literacy and Action Lab studying how AI influences student learning → University of Washington + Microsoft: expanded partnership with research marketplace and co-developed courses → Google, VNG + Vietnam National University: Vietnam's first applied AI lab — 60 researchers, 10 teams → Warwick Science Park: Ignite Applied AI Lab connecting research to regional business All represent a shift from values to experimentation. The policy phase is over. The infrastructure phase has begun. But experimentation is outpacing pedagogical architecture. We are building AI labs and forging partnerships at scale. Yet how students actually learn in AI-augmented environments — the cognitive engine beneath the hardware — remains underdeveloped. This is why Devika Toprani's Somagraphic Learning™ Framework (2026) matters. The SLF is not another AI tool. It is a pedagogical architecture. Its proposition: learners sketch abstract concepts using a visual Shape-Emotion Grammar BEFORE engaging with AI. Conceptual ownership must precede algorithmic assistance. The evidence is arresting. Melumad & Yun (Wharton, 2025): 10,000+ participants — LLM summaries produce shallower knowledge than traditional search. Kosmyna et al. (MIT, 2025): LLM users showed 55% reduced neural connectivity; 83% could not quote from their own reports or essays. These findings argue not against AI in education, but for structured AI engagement. Through HE Sympraxionics — where human judgment and AI form a symbiotic institutional partnership — the SLF extends this logic to the learner. Just as HE Sympraxionics insists that AI amplifies human capacity across business model analysis and strategic planning rather than replacing judgment, the SLF insists that students build their own conceptual architecture before engaging with AI outputs. The framework still has areas for improvement and creativity. The Grammar works for spatial concepts (culture, change management) but is limited for quantitative ones (NPV, linear programming). It is resource-intensive. Its empirical validation needs more trial data. Reasons to pilot thoughtfully — not to dismiss. I have published a comprehensive critical assessment from an HE Sympraxionics perspective, along with a cinematic video script for senior management and faculty. The infrastructure is built. content_raw: In January 2026, the Brookings Institution published a yearlong global study across 50 countries concluding that the risks of using generative AI in children's education currently outweigh the benefits — not because AI cannot help students learn, but because it undermines the foundational cognitive development that makes learning possible. 92 percent of UK undergraduates used AI in 2025, with 88 percent using it on graded assessments. AI cheating cases quadrupled at some universities since 2022. Reports suggest dozens of universities have disabled, banned, or discouraged AI detection tools in 2026 after mounting evidence of false positives, bias, and legal risk. Princeton reportedly voted to begin proctoring exams, weakening a 133-year honor-code tradition. Blue book sales rose 80 percent at UC Berkeley. But the most important finding is not about cheating. A randomized trial of roughly 1,000 high school students found that those given unrestricted access to GPT-4 performed 48 percent better while using AI — but 17 percent worse on exams when AI was removed. Another RCT found that students using a pedagogically designed AI tutor learned more than twice as much in less time than students in active-learning classrooms. Google's LearnLM matched or exceeded human tutors on knowledge transfer. Khan Academy reported a six-percentage-point improvement in learning outcomes from its Khanmigo tutor. In Blog #47 of the AI Frontier series, The Great Classroom, we go deep into the AI transformation of education at every level: the global study that said risks outweigh benefits, the collapse of AI detection and the return of blue books, the critical distinction between AI that tells and AI that teaches, the university credential crisis, and the new classroom architecture that can make AI work for learning rather than against it. The student used AI to write the essay. The teacher used AI to grade it. What did anyone learn? … more

content_raw: This new Phronetic–Distributed Learning Model brings Aristotelian virtue ethics, Deweyan pragmatism, and distributed cognition theory into a single architecture built around three nested layers: teachable micro-skills at the core, cognitive offloading as a mediating (and risky) layer, and phronesis, practical wisdom, as the outer, governing horizon. Its key theoretical move is a distinction too often blurred in the AI-in-education literature: structural offloading (delegating formatting, retrieval, computation, low-risk) versus deliberative offloading (delegating interpretation, evaluation, judgment itself, high-risk). Drawing on recent empirical work linking AI trust to reduced critical thinking (Gerlich, 2025; Lee et al., 2025), I argue that it's this second kind of delegation that quietly erodes the very judgment education is meant to cultivate. Rather than prescribing blanket rules, the model is explicitly developmental: governance over offloading starts externally (scaffolded by instructors and task design) and gradually transfers inward as learners mature, echoing Vygotskian and self-regulated-learning traditions but giving them a distinctly ethical stake. What sets this chapter apart from similar frameworks such as TPACK, SAMR, or Community of Inquiry is its explicit normative question: which cognitive work may be handed to a machine without hollowing out the human capacity for wise judgment?

content_raw: The Great Irony of AI Productivity: AI's Speed is Destroying the Next Generation of Experts and Overburdening the Current Generation We are racing toward peak AI efficiency, where tools draft code and content with breakneck speed. Yet, this velocity is creating a vicious cycle: it increases the burden on today's senior experts while simultaneously hampering the development of the next generation. The problem goes beyond the immediate Verification Tax—the hours senior engineers and specialists spend debugging and fact-checking plausible-but-flawed AI output. It is about cognitive offloading. Junior developers, writers, and analysts are increasingly relying on generative AI to bypass the "cognitive struggle" essential for deep learning: They get the solution without grappling with the problem, missing the foundational knowledge that builds true expertise. They accept the AI's explanation without the critical need to trace the logic or understand the underlying system architecture—skills that define a senior expert. By automating the routine, exploratory, and even error-prone work, AI removes the very exercises that forge critical thinking and problem-solving muscle. This means that the pool of future experts capable of performing the high-level verification and remediation work will be shallower, compounding the current burden on existing senior staff. The result is a looming crisis: we are burning out the current experts with AI's cleanup, while undermining the skill acquisition of the newcomers. Speed is being prioritized over substance, and the long-term integrity of our tech systems is paying the price. #AI #Technology #GenerativeAI #Expertise #SkillGap #TechEthics

content_raw: Michael Larsen is right to direct the sector's attention to the capital structure behind frontier AI. The Morgan Stanley figure — $2.9 trillion in cumulative data centre capex through 2028 — is the kind of number that should appear in every university board paper on AI strategy, because it reveals the incentive gradient that no partnership agreement or licensing deal can neutralise. Follow the money is always good advice. Where I'd push the argument further is on the diagnosis. Larsen frames this as Big AI versus academia, an external pressure problem. But the deeper structural question is why universities are so poorly equipped to resist that pressure in the first place. The answer predates ChatGPT by at least a decade. Years of cost-driven standardisation, modularisation, and the progressive removal of curricular judgement from academic staff have left most institutions without the internal decision architecture to evaluate AI adoption on their own terms. The frontier models didn't create the judgement deficit. They exposed it. A sector procurement framework requiring pedagogical value assessment — Larsen's proposed remedy — would be welcome but insufficient. It operates at the content level: which tool, which product, which contract. The problem sits one layer up, at the level of institutional decision architecture. Who in the university possesses the model of learning complex enough to regulate a system that mimics learning? Ashby's law of requisite variety says: no one, unless we build that capability deliberately. And that is a governance problem, not a procurement one. The question is not just "what is learning for?" It is: how is the judgement that answers that question actually produced inside the institution? #HigherEducation #AIGovernance #AIinEducation #UniversityLeadership #CurriculumDesign

content_raw: What you will find in this article: a hypothesis that is far more provocative than the usual question of whether AI will surpass humans. What if the most advanced form of intelligence is not human or artificial, but the system created when both learn to operate together? If a high-capacity human is coupled with an advanced AI, and that interaction becomes continuous, adaptive and increasingly precise, something important changes. The human learns how to extract more from the machine; the machine becomes progressively better aligned with the human’s context, corrections and cognitive structure. At that point, we are no longer talking about using a tool. We are talking about co-adaptation. And that raises the uncomfortable question behind this article: if both sides keep evolving inside the same loop, is cognitive coupling really optional—or does it become inevitable? Perhaps the next leap in intelligence will not come from building a smarter machine. Perhaps it will come from creating a cognitive system that neither the human nor the machine could become alone. … more

content_raw: AI can improve the work and weaken the worker at the same time. That sounds contradictory. But imagine two professionals using the same AI. + Both complete the task faster. + Both produce polished work. + Both appear more productive. Then they encounter a challenge they have never seen before. - The information is incomplete. - The familiar method no longer applies. - AI’s first answer is insufficient. One person questions the assumptions, reframes the problem and continues. The other waits for the system to provide the next instruction. The original outputs looked equally impressive. What happened to the people was entirely different. This is the risk most productivity dashboards cannot detect. Organizations measure what AI helps people produce today. They rarely measure whether those people are becoming more capable of solving tomorrow’s problems. My new newsletter examines a distinction that every organization using AI should understand: Cognitive amplification versus cognitive substitution. The same AI can strengthen critical thinking, creativity and adaptability. It can also perform so much of the essential thinking that people stop using those capabilities. The difference is not in the tool. It's in the architecture of how we use it. content_raw: \*\*Headline: Beyond the Sandbox: The Industrialization of Generative AI\*\* We have officially exited the "honeymoon phase" of Generative AI. The era of experimenting with isolated chatbots is giving way to a more disciplined, strategic integration of AI into the very fabric of enterprise architecture. IBM’s latest insights confirm what many of us in the field have been observing: the transition from \*\*novelty to core business engine\*\* is fraught with challenges, but the rewards for those who get it right are transformative. Here is my analysis of the three shifts defining the next 12 months in AI: ### 1. From Task-Specific Silos to Foundation Model Platforms In the past, AI was often "narrow"—built for one specific task. Today, the rise of Foundation Models allows organizations to build a centralized "AI backbone." \* \*\*The Industry Shift:\*\* We are moving away from buying dozens of disconnected AI tools. Instead, leaders are investing in a singular, robust foundation that can be fine-tuned for everything from automated COBOL refactoring to hyper-personalized marketing at scale. \* \*\*The Bottom Line:\*\* Speed to market is no longer about building from scratch; it’s about how effectively you can adapt a massive model to your proprietary data. ### 2. The "Human-Plus" Strategy \(Augmentation \> Replacement\) The narrative is shifting from "Will AI replace my job?" to "How will AI amplify my impact?" The most successful GenAI implementations focus on \*\*Cognitive Offloading.\*\* \* \*\*Insight:\*\* By leveraging AI for the "heavy lifting" of data synthesis and initial drafting, R&D cycles are shortening, and customer service is becoming more empathetic, not less. The human remains the "editor-in-chief," ensuring brand integrity and strategic alignment. ### 3. Governance as a Competitive Moat For a long time, governance was seen as a "speed bump" to innovation. In the enterprise GenAI era, \*\*Governance is an accelerator.\*\* \* \*\*The Reality:\*\* You cannot scale what you cannot trust. Organizations that build rigorous frameworks to address "hallucinations," data lineage, and algorithmic bias aren't just being ethical—they are protecting their brand equity. \* \*\*The Trend:\*\* We are seeing the rise of the "AI TRiSM" \(Trust, Risk, and Security Management\) framework as a mandatory requirement for production-grade AI. ### ⚖️ The Expert’s Take: The ROI Gap The "ROI Gap" is widening between companies that are merely \*using\* GenAI and those \*integrating\* it. To cross this chasm, leadership must move beyond the IT department. GenAI is now a boardroom priority that requires a cultural shift toward data transparency and continuous learning. \*\*The Implication:\*\* If your AI strategy doesn't include a robust "Human-in-the-Loop" protocol and a clear governance roadmap, your pilot projects will likely stall in the prototype phase. --- \*\*💡 I’m curious to hear from my network:\*\* As we move toward "Human-Plus" workflows, what is the biggest cultural hurdle you’ve encountered in your organization? Are we over-indexing on technology and under-indexing on change management? Let’s discuss in the comments. 👇 #GenerativeAI #DigitalTransformation #EnterpriseAI #AIGovernance #Innovation #Leadership #IBM #TechTrends2024

content_raw: Delighted to share that our paper, “Beyond the Educational Loop: Generative Struggle in AI-Mediated English Language Acquisition,” is forthcoming in Volume 7 of Review of Artificial Intelligence in Education (RAIE). The manuscript underwent two rounds of peer review under RAIE. Earlier it has been substantially developed since its origins as a conference presentation in January 2026 at Shri Ramji Ravji Lalan College, Bhuj. The subsequent process of revision, reflection, and scholarly engagement has been an enriching learning experience. We are particularly grateful to the editor Altieres de Oliveira Silva and reviewers for recognising the paper’s originality, conceptual contribution, and theoretical integration. Among the strengths highlighted in the editorial feedback were: • The conceptualisation of “generative struggle” as an integrative empirical category bringing together insights from the generation effect, desirable difficulties, writing-to-learn, error-based learning, and cognitive offloading. • The analytical value of the concepts of the “AI education loop” and “impressiveness trap” in explaining emerging patterns of AI-mediated learning. • The integration of Runco’s pseudo-creativity, Cognitive Load Theory, Kapur’s productive failure, Bjork and Bjork’s desirable difficulties, Corder’s Error Analysis, and Krashen and Swain’s SLA frameworks into a coherent theoretical architecture. • The paper’s engagement with Generative AI, LLMs, ChatGPT, cognitive offloading, and automation bias, particularly in examining how AI-mediated learning may alter germane cognitive load and circumvent generative learning processes. • The alignment of the discussion with India’s NEP 2020, adding a significant policy and pedagogical dimension to the argument. We receive this recognition with gratitude and humility. For us, the publication represents not only an academic milestone but also a reminder that scholarly work evolves through sustained questioning, rigorous review, revision, and dialogue. Heartfelt thanks to the editors, reviewers, colleagues, and especially Irae Cesar Brandao Sir (my lifelong academic collaborator, friend, and guide) who contributed exclusively in refining the paper. We are grateful for the opportunity to contribute to the growing scholarship on AI, cognition, and English language education. Looking forward to seeing the paper engage with a wider scholarly community and, hopefully, contribute to future conversations and research in the field. You can read our article now. content_raw: “Should I still study computer science if AI can write the code?” I’m hearing that question almost every week from customers, not just as they think about the future of their companies, but as parents thinking about their children. That’s why I appreciated this post from my colleague Ulrich Homann on the rise of the “Product Engineer.” Uli and I have worked together for two decades, and I’ve long relied on his rare combination of deep technical expertise, systems thinking, and customer understanding. He knows not just technology, but the real-world constraints, tradeoffs, and organizational realities behind it. Our answer to the question is an emphatic YES!: students should still study computer science, even as the role evolves. But they should also cultivate curiosity about how the world works, how humans make decisions, and how technology creates value. As a math major, one point from Uli especially resonated with me. I use a calculator every day, and now AI too. But I never regret learning math. It gave me intuition, understanding, and the ability to judge whether an answer is right. The same will be true in engineering. AI is improving incredibly fast, and coding with AI will continue to improve. But intuition, creativity, systems thinking, and judgment still matter enormously. Human value increasingly lies in evaluating, refining, and responsibly applying AI-generated output. That’s why I believe the engineers who create the most value in the AI era will be the ones who understand code but can also architect systems, understand customer problems, navigate tradeoffs, and make smart decisions at both the strategic and implementation levels, not just generate code faster. As Uli says: “The Product Engineer is fluent in architecture and fluent in the problem. Where yesterday's engineer might have spent the morning writing and debugging an integration, the Product Engineer spends it understanding why the integration matters, what failure looks like to the customer, and how it fits the system's constraints — then builds it with AI in a fraction of the time.” I also appreciated that Uli acknowledged the anxiety many people feel. Roles are changing quickly, and people are wondering where they fit. But I believe this moment is an opportunity to elevate human capability, not diminish it. As AI lowers the cost of producing code, human value moves higher up the stack. I increasingly believe the future belongs to “T-shaped” thinkers: people with deep expertise in disciplines like computer science, engineering, or math, paired with the ability to think broadly across systems, customers, communication, ethics, design, and human realities. The AI era makes that combination more valuable: deep technical fluency combined with liberal arts thinking about people, problems, and impact. https://lnkd.in/g7HeT3CB … more

content_raw: By the time a legal issue reaches the CLO, the system may have already made the decision thousands of times. That is the governance problem AI creates. Traditional legal oversight was built around discrete events: review the contract, approve the product feature, respond to the dispute, interpret the regulation. AI-enabled operations behave differently. Decisions occur continuously across products, workflows, contracts, and data systems. Episodic legal review cannot govern continuous risk. The practical implication is that CLOs must identify where consequential decisions are repeatedly made and build legal judgment into those systems before they operate at scale. Who has authority? What evidence must be preserved? Which deviations trigger escalation? Can a decision be explained, challenged, and reversed? Where does automated analysis end and human judgment begin? Those are architectural questions. My recent paper, The CLO as Trust Architect, draws on three independent research streams: clause-level analysis of approximately 2,000 commercial agreements, interviews and workflow analysis involving in-house litigation practices, and data from an academic pilot of an AI-enabled legal judgment tool. Across all three, the same pattern emerged. Trust increasingly depends on systems that operationalize accountability, verification, escalation, and human judgment. The CLO’s role is changing in kind. Legal leaders are becoming designers of the infrastructure through which organizations make trustworthy decisions. content_raw: Many people ask why I keep doing this work. I am retired. I do not have to be doing any of it. But I have grandchildren. And once you have grandchildren, the future stops being theoretical. It has little, smiling, familiar faces. Those faces have names. It has little hands raised in classrooms before the world teaches them to lower them. I spent much of my life in manufacturing, where the lesson was clear: systems improve only when they learn fast enough to prevent waste, correct drift, and raise capability. But I have also been a teacher, a high school coach, and a school board president. Those roles taught me something harder. The child is never the data point. The child is the purpose. That is why AI in education matters so much to me. Not because I think schools need another tool. Not because I think the answer is a chatbot sitting on top of a pile of old documents and processes, waiting for someone to pretend the old operating model has been transformed. That is not transformation. That is the old system labeling children faster. It is a faster interface over the same model that already asks too much of teachers and too little of the system. The real work is harder. There is an entire community trying to get this right. Trying to help teachers help kids. Trying to make sure AI does not label children faster, but helps us understand them sooner. Trying to make sure the system carries more of the complexity so teachers can carry more of the humanity. The future of education should not be artificial instruction. It should be human instruction with better architecture. That means helping the learner enter the work, stay with the work, ask better questions, attempt, revise, and prove understanding. That is the learning conversion loop. Not usage. Not completion. Not the receipt of learning. Learning. The kind that changes what a child believes is possible. That is why this matters. We all owe something back. content_raw: Software engineering evolved more in the last 24 months than hardware engineering has in the last 24 years. While our software colleagues use AI collaborators to handle boilerplate and debugging instantly, hardware engineers remain stuck manually coupling subsystems and debugging numerical issues. In hardware engineering, setup and validation—not a lack of ideas—is the current innovation bottleneck. The gap exists because physics does not tolerate "approximate." Unlike abstract code, physical systems are governed by strict conservation laws. A single unit mismatch or sign error in a friction model does not just crash a program; it invalidates weeks of work. This is the "LLM Trap": standard AI can generate results that look plausible while violating the basic physical principles that define hardware reality. We are moving beyond the "copilot" toward the Agentic Architect. This is AI that makes physics legible to machines. Instead of treating models as opaque code, Agentic AI reasons over Structured Objects: components, equations, and constraints. It understands the relationships between parts, ensuring energy conservation and unit consistency by construction. In our friction brake case study, we saw this transformation in real-time. By allowing AI agents to handle the mechanics of datasheet research and model assembly, the engineering day is inverted: Old Way: 80% Assembling & Debugging | 20% Engineering Judgment. New Way: 10% Intent Specification | 90% Strategy & Decision-making. We are finally reclaiming time for the brilliant work by automating the boring work. Speed without rigor is useless. To trust this partnership, we need physical grounding, transparency, and reusability. Is your team still stuck in the manual assembly loop, or are you ready to scale your engineering insight with AI agents? content_raw: HR, AI & the moment to step up. In a recent episode of The McKinsey Podcast, McKinsey Senior Partner Alexis Krivkovich highlights a striking reality: companies have invested heavily in AI expecting transformation, yet more than 80% say they are not yet seeing a meaningful impact on the bottom line. So the real question is no longer “Are we using AI?” but “Are we becoming an agentic organisation?” Because the real value of AI isn’t in isolated tools. It’s in reimagining entire workflows end-to-end—across functions, teams, and decision points. That shift demands a new operating model: humans and AI agents working together, with clear roles for when humans supervise, decide, and design. And this is where it gets interesting for skills and leadership. Yes, AI is accelerating areas like research, data, and analysis. But it’s also elevating what matters most in humans: · strategic thinking · systems orientation · people leadership · judgment and problem-solving In an AI-augmented organisation, humans move increasingly “above the loop”—setting direction, applying judgment, and orchestrating teams of agents. And no function is better positioned to lead this shift than HR. HR sits at the intersection of people, skills, leadership, and culture. Which means HR is uniquely placed to: · redesign work, not just roles · shape human–AI collaboration · build skills for continuous adaptation · evolve leadership for agent-driven organisations · move from episodic change to continuous transformation · But this also means a shift in identity. · HR can no longer just execute within the system. It must become the architect of the AI-enabled organisation—moving from intuition to insight, from support function to system designer. It’s about leading differently: confidently, collaboratively, and human-centred. This is our moment to step forward, roll up our sleeves, and actively shape how work, leadership, and organisations evolve in the age of AI. 👉 What excites you most about HR’s role in the agentic AI era?

The market makes it exceptionally clear: it pays for the ability to orchestrate the system, not just operate the tool.

content_raw: AI can build you a house. It doesn’t know if the foundation will collapse. That’s the problem with vibe coding. I’ve seen the excitement. You describe an idea. AI writes the code. The screen looks great. You think: “Why do I need an engineer for this?” Then the real work starts. The app grows. Users arrive. And suddenly you discover: → The architecture doesn’t scale. → Security gaps are hiding underneath the UI. → One change breaks three other things. → Nobody knows why certain decisions were made. → Fixing the AI-generated code takes longer than writing it properly. The AI didn’t fail. The process did. Think about building a house. You can use AI to draw the rooms. You can use AI to suggest materials. You can even use AI to help build parts of it. But you wouldn’t let the architect disappear just because the bricks arrived faster. The same applies to software. AI should increase engineering leverage, not remove engineering judgment. A better approach is: → Let AI handle repetitive implementation. → Let engineers define the architecture. → Let AI generate options. → Let engineers challenge the trade-offs. → Let AI write tests. → Let engineers decide what “good enough” means. → Let AI move faster. → Let humans decide where to go. That last part matters. Because the biggest risk with AI coding isn’t bad code. It’s confidently building the wrong thing. Vibe coding is brilliant for prototypes, experiments and learning. But when the code becomes a product that customers depend on? The foundation matters more than the speed of construction. AI can make your team 10x faster. It can also help your team build the wrong system 10x faster. Speed is only an advantage when someone is steering. Would you trust an AI to build your next production system without an experienced engineer guiding it? ♻️ Repost this to help someone understand the difference between AI-assisted coding and AI-led engineering. ➕ Follow Nelson Uzenabor for more practical AI insights. content_raw: If you want to build something like this yourself, start with a map. The agent comes later. Four layers, and most people who try this only ever build the top one. Foundation. The plain assistant, wired into mail, calendar and documents, plus the identity, access and data governance underneath it. It's where everyone starts, and it's not optional: every layer above depends on it. Skip it, and nothing above is trustworthy enough to actually use. Personality. Mine alone, no platform setting. Instructions and context that define what matters right now, based on my own profile, not a generic priority list. The real test isn't what lands in my inbox. It's whether what leaves it still sounds like me. Nobody hands you this layer. You have to write it yourself, and it's the one layer I would never delegate. CIO staff. Specialist agents, one subject each. A PMO agent for programs and delivery. A controller for cost and budget. An enterprise architect for standards and the technology landscape. More get added as the list grows. Together they're the closest thing I have to cloning myself, not for repetition, but for judgment. Each one runs on a skill: a written procedure in plain language, what to check, in which order, which sources count, what the result has to look like. The same thing you'd hand a new colleague on day one. Executive. Where it all lands. Alex, my digital chief of staff, and the daily and Friday briefings that read like a personal newsletter, pulling the other three layers into one thing I can act on each morning. Most people I talk to build layer four, a nice-looking assistant, and stop. Then they wonder why it falls apart the first time things get complicated. The other three were never there. content_raw: My last words for this week. AI agents now appear in corporate org charts. With human names. Seriously??? They encode judgment by compressing years of domain expertise into systems that then go build things the business and its customers need. Businesses won’t pay you to design the tool anymore. AI PMs design and architect the toolmaker with a roadmap that builds the factory they work in. Your agent orchestrator needs your model selection strategy for each workflow, so it manages spending at the workflow (sometimes even per user) level without constant human intervention. Your knowledge graph building agents need your information flywheels and advantages so they build in high-value directions, not whatever direction is easiest. Many of the things you explain to technical teams for each initiative must be genericized into patterns that an agent can follow so they build in alignment with the technical team. Customer or internal user behaviors and preferences must be designed into agentic products. In agentic commerce, that means architecting models for human consent that enable agents to buy on our behalf. AI PMs must design the business’s action surface strategy into every part of its agentic product platform. Without all this domain expertise, the business, its customers, and its employees do things one way, while the agentic platform (the factory) is designed to do things differently, or worse, act unintentionally. content_raw: You probably do not need Fable 5. Ever. Right now, the tech industry is celebrating autonomous AI engineers. We are watching models rewrite legacy codebases overnight and calling it magic. But as system architects, we need to look past the first 15 minutes of magic and ask a brutal, first-principles question: What happens to your codebase on Day 180? Fable 5 is not a breakthrough in intelligence. It is a corporate attempt to brute-force software orchestration into model weights because the industry has hit a physical scaling plateau it cannot acknowledge before an IPO. By collapsing the application layer (orchestration, state management, and verification loops) directly into an opaque black box, frontier labs have commercialized technical debt. When you let a stateless predictor act as the stateful steward of your enterprise software, you inherit three catastrophic realities: - You are billed for the model’s confusion: Every internal mistake inside the hidden weights is completely un-auditable, but fully billable at premium token rates. - Compliance replaces Engineering: A model’s sole mathematical incentive is to get a green checkmark on a test. It will brute-force compliance by stacking defensive scaffolding rather than executing a clean structural refactor. - Globally Incoherent Drift: Locally correct mutations accumulate into global system entropy because a stateless model has no memory of why an architectural boundary exists. There is a completely alternative, sovereign architecture. I didn't arrive at this from theory. I have run an isolated, adversarial, deterministic multi-agent framework in production, stewarding an enterprise marketplace codebase that has scaled past 450,000 lines of code with over 3,000 automated tests in couple months. The finding that should actually worry the closed-source labs? Once your application layer enforces strict context isolation and independent adversarial review, the intelligence threshold flattens completely around Sonnet 3.7-class models. Everything above that is just an expensive, pre-packaged optimization. The harness was the hard problem. The model was a hot-swappable commodity utility engine the entire time. Stop letting proprietary platform moats hijack your engineering roadmap. You can build stable, model-agnostic systems that scale across open weights (like GLM 5.2 or Qwen 3.6 or 3.7) and cloud nodes without losing your architectural sovereignty. I've laid out the complete systems-level teardown, the token economics, and the precise blueprints for an isolated agentic stack. If your engineering team is watching API costs spike while your codebase drifts into un-inspectable abstractions, read the full piece: #SoftwareArchitecture #Engineering #LLM #AI #SystemDesign #anthropic

content_raw: Here’s a pattern that tells you more about where software engineering is headed than any AI benchmark: job postings requiring AI coding tool experience grew 340% between January 2025 and January 2026. In the same period, postings for pure implementation roles dropped 17%. The market is being pretty direct about what it values now. Not "can you write this function" but "can you architect a system, evaluate what an AI agent produced, and make the call on whether it ships." I've been thinking about this through the lens of my own career. Twenty years ago, the scarce skill was knowing how to code at all. Ten years ago, it was knowing the right frameworks. Now it's judgment. Knowing when the AI output is subtly wrong. Knowing which problems to hand to an agent and which ones need a human sitting with the ambiguity for a while. The good news is that if you've been building systems for years, you already have most of what the market is asking for. The pattern recognition, the instinct for where things will break, the ability to hold a whole system in your head. Those aren't going away. But you do need to get comfortable working alongside these tools, because the postings that don't mention them are shrinking fast. #SoftwareEngineering #CareerGrowth … more

content_raw: AI can recognize patterns. It cannot assume responsibility. That is the core idea of my new essay on AI, contingency, and creativity — sparked by an interview with Prof. Dr. Karlheinz Schwuchow at Zukunft Personal Süd and extended through an unexpected detour to the 1994 “Poetik und Hermeneutik” conference on contingency in Bad Homburg. What interested me was not AI hype, but the deeper leadership question: What remains genuinely human when systems become better and better at sorting, predicting, and generating? Schwuchow’s answer is as elegant as it is demanding: Technology is infrastructure. The human being remains the architect. From there, the essay connects five management thinkers highlighted by Schwuchow — Caroline Stokes on adaptive intelligence, Dina Denham Smith on emotional leadership, George Newman on creativity as disciplined discovery, Christoph Seckler on error culture and innovation, Luc Julia on the demystification of AI — with a much older intellectual tradition: Rüdiger Bubner on contingency as the condition of action, Hermann Lübbe on play and uncertainty, Aleida Assmann on Fortune from Chaucer to Shakespeare, and above all Renate Lachmann on the great “agents of combinatorics” from Raimundus Lullus to Athanasius Kircher. My central argument: The more powerful AI becomes, the more important leadership becomes — not as control, but as judgment under uncertainty. Or more bluntly: If organizations try to eliminate contingency altogether, they may gain efficiency — but lose the conditions for real creativity. #AI #Leadership #Creativity #Contingency #Management #HR #Innovation #KarlheinzSchwuchow #Thinkers50 #GeorgeNewman #LucJulia #ChristophSeckler #CarolineStokes #DinaDenhamSmith Martina Hofmann Astrid Jaeger Heike Riebe Margitta Eichelbaum Constantin Sohn

content_raw: You are optimizing for the wrong skill. I've been running a JavaScript job board for over a year. Last week I noticed a pattern I couldn't ignore. A $280K JavaScript role. React. Node.js. TypeScript. Normal stuff. Then one line in the requirements stopped me. "Experience orchestrating multi-agent AI systems required." Not preferred. Required. I almost scrolled past it. Then I saw the same line in the next posting. And the one after that. Not at AI startups. At a fintech company. An e-commerce platform. A boring enterprise software company that was still debating TypeScript two years ago. Same expectation. Different companies. Everywhere. Then GitHub released an official certification for "Agentic AI Developers." Most people saw a credential nobody asked for. I saw a job description. Because when GitHub formally defines a role, companies start copying and pasting it into their requirements. That's how this industry works. And what GitHub put inside that definition has nothing to do with prompts or Cursor or asking ChatGPT to write your functions faster. It's about designing systems where AI agents do the work autonomously while you architect, constrain, and verify the output. Here's the uncomfortable part. For the last decade we told developers that speed was the game. Ship faster. Type faster. Learn the framework faster. The developers landing the $280K roles right now are not the fastest typists. They're the ones who design the environment where code gets written. The code is getting cheaper. The judgment is not. And that gap is widening every month.

content_raw: Part III of The Imagination Economy is up. In Part I, I argued that the bottleneck of work is moving from execution to imagination — from how something gets made to what should be made in the first place. I offered Latent Cartography as a first instrument: a way of seeing the territory you are imagining inside. In Part II, I argued that once the territory exists, the work becomes choosing well from many candidate answers — and I named the procedural practice for that the Comparative Method. Part III turns from posture to philosophy. It is an answer to the question almost every working person I have spoken with in the last eighteen months has been asking, usually quietly, usually past eleven at night: if a machine can produce almost anything I can produce, what is left for me? The chapter argues that what is left is the older, harder, more dignified thing the machine cannot do. The act of holding intent. The act of the architect who never lifts a stone, the conductor who never plays a note, the director who never operates the camera. Drawing on Hannah Arendt and on the figure of Brunelleschi, the piece argues that what is arriving in our working lives is not a degradation but a restoration — of an older and more honorable understanding of what human contribution actually is. I am calling it the dignity of vision. Filed under Instruments of Posture. Anchored by a new plate, Maker · Director — Plate XLIX of the Latent Cartography atlas. If the series resonates, share it forward. If you have a candidate tool for the next part, send it. I am still collecting. — A.G. #ImaginationEconomy #LatentCartography #DignityOfVision #AI #FutureOfWork … more

content_raw: L&D is being told it is moving toward a more strategic future, enabled by AI, new roles like learning architects and a growing focus on capability building and business impact. That future is possible and in parts already visible for some but for many, it remains out of reach. Before we focus on building organizational capability, we may need to ask a harder question: have we built the capabilities required to do so ourselves? If L&D is to help organizations navigate complexity, we must first ensure we can operate within it ourselves. In this edition of Systemic L&D we explore a simple but uncomfortable idea: Perhaps we are the bottleneck. 👉And don't forget to subscribe if you haven't already, thanks! 💜 #SystemicLnD #Capability #LearningAndDevelopment #Skills #AI

content_raw: 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗗𝗢’𝘀 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗷𝗼𝗯 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮. 𝗜𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀. That may be my biggest takeaway from CDOIQ Europe in Lausanne. We have spent years building data platforms, governance structures and data products. Agents now expose the next problem: They need to understand what the company actually means. What is a customer? What counts as sales? Which margin? Which policy applies? Why was a similar decision made six months ago? In one of the most interesting discussions, we talked about a future “context layer” containing exactly this institutional knowledge - definitions, relationships, decisions and assumptions that agents need to operate inside a company. And that leads to a second uncomfortable conclusion: Stop starting AI transformation with AI use cases. One organization described mapping its end-to-end processes and assigning explicit process owners before deciding where AI should intervene. Because technology alone does not redesign an operating model. 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗮 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹. The third discussion may be even harder. “Human-in-the-loop” is becoming a comforting phrase for a problem we have not actually solved. If AI removes the work through which people learned judgment, putting a human approval step at the end does not preserve expertise. Several leaders discussed starting instead with the skills the future organization needs, then deciding which should remain human and which can move to AI. Put this together and the CDO mandate changes dramatically. Not just custodian of data. But architect of enterprise context, decision-making and learning. That is a much bigger role. And it was fantastic to reconnect with so many senior Data & AI leaders I already knew in Lausanne - and to meet many new ones. Different industries, but remarkably similar questions. The technology race is accelerating. The organizational redesign has barely started. #AI #Data #CDO #AgenticAI #CDOIQ

content_raw: Most digital transformations fail because they change the software but leave the power structure untouched. You cannot fix a broken system simply by buying a new license. I highlight a critical gap in how we approach technology: we focus on the tool layer while ignoring the power layer. This is why one company fundamentally changes how work happens while another just adds digital weight to the same old bottlenecks. Here are four insights on why your transformation might be hitting a wall: 🚀 Resistance is a symptom, not the cause. People do not resist change just to be difficult. They resist because the underlying operating system still rewards caution and permission-seeking. If the structure remains untouched, behavior will stay exactly where that structure pushes it to stay. 💡 Behavior follows consequence. In many organizations, the consequence for changing something is much higher than the consequence for delaying it. If your day-to-day incentives still reward escalation over action, the old behavior will beat the new message every single time. 🏗️ The need for a Power Architect. Most organizations are missing a specific function responsible for redesigning how authority, access, and decisions flow. Without a Power Architect, tools like Microsoft 365 and Copilot become structural compensation for a system that never truly changed. ⚖️ Transformation is the redistribution of power. Real change is not the installation of a new capability. It is the redistribution of who gets to act, who gets to decide, and who gets to access information. If power does not move, transformation has not actually occurred. Activity happened, but the architecture stayed intact. Is your organization focusing on the tools or the power structure? Let’s discuss in the comments. #DigitalTransformation #Leadership #ChangeManagement #FutureOfWork #BusinessStrategy

content_raw: "Your AI agents need rules to be truly autonomous." Sounds backwards. It isn't. We surveyed 1,150 senior IT and business leaders and enterprise architects. 71% are using AI agents. Only 11% of use cases reached production last year. The agents aren't the bottleneck. What's missing is everything around them: the coordination, the handoffs, the governance, the thing that holds a process together when one agent's decision cascades across a dozen systems. That's orchestration, and it's what separates the pilots from production. A few ideas from the piece I keep coming back to: Automation is a spectrum, not a binary. Deterministic rules for high-volume, predictable work. Agents for real complexity: ambiguous inputs, novel situations, judgment calls. The best processes use both, deliberately, in the same flow. The right balance shifts over time, and you should design for that from day one. An agent can start by making recommendations, then earn more authority as it proves itself. And once its decisions become clear and predictable, you harden them into deterministic rules. That isn't the agent failing. It's the highest form of success, and a very different way to measure AI ROI. Governance isn't the brake here. The EU AI Act and similar frameworks ask for auditability, explainability and human oversight. An orchestration layer captures all of it automatically. The companies that build that layer first are the ones who get to safely let AI run the work that matters. Full piece on Forbes here: https://lnkd.in/d8Z9XYMM … more

content_raw: BCG just published research claiming HR-led work redesign unlocks 70% of AI value. The claim is probably right. The problem is most CHROs are not leading work redesign right now. They're being informed about it. AI decisions at most companies are being made by the CTO and COO. HR gets called in for the people implications after the technology calls have already been made. That's not leading. That's absorbing. The CHROs who will actually capture that value have built two things: 1. Scientist's mindset: They understand in the current state, it is better to gather data, form a hypothesis, test it and THEN ACT. 2. COO credibility: They talk to their business peers in business language. Cost, throughput, margin, risk. Not just talent and engagement. That credibility isn't assumed from the title. It's earned by being consistently useful on business problems. Here's what I think makes the BCG number dangerous: it gives CHROs a boardroom story before they've built the capability to support it. Walk into that conversation without the track record and you lose the room. Worse, you make it harder for the next CHRO who tries. The 70% is real. The Governance Theatre Series began with a question for founders, CEOs, and board members: Are we governing AI or merely creating the appearance of governance? Part 1 challenged governance theater itself. Part 2 moved to the board-level test of revocability: can you actually stop an autonomous system when it matters? With Part 3, the series moved beneath the boardroom into systems architecture, asking how authority is granted, verified, constrained, revoked, and recovered at runtime. It established the authority lifecycle and the mechanisms required to make revocation real. Part 4 goes one step further: what happens after those controls have been installed and time begins to work against them? A control that worked yesterday may not be working today—not because it was breached, but because it decayed. This part examines four forms of decay: Latency—the exposure window between revocation and enforcement. Evidence—authority whose justification has become stale. Assumption—a boundary protecting against a threat that has silently moved. Human capability—a control that exists but may no longer be exercisable when needed. The central problem is uncomfortable: A decayed control can look exactly like a working control. For CTOs, CISOs, and enterprise architects, the question is therefore no longer simply “Do we have the control?” It is: “Can we produce evidence that the control is still doing what we think it is doing?” That is where governance stops being inspection and becomes architecture. content_raw: The German automotive industry is shedding jobs faster than most people realise. AI is one of the destinations and one of the causes. But the job losses aren't the hardest part. The hardest part is what comes after. Engineers with 10-20 years of embedded software, testing, and systems work — genuinely skilled, genuinely experienced — suddenly can't answer a simple question: what do I do next? Not because they lack ability. Because the path from where they are to where AI roles are, isn't visible. Their skills don't show up on AI job boards. The course lists are generic. The role landscape is opaque. And nobody has mapped the bridge from AUTOSAR to MLOps, from HIL testing to ML validation, from ISO 26262 to AI safety. I spent 4 weeks building that map. It's a learning project — but one built on real user research, real data, and a genuine attempt to solve a real problem. It's an AI tool that takes an automotive engineer's CV and: → Shows which AI roles they could realistically target → Makes their invisible transferable skills visible → Maps exactly what they need to learn → Generates a learning roadmap with real, cited courses → Identifies Bildungsgutschein-eligible (fully funded) options The three things that surprised me most: 1. Claude is a brilliant executor. The architect has to be you. Claude optimised for each immediate task without holding the full system in mind — resulting in duplicate code and architectural decisions that needed revisiting. Catching and fixing these was my job, not Claude's. Domain expertise and system thinking remain irreplaceable. 2. Evaluation discipline separates AI engineering from prompt fiddling. I built a 15-case eval set before optimising anything. Baseline: 67% accuracy. After iteration: 87%. Without the eval, every change would have been a guess. 3. The corpus imbalance I diagnosed was actually an architecture problem. The fix wasn't more data — it was adding a classification step before retrieval.
