content_raw: A pull request approved in six minutes. An incident three weeks later. The reviewer read it, understood none of it, and thought they had. The failure wasn't speed. It wasn't the agent. It was something quieter: the reviewer's calibration was off, and they couldn't see it from inside it. Convincing output attacks your judgment in two directions at once. First direction: the output sounds authoritative, so you accept it as correct. Kruger and Dunning showed in 1999 that low performers can't recognize their own competence gaps. Fluent, formatted, plausible text widens that gap silently. Your confidence becomes someone else's input. Second direction: the output looks more polished than yours, so you stop trusting your own read. You defer where you should be the judge. Clance and Imes named this in 1978. The agent's draft feeds it directly. These aren't opposites on a spectrum. You can feel both on the same code review. "Be more careful" doesn't fix this. It's a resolution, not a mechanism. Resolutions don't survive a context switch. They don't fire at the moment you need them, which is exactly the moment you feel most confident. A mechanism fires whether you're confident or not. My new article walks through four levers that force you to actually know what you're approving: one for junior developers, one for seniors, one for engineering managers, one for architects. Each one is condition-triggered. None requires willpower. I also name the limits. These mechanisms catch overconfidence better than they catch underconfidence. None is a guarantee. Worth having anyway. Amazon's mechanisms are Amazon's. The pre-mortem is Klein's. What explicit mechanism do you have in place? #SoftwareEngineering #AI #EngineeringLeadership

content_raw: If AI agents can write code, analyze incidents, configure systems and automate workflows, what skills will actually become more valuable in the BSS/OSS world? I don't think the answer is simply "learn AI." I think it depends on where you are in your career. For graduates and young professionals: Build strong engineering fundamentals + AI fluency. Understand software, APIs, data, cloud and how agents actually work. Use AI to learn and execute faster, but don't let it replace your understanding of the fundamentals. For experienced professionals: Domain depth becomes a differentiator. Understanding charging, billing, order management, assurance or network operations — and knowing why the business rules exist — gives you context that an AI agent may not have. Experience + AI fluency could be a very powerful combination. For architects and senior technical leaders: System thinking and orchestration become increasingly important. How do applications, data, APIs and multiple agents work together? Where should agents be autonomous? Where do we need guardrails? How do we design for reliability, security and scale? For leaders: Judgment may become one of the most valuable capabilities. What should we automate? Where should humans remain in the loop? Which problems are actually worth solving? And how do we redesign organizations and ways of working around these new capabilities? There is an interesting paradox here: as AI makes execution cheaper, context and judgment become more valuable. So perhaps the career question isn't "Will AI replace my BSS/OSS skills?" Maybe the better question is: "Which part of my expertise becomes more valuable when AI can do more of the execution?" Curious how others in BSS/OSS domain are thinking about this.

content_raw: Nobody assigned this to me. Requirements review is a large part of my work as a software architect in safety-critical automotive development. And for a long time, the first 20–30 minutes of every review session looked the same: open the change task, find the affected requirements, pull them from the database, load the context — then finally start the actual thinking. So I built an agent to do that part for me. It takes a single change task ID, assembles the full context — requirements text, ASIL levels, rationale, traceability — and produces a structured findings report before I open it. In interactive mode I can ask follow-up questions, check for ASIL conflicts, or draft a review comment on the spot. A few things I learned building it: — The checklist matters more than the prompt. The LLM amplifies the architect's expertise; it doesn't replace it. — The hard part wasn't the AI. Integrating with real systems — inconsistent exports, tool-specific formats, cross-system context — took most of the time. — Structured output beats narrative. A findings table per requirement is more useful than a long prose answer. — Freeing attention compounds. When routine work is off the plate, you apply judgment where it actually matters. The final decision always stays with the architect. The agent handles preparation. Safety-critical judgment is not something you automate. I believe AI agents in engineering workflows should be built from the bottom up — by the engineers who know the domain and feel the pain, not handed down as an IT initiative. This is what that looks like in practice. A few weeks ago I wrote about the architecture behind building AI agents for embedded systems workflows. This is what one of those agents looks like in production. Full write-up in the comments. content_raw: Last week in Midtown Manhattan, construction crews were inside the old Pfizer headquarters at 235 East 42nd Street. A 33-story tower being converted into apartments. Part of the project involved widening and extending upper floors, adding fresh load on top of an existing frame. Then steel columns on the 21st floor started to buckle. Floors sagged. Bricks dropped. Within hours, FDNY and NYPD cleared the building, evacuated several nearby buildings, and shut down surrounding streets. Engineers swarmed the 21st floor to shore up the damaged columns before something worse happened. Nobody planned for a public safety event. The original intent was simple: add new, attractive floors on top of a building that already existed. The problem was the mismatch between the new load and the old frame. That is where a lot of AI strategy sits right now. Executives want AI on the top floors. Smarter hiring. Predictive models. Agentic workflows. But the frame they're loading it onto was built for a different era. Disconnected data. Manual processes held together by tribal knowledge. Incentive structures that reward activity over outcomes. The weight is going somewhere, and most organizations haven't asked where. The buckling just looks different than steel bending. It looks like HR teams running constant fire drills to meet deadlines for pilots and demos that never graduate. It looks like conflicting data and shadow systems multiplying under the banner of "experimentation." It looks like a CHRO who feels in their gut that the organization isn't being built right, even when the pilot metrics say otherwise. I'm calling it the AI fire drill era. And it's what happens when we keep adding floors without checking the frame. That's why this week I want to dive more into the Architect mindset.

content_raw: How do you stay valuable as a network engineer when AI keeps getting better at the job? Every new model is better than the previous generation. Today, we mainly have general purpose LLMs and they are already pretty good. In the future, we'll likely have specialized models, from for example networking vendors, that will be even better and more efficient. So how do you stay relevant? Become more of a designer/architect. An LLM can confidently generate a BGP config, but was BGP the right choice? How do we build something that is not only redundant, but also resilient? Get very good at verifying. AI will hand you an answer with total confidence, and sometimes it's confidently wrong: a command that seems plausible, but it doesn't exist. The engineer who can read the output, test the claim, and catch the subtle failure is worth more in an AI world, not less. Bring your ops discipline to AI itself. This is where our background is an advantage most people don't have. We already think in blast radius, change windows, least privilege, and rollback. Those are exactly the guardrails autonomous systems need, and a lot of AI teams are relearning them the hard way. You already know this. Point it at agents. None of this is about out-typing the machine. It's about owning the judgment, the verification, and the accountability no model can hold, because in the end it's still your name on the change. The real skill is being willing to keep moving up the stack, a little faster than the tools move up behind you. So where are you putting your learning time right now?

content_raw: Enterprise Architecture is not collapsing under AI. It is splitting in two. On one side, a volatile layer of AI agents, orchestrated workflows, and models that change weekly. The architectural mistake many organizations are making right now is trying to govern both layers the same way. That approach fails in both directions. Too slow for AI. Too reckless for the core. The future enterprise is not collapsing. It is bifurcating. Design for the split. #EnterpriseArchitecture #AIArchitecture #AgenticAI #EnterpriseAI #TechnologyStrategy #FutureOfWork #MaverickEA

content_raw: The real bottleneck in AI-assisted development isn't the model. The real bottleneck in AI-assisted development isn't the model. It's the architect. Michael Mattern makes one of the sharper arguments I've read lately on this: as AI handles more of the coding, the constraint shifts upstream — to the people who can actually judge whether what gets built is the right thing, built the right way. Worth adding one uncomfortable corollary: many organizations responding to AI productivity gains are doing exactly the wrong thing. They're cutting architect headcount or freezing junior hires, betting that AI makes experienced judgment redundant. It doesn't. It makes it scarcer and more valuable. The organizations that will win long-term aren't the ones squeezing efficiency out of today's senior cohort. They're the ones investing now in the next generation of architects — people who still know how to code, who grew up shipping software, and who will eventually be the ones steering the AI. Efficiency is a tactic. Talent pipeline is strategy.

content_raw: Most people using AI today are consumers. They rent the model. They rent the interface. They accept the rules set by the provider. The purpose of the AI is whatever the provider decided it should be. Consumers rent their capabilities. An architect builds them. When you build an autonomous pipeline, that relationship changes. You own the models. You write the rules. You decide what the system is for. But ownership comes with a catch. When you own the architecture, you own the responsibility. A governed framework handles the mechanics. It catches bad outputs. It tracks every decision. It forces humans to review the work. What the framework cannot do is answer the most important question. What is this machine for? What should the agents build? Who is it serving? What is the end goal? The framework governs how the AI works. The architect decides what the AI builds. A governed system without a clear purpose is a sophisticated pipeline. A governed system with a clear purpose is a tool you control completely. content_raw: Do you think AI is actually reducing work? It is certainly reducing the cost of producing work. Analysis that took days can now be generated in minutes. Code appears in seconds. Ten scenarios can be created where previously there might have been two. But something interesting happens next. Organizations rarely take that productivity gain and simply stop. They ask for more analysis, more variants, more scenarios, more recommendations, more output. The bottleneck does not disappear. It moves. Before AI, scarcity often sat with the people producing the work. Increasingly, it sits with the people who must review it, prioritize it, make decisions, and act on it. That is the AI Work Paradox. AI can make every producer more productive while simultaneously increasing the amount of work flowing toward managers, reviewers, architects, editors, and decision-makers. Which leads to a very different AI productivity question: Not: How much more can we produce with AI? But: How much additional intelligence can the organization actually absorb and convert into value? In the latest edition of Technology Bytes, I explore why AI may be shifting the real constraint from production capacity to absorption capacity, why “hours saved” tells only half the story, and where those saved hours actually go. content_raw: Have you ever used AI that works precisely the way you do? You bought the AI subscriptions. Every tool in your stack bolted "AI" on. And if you run complex customer, technical, or operational work for a living (solution architect, sales engineer, technical account manager, IT leader who still does the work), you are most likely not getting the leverage or productivity gains to the degree that you expected after a year or more of AI at your disposal. That is not because the AI is weak per se. It is because nobody taught you a method for applying it to your specific work. Most "AI productivity" advice tells you to automate everything. That is the wrong approach. Most things should not be automated. Most workflows are not worth the build effort. And most prompts produce mediocre output because the thinking that should have happened first never did. So I built the alternative. It is called Bring Your Own Stack. BYOStack is a methodology, not a library of done-for-you skills. It teaches you a repeatable system to: • Decide what is actually worth automating • Deconstruct a real workflow with deliverables (RFPs, SOWs, status reports, QBR decks, solution designs, etc.) • Build and iterate a Claude skill where you actually trust the output And it goes after the layer every other attempt skips: your judgment. First pass: your process. Second pass: the judgment calls you make without noticing you make them. Your process is what you do. Your judgment is what makes it yours. That is the difference between AI that "does the steps" and AI that does your work the way you do. What you walk out with is not a magic finished skill handed to you. It is: • A Version 1 you briefly iterate into something you actually use every week • A way of thinking worth internalizing, because you can reuse it on every other workflow In about 7 days, you take one real workflow and turn it into a Claude skill that carries your process and your judgment. After that, you stop rebuilding the same workflows from scratch and let Claude do the heavy lifting your way. It is $97 USD, one time, built to run on Claude Pro. และขาดกระบวนการย่อยข้อมูลจากสมองซีกแรก (First Brain) จะทำให้ระบบ AI กลายเป็นเพียง "ถังขยะข้อมูลที่ระบุพิกัดได้" เท่านั้น ไม่ใช่สถาปัตยกรรมความรู้ที่งอกเงยจริง สอดคล้องกับบทความที่ชี้ให้เห็นชัดเจนว่า "Critical Thinking" และ "Internal Understanding" คือหัวใจสำคัญ (Feedback Loop) ก่อนที่จะทำการ Deposit ข้อมูลลงสู่ระบบ Second Brain หาก Content ที่ป้อนเข้าไปเป็นขยะ (Junk) ต่อให้ AI ค้นหาเจอ (Retrieve) มันก็ไร้ประโยชน์ (Useless) 🏗️ 4 ความท้าทายเชิงสถาปัตยกรรมข้อมูล (Knowledge Architecture): ---- 1️⃣ The Knowledge Retrieval Fallacy: การที่ระบบ AI ค้นหาข้อเท็จจริงพบไม่ได้แปลว่าผู้ใช้งานเกิด "ทักษะและการตัดสินใจ" (Strategic Decision) ในระดับ Production หากขาดการตกผลึก ข้อมูลนั้นจะไม่สามารถนำมาประยุกต์ใช้แก้ปัญหาหน้างานจริงได้ 2️⃣ Semantic Loss in Vector DBs: ในระบบ RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) การ Embed ข้อมูลที่ไร้โครงสร้างและปราศจาก Context ของมนุษย์ จะลดทอนคุณภาพการสืบค้น (Accuracy) และทำให้คำตอบที่ LLM เจนเนอเรตออกมามีความตื้นเขิน 3️⃣ Security & Data Governance Risks: การจัดเก็บข้อมูลอย่างไร้ทิศทาง (Passive Hoarding) เสี่ยงต่อการหลุดรอดของสิทธิ์เข้าถึง (Data Leakage) องค์กรจำเป็นต้องบังคับใช้หลักการ Least Privilege ในทุก Layer ของ Knowledge Base 4️⃣ Operational Inefficiency: การประมวลผลและทำ Indexing ข้อมูลขยะที่ไม่สร้าง Value ต่อธุรกิจ ส่งผลเสียต่อ Compute/Storage Resource โดยตรง ซึ่งขัดต่อหลักการ Operational Efficiency ในการบริหาร Cloud Infrastructure ---- ⚙️ 3 แนวทางกู้คืนระบบ "First Brain" เพื่อขับเคลื่อน AI Memory: 🔹 Digest Before Deposit: ต้องสรุปเนื้อหาสำคัญสั้นๆ 1-2 บรรทัดด้วยภาษาตัวเองเพื่อสร้าง "Long-Term Memory" ที่มีคุณภาพก่อน Record เข้าระบบ 🔹 Implement Data Lifecycle: คัดกรองและกำจัดข้อมูลที่ไม่ได้ใช้งาน (Rotten, Outdated, Trivia - ROT Data) ออกจากคลังความรู้เสมอ 🔹 Prompt with Architecture Constraints: การ Query ข้อมูลผ่าน AI ต้องระบุบริบท (Why) และผลกระทบ (Impact) ที่ต้องการอย่างชัดเจน ไม่ใช่ถามหาแค่ความหมาย เรากำลังสร้าง "ปัญญา" หรือแค่สร้าง "คลังเก็บขยะข้อมูล" ที่ฉลาดขึ้นด้วย AI? content_raw: I scroll through LinkedIn and I'm honestly not sure what’s scaling faster: the rapid evolution of AI or the steady decline of human critical thinking. Five years ago, the feed was full of genuine technical depth. We saw real debates on ML architectures, production-grade pipelines, and builders actually shipping robust solutions. Then ChatGPT launched three years ago… and overnight, everyone rebranded as a "GenAI Expert." Apparently, three years of non-stop GenAI talk wasn't enough to keep the hype alive. We needed a new buzzword to chase. Now, we’ve shifted into the era of "AI Agents." At this stage, I’d bet half the people posting about them would struggle to explain the fundamental difference between a standard LLM and an actual agentic workflow. It gets even more surreal: The comments are now likely generated by AI agents… debating other AI agents… on behalf of human profiles. We’ve reached a stage where machines are arguing with machines while humans just sit back and watch. Is this what we’re calling progress? #AI #Agents #Hype #TechTrends #MachineLearning

content_raw: Success is no longer determined by getting better at playing yesterday’s game using AI. It’s defined by whether you’re playing the right game. Almost everyone now has access to powerful LLMs, GenAI tools, and intelligent workflows. As a result, content is abundant: perfectly structured emails, solid analytical reports, polished slide decks, and slick video assets. Yet, when output becomes effortless, distinctiveness disappears. Without clear human intent, much of what we see feels generic, pale, and transactional. AI amplifies capability, but true differentiation comes from how we apply it. I spent this past week for an intensive training series. We moved beyond simple prompting and coding, to focus on what matters most for scalable, enterprise-grade AI: + Output Quality & Authenticity: Bringing critical thinking and domain expertise back into AI-generated deliverables. + Agentic System Design: Moving from standalone prompts to multi-agent architectures. + Evaluation & Security: Ensuring governance, risk mitigation, and continuous quality measurement. The tech landscape is evolving rapidly. The goal isn’t just to produce more, but to figure out what to do - it's executing with quality, judgment, and human nuance. #Google #GoogleCloud #AI #GenAI #AgenticAI

content_raw: Last week I attended Fraunhofer FOKUS's 2nd Learning Technology Symposium in Berlin. I had meant to leave it at a selfie and a single sentence 😉, but what came out in the end was a whole article that briefly sums up the themes and talks I found most important. The common thread is the role of the human in AI and learning architectures. It turns out that, alongside skills like critical thinking, we also need the ability to learn and, above all, to reflect on our own learning process. AI tools (recommender systems and reasoning agents) can be an enormous help here, but they do not replace certain skills that most of us wrongly assume we already have. In the article I take a closer look at these contributions, among others: Truong-Sinh An & The-Anh Nguyen "Interoperability in Education – Building Sustainable Digital Learning Ecosystems" Marc Ghanime & Bach Do "AI in Education – A practical introduction to modern AI‐powered learning" Nathalie Theisen & Marian Guenther "Frontier agentic Learning Experiences (Microsoft Perspective)" Jessica Schlauer "AI in Action – Shaping a Learning and Adaptive Organization" Kristin van der Meer "AI in Primary School" Panel discussion "Are we changing learning, or are the technologies changing us?" with Jan Veira, Dr. Yvonne Konstanze Behnke, Naomi Schoppa, Lewis Erckenbrecht, Kristin van der Meer and Justine Alice Weber Many thanks for the really interesting input! There were several other really good talks as well, among them a whole track on Immersive Learning. And perhaps the piece is also of interest to my dear colleagues at Hapag-Lloyd AG. 😎 #FOKUSLTS #FOKUSMWS #MediaWebWeek #LearningTechnology … more

content_raw: 𝘼𝙄 𝙬𝙤𝙣’𝙩 𝙧𝙚𝙥𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙚 𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙨𝙪𝙡𝙩𝙖𝙣𝙩𝙨 𝙖𝙣𝙮 𝙩𝙞𝙢𝙚 𝙨𝙤𝙤𝙣. 𝘽𝙪𝙩 𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙨𝙪𝙡𝙩𝙖𝙣𝙩𝙨 𝙬𝙝𝙤 𝙗𝙡𝙞𝙣𝙙𝙡𝙮 𝙩𝙧𝙪𝙨𝙩 𝘼𝙄 𝙬𝙞𝙡𝙡 𝙦𝙪𝙞𝙘𝙠𝙡𝙮 𝙧𝙚𝙥𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙚 𝙩𝙝𝙚𝙢𝙨𝙚𝙡𝙫𝙚𝙨. LLM models are developing at a break-neck pace. I am sure you would have read about (if not already used) the newly minted Claude Fable 5 (Mythos-level model) that has aced reasoning benchmarks. But let me tell you about a fairly recent, quiet disaster in the advisory world. A top-tier global firm published an authoritative industry report on cybersecurity. It was a masterclass in thought leadership - highly persuasive and packed with compelling statistics supporting the narrative. There was just one small issue: 𝙖 𝙨𝙪𝙗𝙨𝙚𝙦𝙪𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙞𝙣𝙫𝙚𝙨𝙩𝙞𝙜𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙧𝙚𝙫𝙚𝙖𝙡𝙚𝙙 𝙤𝙫𝙚𝙧 60% 𝙤𝙛 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙧𝙚𝙥𝙤𝙧𝙩'𝙨 𝙘𝙞𝙩𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨 𝙬𝙚𝙧𝙚 𝙝𝙖𝙡𝙡𝙪𝙘𝙞𝙣𝙖𝙩𝙚𝙙. The AI tool used to draft the document had fabricated articles from top-tier tech magazines, invented non-existent research from competitors, and generated dead URLs. But because the citations carried prestigious logos, no one in the team working on the document thought to cross-check the footnotes. In Consulting, our product isn't a 50-slide deck or a polished whitepaper. 𝗢𝘂𝗿 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁, 𝗷𝘂𝗱𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆. When AI is deployed without rigorous human validation and guardrails, we aren't achieving "efficiency". We need to remember that Gen AI are prediction engines designed to generate mathematically probable strings of words, not to verify objective truth. As consulting companies integrate AI into strategy, data analysis, and deliverables, critical thinking is no longer a soft skill but most vital hard skill in the tech stack. What I believe 𝘾𝙧𝙞𝙩𝙞𝙘𝙖𝙡 𝙏𝙝𝙞𝙣𝙠𝙞𝙣𝙜 looks like in the AI Era: • 𝗭𝗲𝗿𝗼-𝗧𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴: Assume your AI tool is a highly articulate analyst who occasionally makes things up to impress you. Verify every data point and citation before it leaves your desk. • 𝗧𝗵𝗲 "𝗦𝗼 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁?" 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁: AI can summarize 1,000 pages of legacy IT architecture in seconds, but a human must still synthesize how we can generate client value that impacts the bottom-line • 𝗚𝘂𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗞𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗹𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗲: Hallucinated work-slop doesn't just ruin a single deliverable; it poisons the well. If unverified AI outputs enter internal systems, they become the foundation for future errors. 𝙏𝙝𝙚 𝙥𝙧𝙚𝙢𝙞𝙪𝙢 𝙞𝙣 𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙨𝙪𝙡𝙩𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙝𝙖𝙨 𝙨𝙩𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙚𝙙 𝙨𝙝𝙞𝙛𝙩𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙛𝙧𝙤𝙢 𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙘𝙧𝙚𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙩𝙤 𝙘𝙤𝙣𝙩𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙘𝙪𝙧𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙖𝙣𝙙 𝙫𝙖𝙡𝙞𝙙𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣. content_raw: 🚀 The Skill Shift: From Prompt Engineer to Problem Architect Most people think AI rewards those who know the most. It doesn’t. It rewards those who think clearly. In the pre-AI world, weak reasoning could hide behind effort — the 40-page report, the complex model, the 20-slide deck. We often mistook the grind for the insight. AI changes that. It removes the cost of producing analysis — but not the cost of thinking. And that exposes the real equation: Weak Thinking → Weak Prompts → Weak Outputs To work effectively with AI, the skill is not prompting. It is problem architecture — structuring thinking before interacting with the machine. Three capabilities matter: 1. Precision: Framing Over Typing Two analysts use the same LLM. One produces a summary. The other produces a decision-grade insight. The difference is not the tool. It is problem framing. 2. Skepticism: The Validation Loop GenAI is extremely good at producing plausible answers. Strong users don’t just ask for conclusions — they ask: “What would prove this wrong?” Without validation, AI simply amplifies user bias. 3. Mechanics: Mapping Cause & Effect Narratives describe outcomes. Mechanisms explain them. AI becomes powerful when prompts are built around cause-effect logic, not commentary. AI is not replacing thinking. It is exposing the structure of thinking. The bottom line “Prompt engineering” is a temporary label. The durable skill is critical thinking applied to AI workflows. AI is making reasoning quality visible again. The real question is: Are you structuring problems — or just generating outputs? #GenerativeAI #CriticalThinking #FutureOfWork #AIStrategy #Leadership

content_raw: A paradox is haunting the adoption of GenAI in software development, and it strikes at the heart of how we build and innovate. This hits the core of what I’ve been exploring. In a past post, I argued that the AI revolution is happening on two fronts: what we build (Agentic AI) and how we build. While Agentic AI pushes the boundaries of "what," this paradox threatens to undermine the "how." The paradox is this: senior engineers, who can critically judge an AI's output, are best equipped to use these tools. Juniors, however, are vulnerable to the "trust trap"—the plausibly correct but subtly flawed code that LLMs excel at creating. In my last post, I proposed a solution: treat the AI as a "sparring partner" to build the cognitive muscles for the future. But a sparring session without rules can be chaotic. How do we structure this partnership to be safe and effective for everyone, not just seasoned experts? A concrete answer is emerging. A recent, brilliant post from the GitHub Blog introduces "Spec-Driven Development". The core idea is a seismic shift from "code is the source of truth" to "intent is the source of truth". This isn't just a new workflow; it's the disciplined regimen our sparring partner needs. Instead of a vague prompt leading to a black box of code, it forces a structured dialogue: 📝 Specify Intent: First, the developer and AI collaborate to forge a detailed, executable specification. This isn't about code; it's about user journeys and what success looks like. Critical thinking is forced before a single line is written. 🗺️ Architect the Plan: Next, that intent is translated into a concrete technical plan and manageable tasks, respecting the system's architecture and constraints. 🛠️ Implement with Precision: Only then does the AI generate code, but now it's against a pre-validated, human-approved blueprint. This is the operating system for the AI teammate I wrote about. It solves the paradox by making critical thinking and problem decomposition—the core of a senior engineer’s skillset—the first step for everyone. It transforms the AI from a potentially misleading oracle into a true partner in thought, one that helps architect the solution from the ground up. This is how we revolutionize the "how" of building software. We stop simply asking AI for code; we start leading a structured dialogue about intent. This is how we build the next generation of engineers—not by protecting them from AI, but by teaching them to lead the dance. #FutureOfWork #AIinEngineering #SoftwareDevelopment #GenAI #AgenticAI #Leadership #TalentDevelopment #SpecDrivenDevelopment #GitHub … more

content_raw: Adapting to the Next Wave...Claude impacts SaaS IT Services industry has thrived for over five decades, evolving through every major technological shift. Each disruption reshaped the way we work yet every generation of technologists adapted, learned, and pushed the industry forward. * Y2K: They mastered large-scale problem‑solving, collaborating across systems, geographies, and deadlines to safeguard global infrastructure. * Mobile revolution: They reimagined user experiences and built entirely new ecosystems from apps to responsive platforms that transformed how the world interacts with technology. * Cloud transformation: They embraced rapid upskilling, shifted from hardware‑centric thinking to scalable, distributed architecture, and rebuilt enterprise systems for speed, resilience, and global access. Each wave demanded new skills, fresh thinking, and the courage to unlearn old ways. Today, we stand at the edge of the GenAI era and the pace is unlike anything we have seen before. This disruption hits at the core of what we do: how we build, design, write, communicate, and solve problems. It is exponential, fast, and deeply transformative. So, what can the current workforce do uniquely to tackle GenAI disruption? - Adopt a “human‑plus‑AI” mindset: Instead of competing with AI, learn to orchestrate it, using GenAI to amplify creativity, speed, and decision‑making. - Develop cross‑functional intelligence: Pair domain expertise with AI literacy to build solutions that are not just technically sound, but business-smart and human-centric. - Experiment relentlessly: GenAI rewards fast learners. Those who build prototypes, test ideas, and iterate quickly will lead the next wave. - Focus on judgment, critical thinking, and ethical decision‑making: These human capabilities now matter more than ever because AI still needs wise, skilled humans to steer it. The question isn’t whether GenAI will reshape our work; It already has. The next disruption is here.

content_raw: There was a moment at the Women in Technology Breakfast as part of Palo Alto Networks Ignite conference that really stayed with me. The conversation wasn’t just about AI. It was about leadership. I loved hearing the thoughts on who is creating the trust, safety and resilience in an AI-powered world. AI doesn’t create trust. Leaders do. We talked about resilient operations. About lifting top line, reducing cost, increasing productivity. About GenAI not as a shiny experiment but as product outcomes. We heard from brilliant women like: • Vanessa Van Beek from Fortescue • Peggy Renders (Telstra Enterprise) • Stephanie Dietz from Canva • Lisa from Cyberfit Nation Each reinforcing a powerful theme: AI is not a just a technology conversation. It’s a thinking conversation. It’s a human conversation. We’re moving from: Technical capability → Productivity capability. Generic tools → Personalised GPTs by role. Experimentation → Enterprise integration. AI is democratising roles. It’s elevating creativity, imagination and innovation. But it’s also demanding stronger critical thinking, sharper decision-making and deeper integration. The World Economic Forum continues to name critical thinking, problem-solving and creativity as essential future skills. AI doesn’t replace those. It amplifies the gap between those who have them… and those who don’t. And then there was the simple but profound idea: Trust is confidence in the unknown. In an AI world, we are constantly stepping into the unknown. Trust isn’t accidental. It must be designed into systems, into governance, into security. But more importantly? It must be designed into our thinking. Because leadership in the age of AI isn’t about knowing everything. It’s about: • Creating psychological safety • Building resilient operations • Asking better questions • Integrating technology with human judgement • Focusing on value and outcomes not hype AI will absolutely lift productivity. But only leaders who intentionally design trust and safety into their decisions will unlock its full value. The question isn’t whether AI will change your organisation. The question is: Are you consciously designing the trust architecture that allows it to thrive? I’d love to hear from you. How are you building trust and resilience into your AI strategy right now? And how are you lifting your leadership and team capability to lean into better thinking? content_raw: The Great Gen AI Con Gen AI Sounds Smart but Knows Nothing-The Illusion of Authority Gen AI sounds confident. Gen AI sounds smart. But it is all an illusion. Humans with deep knowledge and expertise possess authority to analyze and diagnose. These are the people we trust to authoritatively opine on important matters based upon their depth of knowledge. The people with the most knowledge will often be the first ones to acknowledge that they don’t know everything. What about LLMs? LLMs are constructed on algorithms, massive statistical engines performing probability calculations. Because they are performing mathematical equations, by definition LLMs are incapable of reasoning. LLMs can only predict the next word based on patterns in their training data, not understanding or comprehension. Because of this, LLMs cannot “know what they don’t know.” Fundamentally, LLMs can never “know” anything because mathematical equations cannot possess knowledge. Even more troubling? LLM "knowledge" is frozen the moment training ends, and no amount of scaling, extra GPUs, or parameter growth changes that fact- hence, sclerotic data. Fluent and convincing as they may appear, their outputs are mathematical guesses masquerading as expertise. When patterns shift or novel situations arise, the illusion crumbles—because pattern-matching is not reasoning, and statistical probability is not knowledge. Gen AI will never truly know anything, no matter how impressive the demo. But without education about the true nature of Gen AI or critical thinking on the part of the user, the user may never question the outputs they are receiving as shown in this cancer case. Without understanding Gen AI’s true nature, users risk being duped into blind trust. Hype only amplifies the problem. CEOs and media claim scaling—more GPUs, more parameters, bigger models—will solve everything. But scaling doesn’t fix the architecture. Autocomplete can’t become reasoning. Fluency will never equal accuracy. INSA is different. Designed with semantic comprehension and incremental learning at its core, every interaction strengthens capability. Its architecture supports memory, contextual reasoning, and explicit “I don’t know” states—so it can clarify, qualify, or escalate when meaning is incomplete. I came back to it after yet another conversation where an AI initiative was described as “successfully deployed”, while in reality people were barely using it and value was still somewhere “expected next quarter”. At some point I realised that this gap between deployment and adoption has become almost normalised and that’s exactly why it’s dangerous. What resonated with me in this Gartner piece is not the framework itself, but the honesty behind it. The data confirms what many of us see every day: most GenAI initiatives don’t struggle because of models, platforms, or licenses. They struggle because organisations underestimate the human and architectural side of change. In my work, I rarely see AI fail because it doesn’t work. I see it fail because nobody really owns how it fits into daily workflows, decision-making, incentives, and responsibility models. Adoption is treated as an afterthought, while architecture quietly absorbs the consequences fragmented usage, shadow experimentation, rising risk, and invisible debt. That’s why the focus on community matters so much to me. Not as a cultural add-on, but as part of the enterprise design. Communities of practice, champions, feedback loops, psychological safety these are not “soft” elements. They are structural mechanisms that either exist by design or emerge by accident. And this is where architecture becomes critical. Without architectural thinking, communities remain disconnected, feedback never reaches governance, and AI adoption turns into scattered local optimisation instead of enterprise capability. Architecture is what connects people, platforms, risk, learning, and value into one coherent system. This article didn’t teach me something new. It articulated something I’ve been observing for a long time: GenAI adoption is not a technology problem. It’s an enterprise problem. And enterprises that treat it as such will move faster and safer than those who don’t. content_raw: This year at the Academy of Management (AOM) 2026, I will be presenting my co-authored scholarly paper titled 'Role-Biased Chatbots as Pedagogical Provocations for Collaborative Learning' under the paper session Designing with AI: Innovative Pedagogical Architectures for the GenAI Classroom. 🎯 This study examined how students engage with biased AI perspectives during management learning tasks. Students individually interacted with chatbots intentionally configured to reflect differing corporate roles and associated biases in decision-making and strategic management. They later collaborated with human peers, with reflective checkpoints embedded throughout. 🎇 We investigated how students integrated insights from their initial human–AI interactions, how these shaped their reasoning during group discussions, and how learning was consolidated following human–human collaboration. 🎆 Findings indicate that students primarily recognized and interrogated the chatbots’ role-driven biases, using them as a basis for critical comparison during group work. Collaborative dialogue further deepened their awareness of decision-making biases and the varied strategic priorities embedded within each role, resulting in more nuanced, evidence-informed perspectives on managerial decision-making and strategy formulation. 💥 The design promoted reflection, perspective-taking, and collective sense-making. Collectively, the results illustrate the value of structured human–AI engagement in cultivating critical thinking. When students are prompted to interrogate decisions through “why” and “how” questions, reflection becomes a tool for sense-making, thereby elevating the quality of learning in management education. content_raw: \*\*Headline: Beyond Analysis: Why the Shift to Generative AI is the Most Significant Tech Pivot of the Decade\*\* 🚀 The conversation around Artificial Intelligence has fundamentally changed. We are no longer just teaching machines to "sort" the world; we are teaching them to "build" it. I recently reviewed a comprehensive guide from GeeksforGeeks on the evolution of Generative AI, and it reinforces a critical reality for every professional: \*\*We are moving from an era of discriminative AI to an era of creative orchestration.\*\* Here is my analysis of the three pillars driving this shift and what they mean for the industry: ### 1. The Death of the "Labeling" Constraint Traditional AI excels at classification—identifying a cat in a photo or flagging a fraudulent transaction. However, GenAI \(powered by Transformers and GANs\) has broken the "labeling" barrier. By mastering the underlying patterns of massive datasets, these models don't just recognize code or text; they synthesize it. \*\*Industry Implication:\*\* This democratizes high-level technical and creative output. The barrier to entry for complex tasks—from drug discovery to software architecture—is collapsing. ### 2. The Rise of the "Director" Mindset The guide highlights a profound shift: \*\*Success now requires moving from "doing" to "directing."\*\* As GenAI becomes a massive productivity multiplier, the value of a professional is no longer found in the manual execution of a task, but in the strategic orchestration of the tool. \*\*Key Skill:\*\* \*\*Prompt Engineering\*\* is the new literacy. Learning to craft precise, context-aware inputs is how we bridge the gap between "generic AI output" and "high-value business solutions." ### 3. The Ethical Safeguard: Human-in-the-Loop \(HITL\) We cannot talk about the power of GenAI without addressing its volatility. AI "hallucinations" remain a technical hurdle. The GeeksforGeeks guide rightly emphasizes a "human-in-the-loop" workflow. \*\*My Take:\*\* In a world of automated content, \*\*human verification becomes a premium service.\*\* Our role is to provide the critical thinking and ethical oversight that models—no matter how advanced—simply lack. --- \*\*The Bottom Line:\*\* Future-proofing your career isn't just about learning new tools; it’s about adopting a new philosophy of work. Whether you are a developer, a strategist, or a healthcare professional, GenAI is the wind at your back—if you know how to steer the ship. \*\*Let’s discuss:\*\* As we shift from being "doers" to "directors," what is the one skill you believe will become more valuable than ever? content_raw: Two years ago, I balked at #ChatGPT. I was one of the professors quietly panicking about what AI would do to writing, to thinking, to the classroom, to the world. I worried about linguistic justice. I worried about ethics and authorship. About students losing the productive struggle of drafting and revising. And honestly, those worries weren't wrong. There are moral and ethical questions we haven't fully reckoned with. There are guardrails we still need. We're not talking nearly enough about opportunity divides and environmental impact. Nonetheless, my curiosity led me to start using it while listening to my brilliant Carnegie Mellon University colleagues Nupoor Ranade and David Brown teach me about the architecture behind the tool. And then I got good at using it, in large part because I'm trained as an English professor and someone who studies rhetoric. I think about audience, context, and effect all the time. I know how language persuades and what it takes to build an argument. Even though I use #GenAI almost every day—as a thought partner, as a tool to structure my writing, as a way to pressure-test my own ideas—it still keeps me up at night. And here's the reason why: #AI accelerates production faster than it builds judgment. As someone who taught writing for 15 years—and wrote extensively for 15 years without AI—I know the discomfort of revision. I also know that that discomfort is exactly what builds critical thinking and maturity in writing. AI removes much of that friction, and in business, that's seductive: faster drafts, faster analysis, ultimately, faster output. When production becomes cheap, low-quality work can scale faster than leaders can evaluate it. That's not a problem just for the classroom; it's an enterprise risk. While resistance still (understandably) circulates, to me, the real question is whether organizations are willing to design for judgment as we adopt it. I wrote more about this—and what business leaders should actually be worried about—here: https://lnkd.in/gxQChJcg If you're still skeptical. I understand. If you're all-in, I understand that too. It will take us years—decades even—to understand fully the impact of AI on our worlds and our workplaces. But that doesn’t mean we should wait to act. If you care about how we preserve critical thinking, human agency, and performance as we witness profound technological transformation to our worlds and workplaces, I hope you'll at least join the conversation. content_raw: In 1776 - Adam Smith published “The Wealth of Nations,” which contained his famous analysis of division of labour (including the pin factory example). And in 1791 The father of computer was born an year later Adam smith died. Babbage wasn’t just a mathematician and inventor, He was also an economist who studied industrial organization. In his 1832 book “On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures,” he analyzed how factories divided complex tasks into simple, repetitive operations performed by specialized workers. This study of manufacturing efficiency directly shaped his approach to designing calculating machines which turned into something that today we call “Modern Computers”. ( We know ENIAC was the closest predecessor) Babbage applied division of labour to mechanical computation in his Analytical Engine (designed in the 1830s-1840s) where complex processes of calculations were decomposed into specialised distinct components. Each component had a specific function, just as each worker in a pin factory had one specialized task. This modular architecture became fundamental to computer design. Before Palm Pilots and iPods, PCs and laptops, the term "computer" referred to the people who did scientific calculations by hand. These workers were neither calculating geniuses nor idiot savants but knowledgeable people who, in other circumstances, might have become scientists in their own right. LET’S Circle back to the PRESENT now. The swift uptake and widespread acceptance of Generative AI (GenAI) is significantly re-shaping human cognition, influencing how we engage with information, think, reason, and learn. Human cognition has been historically influenced by the integration of technology into our daily lives, for example, 1.GPS-based navigation affected spatial cognition 2. Search engines impacted memory recall patterns 3. Social media and its move towards increased short-form content has contributed to reduced attention spans More recently, with the advent of GenAI, new cognitive challenges are emerging, particularly in knowledge acquisition, reasoning, learning, creativity, metacognition and critical thinking. But why are we talking about this? Why now? Because it’s NOW or NEVER. Adaptmind

From creating more inclusive housing to transforming the way architects generate design concepts, digital innovation is opening new possibilities for improving quality of life, enhancing creativity, and supporting sustainable development. The paper proposes a framework for integrating intelligent systems—including automated environmental controls, smart monitoring, assistive technologies, and adaptive devices—to improve accessibility, independence, safety, and quality of life. content_raw: Measuring developer productivity by AI token spend is the most expensive mistake engineering leadership can make. Yet tech giants are falling for it. Reports show Nvidia and Meta are tracking "token-maxxing." Meta even built an internal leaderboard to rank employees by consumption. The result is predictable. Engineers are burning API budgets on trivial tasks just to protect their rankings. Now, the bill is due. Uber reportedly burned its entire 2026 AI budget by April. We are replacing "lines of code" with "tokens consumed." It is the exact same management flaw. High token usage does not equal high architecture quality. It usually points to the absence of a critical element: the human in the loop. When you reward raw compute, you incentivize developers to outsource their critical thinking. AI is exceptional at drafting code. But senior-level judgment is required to filter out the noise, optimize context windows, and prevent bloated architecture. True velocity is shipping stable features. Not subsidizing a massive cloud bill for automated churn. How is your engineering org auditing AI spend against actual deployment? Are you keeping a human in the loop, or just paying for compute? #SoftwareEngineering #FinOps #GenAI #TechLeadership

content_raw: Data Centres, Sovereignty and the Quiet Displacement of a Generation Data centres are being sold as engines of digital growth, but the reality is harder. They are capital-heavy, energy-hungry strategic assets, not broad-based job creators. Beyond construction, security and a limited number of specialist technical roles, they create relatively few permanent jobs. The more important issues are sovereignty, power and displacement. As concerns grow over the US CLOUD Act, GDPR and cross-border legal reach, sovereign cloud will become a matter of statecraft, not fashion. At the same time, electricity, grid stability, cooling and water will remain hard constraints for at least the next two decades. Most serious of all, AI will not simply assist the next generation; it will quietly displace many routine cognitive roles. The real divide ahead will be between those who can think, judge and adapt, and those trained only to process tasks. The Mckinsey Article argues that global data centre spending could reach $7 trillion by 2030, driven by AI infrastructure demand. But the real constraint is no longer just capital or land. It is the ability of industrial equipment suppliers to deliver the power, cooling, and mechanical infrastructure fast enough, and in forms that fit next-generation AI architectures. content_raw: AI can generate code in seconds. But what happens when the developer who generated it doesn't fully understand how it works? A feature works. The tests pass. AI may even generate the documentation explaining what the function does. But months later, someone asks: Why was this function created in the first place? Why was it designed this way? What architectural decision does it support? What breaks if we change or remove it? And nobody knows. The original developer may have moved on. The documentation explains what the code does, but not necessarily why it exists. Knowledge transfer becomes difficult because the person who built the system may never have fully understood the decisions behind it either. Multiply that across an application, and the problem becomes bigger than code quality. Architecture slowly becomes harder to understand, systems become harder to change, and technical debt accumulates faster than teams realize. This isn't an argument against AI or vibe coding. AI can be an incredible accelerator. But there is a difference between using AI to move faster because you understand the system and using AI to replace the process of understanding it. For developers, engineering leaders, and executives, the question is bigger than productivity: Are we building software faster than we can understand, maintain, and trust it? My latest article explores this challenge and what it could mean for the future of AI-built engineering teams. content_raw: The AI Training Paradox: Who Is GenAI Actually For in Legal Practice? I recently read coverage of a major legal industry event where Singapore’s Law Minister said 44% of legal tasks can be automated, and senior practitioners described AI freeing them for “high-value work” like critical and strategic thinking. That sounded right. It also sounded like a problem nobody on stage was noticing. So I put the question to an LLM directly. What follows is an edited excerpt. AP: The partners quoted are essentially describing their own experience. But the people best positioned to leverage or utilise AI are senior practitioners — and that’s actually reflected in what they’re saying. The real challenge is at the other end: the interaction between AI and the junior lawyer. LLM: That’s the fault line. A junior doesn’t yet have the substrate to evaluate what AI produces — the pattern recognition, the jurisdictional instinct, the nose for when a proposition is plausible but wrong. Those things are built through repetition: reading cases, tracing arguments, drafting and being corrected. That formative work is precisely what AI automates most efficiently. AP: And firms will deploy AI to maximise junior output. The junior who researches manually in four hours loses, on paper, to the one who generates a memo in twenty minutes — even if the first is building something the second isn’t. LLM: Which creates a circularity nobody is addressing. AI works best for people who already have expertise. Expertise is built by doing work AI now replaces. The people who most need AI as a developmental tool are the least equipped to use it safely. AP: So the solution isn’t restricting access. It’s changing how AI responds to junior users. It needs to stop delivering finished products and start requiring a minimum level of research and analysis before guiding them to the next stage. LLM: That’s Socratic method encoded as system behaviour. The AI becomes a structured interlocutor that requires foundational cognitive work before unlocking the next layer. The junior’s judgment is what’s being built, not bypassed. The architecture exists now. What’s missing is institutional will — a Socratic AI produces less output per hour than an answer machine. AP: It’s not about “digital fluency.” It’s about whether we’re designing AI-assisted practice in a way that still produces competent lawyers at the other end. LLM: Until that question is central to the conversation, we’re building a profession that depends on practitioners trained in a world that no longer exists — and hoping the pipeline sorts itself out. We talk a lot about AI replacing legal work. We don’t talk enough about what happens when it replaces the work that trains lawyers. #LegalTech #AI #FutureOfLaw #LegalProfession … more

content_raw: If you feel like Generative AI is moving faster than your career plan, you’re not alone. The risk is not “AI taking your job” – it’s your role being redesigned around someone else who learns to work *with* AI. The most relevant professionals in the next decade won’t be the ones who know every model architecture. They’ll be the ones who combine **AI fluency** with **distinctly human strengths**: judgment, context, trust, and leadership. Here’s a simple way to stay relevant and keep that balance: - Treat GenAI as your **co‑worker**, not your competitor: offload drafting, summarizing, analysis, and prototyping so you can spend more time on decisions and relationships. - Build **AI literacy, not guru status**: understand capabilities, limits, risks, and how to design useful prompts and workflows for your domain. - Double down on **human skills that AI amplifies but can’t replace**: critical thinking, storytelling, facilitation, and ethical judgment. - Make every project an **AI experiment**: ask “What 20–30% of this work could AI safely handle?” and then redesign your process around that. - Share what you learn: document playbooks, run short internal sessions, and become the person who helps your team use AI responsibly. If you’re mid‑career, your experience is an asset, not a liability. You understand context, trade‑offs, and how your business really works. Pair that with deliberate AI upskilling, and you’re not just “keeping up” – you’re the one shaping how your organization uses Generative AI. content_raw: How does an AI figure out what is "right"? It is a question that matters more each day as we engage GenAI in business decisions. As I indicated in previous articles in this series, I spent time systematically analyzing how Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.5 (and three other leading LLMs) reasons through ethical dilemmas, from the classic Trolley Problem to questions of loyalty versus fairness. With Anthropic’s announcement of their new constitution approach (https://lnkd.in/e5_y2xUq), I thought it would be interesting to share my findings on how to conceptualize the way their current Claude Opus 4.5 model reasons through ethical dilemmas. As indicated before, across the four LLMs I assessed, there was no rigid rulebook. It is more sophisticated: a multi-layered framework that balances outcomes with firm boundaries. Three things stood out for me in analyzing Claude Opus 4.5: 🔹 Hard limits exist. The model won't sacrifice an individual for group benefit when it requires initiating new harm. 🔹 Context shapes method. Different ethical tools for different situations: duty-based rules for rights, care ethics for relationships, Rawlsian justice for policy questions. 🔹 Uncertainty is a feature. The model's “epistemic humility,” or its tendency to flag self-doubt, isn't a weakness; it is a safety mechanism that invites human oversight. For business leaders, understanding this architecture isn't an academic exercise. It directly affects risk management, trust, and how we partner with AI systems. The full analysis is provided in the article below. What ethical considerations do you weigh when deploying AI in your organization? #AIforGood … more

content_raw: Law and higher education have legitimate concerns about what genAI does to critical thinking. The worry is real: students and professionals who outsource reasoning to a tool that flatters them get worse at reasoning over time. But that outcome is a function of how the tool is used, not what the tool is. Used differently, genAI can do the opposite. A worked example. I just used Claude to work through five constitutional amendment proposals on a state ballot. Anyone who has tried to parse Louisiana's amendments knows the deliberation problem: dense interactions between the proposed change, existing constitutional architecture, statutory consequences, and political incentives that the ballot language obscures. The conversation followed a pattern worth noting. I'd state an instinct. Claude would lay out what was actually at stake, identify the load-bearing premise in my reasoning, and push on whether that premise survived scrutiny. When I gave a reason, it offered the strongest counter before letting me commit. When my reasoning aligned with my professional interests, it flagged the alignment and asked me to articulate the case independently. Two things made this work. First, the current generation of frontier models is meaningfully less sycophantic than what came before. The defaults have shifted from agreement toward honest engagement. Second, I run custom instructions designed to push that further: critical posture by default, clarifying questions before answers, no flattery, evidence-based pushback. A useful side effect: Claude identified framings in a "nonpartisan" voter guide that loaded the analysis in subtle ways, including arguments-for that didn't match what the proposal actually did, and arguments-against that named a real concern without naming the strongest version of it. Neutral framing is harder than it looks. The bottleneck in hard deliberation is rarely information. It is structured pressure on your own reasoning. GenAI used well supplies that pressure. The damage-to-critical-thinking story is not wrong about what happens with passive use. It is wrong about what the tool has to be.

content_raw: There is a deeply naive — and frankly lazy — narrative taking hold in software development right now: “Just let GenAI write the code.” In enterprise environments, that mindset is not innovative. It’s reckless. Generative AI does not understand architecture. It does not understand system boundaries, failure domains, data integrity, distributed consistency, or long-term operational cost. It predicts tokens based on probability. That’s it. When you hand over authorship of critical systems to a probabilistic text generator without deeply understanding what it produces, you are not accelerating engineering — you are accelerating entropy. Enterprise software is not a collection of syntactically correct files. It is a web of deliberate tradeoffs: throughput vs. durability, scalability vs. cost, abstraction vs. clarity, velocity vs. maintainability. Those decisions require experience, restraint, and accountability. GenAI owns none of that. It will confidently generate race conditions, subtle security flaws, leaky abstractions, and architectural inconsistencies — and it will do so at machine speed. If you don’t have the expertise to detect those issues, you won’t even know they exist until production teaches you. The hard truth is this: developers who outsource their thinking to AI will eventually be exposed. You cannot fake systems understanding. You cannot bluff your way through debugging distributed failures, memory pressure under load, deadlocks, corrupted state, or data drift in production. AI-assisted coding without deep comprehension creates engineers who can assemble fragments but cannot design systems. And enterprise environments have a way of self-weeding that quickly. GenAI is a powerful tool. Used correctly, it is a force multiplier for engineers who already understand architecture, concurrency, performance boundaries, and operational realities. Used lazily, it becomes a crutch that erodes critical thinking. The market will not reward erosion. It will reward engineers who can wield AI with precision while retaining full authorship and responsibility for their systems. The future does not belong to developers who let AI do their programming. It belongs to engineers who understand what they are building — and use AI as an instrument, not a substitute for discipline. #SoftwareEngineering #Architecture #AI #Leadership #EnterpriseTech … more

content_raw: Your AI policy is probably fine. That's not where the problem is. In May 2026, the House of Commons Education Committee reported that English universities face a real risk of institutional insolvency. What struck me was not the finance. It was where the Committee pointed: governing bodies needing the capability and the culture to challenge senior leadership on forecasts, student numbers, restructuring plans. Read that carefully and it isn't a funding diagnosis. It's a judgment diagnosis. Which makes the timing uncomfortable. The sector is being asked to govern a technology that is reshaping how judgment gets produced, using decision structures that are already producing judgment badly. Most institutional AI work I see is content work — policies, guidance, definitions of acceptable use. It's necessary and there's a lot of it. What's thin is decision architecture: how an institution actually decides, at what speed, with what depth of deliberation. The difference matters, because a policy gap closes by writing a better policy. An architecture gap doesn't close. It compounds. I've written up the argument, including why assessment is the layer that breaks first, and a diagnostic I've set out honestly as judgment rather than measurement. If AI transformation needs a generational commitment, and your governance can't commit beyond the next leadership cycle — what's your theory of change?

content_raw: Extremely excited to share that our paper titled “The Impact of Generative AI on Architectural Design Education: Insights from Hands-on Experience with Architecture Students” has been officially published in the Ain Shams Engineering Journal, a Q1-ranked journal published by Elsevier. This study provides empirical, field-based evidence on how Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) influences architectural design education through a supervised studio experiment conducted at King Fahd University of Petroleum & Minerals (KFUPM). By comparing AI-assisted and non-AI-assisted student groups, the research evaluates the impact of GenAI on creativity, design quality, and time efficiency, revealing notable improvements—particularly a 14% enhancement in design form and aesthetics. The paper also proposes a practical framework for integrating GenAI across different stages of the architectural design process, informed by both student performance and international expert interviews. These insights aim to support educators in adopting AI responsibly while preserving critical thinking, contextual sensitivity, and core design skills. I’m deeply grateful to the research team and all contributors for their collaboration and valuable insights that made this work possible.

content_raw: I spent 5 hours reviewing an AI-generated spec. 8 epics. 27 user stories. Architecture decisions. API design. RBAC. Acceptance criteria. I read everything. Two days later, during implementation, it broke. Epic 3 assumed synchronous REST. Epic 5 depended on event-driven messaging. Same system. Two incompatible assumptions. I had read every line. I still missed it. That's the problem. We have excellent tools for reviewing code. Pull requests, CodeRabbit, Brokk.AI — they highlight hotspots, surface complexity, force critical thinking. But specs are still reviewed like PDFs. AI now generates entire systems: Requirements. Architecture. Tasks. APIs. And the review process is still: Scroll. Read. Nod. Move on. Hope you didn't miss the contradiction between page 8 and page 23. As Advait Sarkar (Microsoft Research) put it: "We've become professional validators of a robot's opinions." So I sketched what a spec review tool could look like. Not a reader. A challenger. → A system view across epics → The same spec, seen through different lenses → And most importantly: provocations Not summaries. Challenges. Contradictions. Blind spots. Missing flows. The kind of things that make you stop and think. The insight is simple: AI shouldn't just help you write specs faster. It should help you question them. This is just a concept. But the problem is real. How do you review AI-generated specs today? content_raw: Time to take accountability for our architecture recommendations, recognising the second-order effects. Publishing the first version of the regenerative architecture principles that have been a collective project for the last few months. Very much aware there are a lot of organisational, cultural and political constraints that often make new approaches hard to realise. But we have to try and nudge and strive to build a better future. Even if we just document the externalities that our organisations are not fully taking responsibility and accountability for, it is a start? Like a log of the technical debt, documenting the fundamentals that we need to address if we want our organisations to have credible long-term futures. To those that say this is too political: If we don't wake up and materially change our systems fundamental constraints will sadly force us to change, science doesn't care about our personal beliefs or positions. Personally I think it's better we try and drive informed change via debate and dialog than continue to sleepwalk into situations and crises that could be managed better if only we discuss and implement different pathways. I also appreciate this is possibly a bit too dense, intellectual and not practical or widely accessible enough. I am hopeful that many of you will start bringing this to life with examples and different pathways. I plan to share more hopeful stories over the coming months that align with this sort of thinking and invite you all to do the same. That said, feedback is always welcomed. Thanks again to so many of you - regulars of Architect Tomorrow and beyond for contributing to this; if nothing else, it's made me realise there are more people out there then you might think that believe we can do better. But it requires us to be engaged and take accountability, be brave and not take the easy path even when it feels like the stampede might crush you (to quote Eddie Obeng). The biggest thank you continues to go to Selena Evans and Darryl Carr for expanding my thinking and introducing me and the community to new (in many cases old!) material and concepts like cybernetics. More to come from me on Ecosystem architecture (one of the principles and something I've been noodling on for a long time) when time allows.

content_raw: “Panic” is not an AI strategy. 😅 (Cartoon by the always-brilliant Tom Fishburne / Marketoonist 👏) Yet “panic” describes how many people approach AI: type a prompt, receive a generic answer, and hold it up as proof that AI is either overhyped or dangerous. Here’s the truth: the greatest threat isn’t AI. It’s our reluctance to invest the time and thinking required to use it effectively. Treat AI like a vending machine—insert a question, receive a standard response, and move on—and generic is exactly what you’ll get. That is the limitation of prompt-only usage. Context engineering changes the relationship. You give AI your objectives, expertise, trusted knowledge, constraints, priorities, and judgment—transforming a general-purpose tool into a personalized AI Thinking Partner. The difference isn’t just the model. It’s the context you invest—and the thinking architecture you build around it. That is why I created YODA (Your Own Digital Assistant): a context-engineering platform and methodology for configuring GenAI into a grounded, critical-thinking partner. Feed YODA your context, and it doesn’t merely answer—it helps you reason. Six Intelligence Disciplines—Sherlock Holmes, Socrates, Jesus, Mr. Spock, Steward, and Aristotle—challenge your thinking, while a council of domain experts brings new perspectives, experience, and constructive disagreement. Make that investment, and YODA helps you: 🚀 Accelerate your development — Learn the questions and decision factors that experienced practitioners use to master a new domain. 🧠 Amplify your expertise — Apply disciplined questioning, empathy, logic, stewardship, diagnosis, and evidence-based reasoning to every decision. 💡 Unleash your creativity — Convene expert perspectives that challenge one another and surface ideas, opportunities, and use cases you might never reach alone. content_raw: ​ THE PILLAR OF TRUST: BUILDING A RELIABLE DATA FOUNDATION FOR GenAI Moving along the architecture flow from my last post, we’ve ingested and processed our data. Now we hit the absolute critical success factor for enterprise AI: the Trusted Data Foundation. Building powerful LLMs is exciting, but unless the data powering them is accurate, accessible, and governed, your GenAI applications will face significant risks. I believe trust is the ultimate currency of successful modern AI systems. We often focus on model accuracy, but we must focus on data fidelity. We need a foundation built on trust. Here’s a detailed breakdown of the five critical pillars of a Trusted Data Foundation for GenAI: ​ Data Quality: The data must be reliable, complete, and current. GenAI cannot distinguish between a typo and a truth. If your inventory numbers are wrong, the GenAI answer will be wrong. We need continuous quality monitoring and healing. ​ Data Governance: You need policy-driven controls. Who has access? Is PII protected? Are data sovereignty rules met? Robust governance ensures that AI uses the right data, in the right way, for the right purpose, with clear ownership. ​ Metadata Management: This is data about the data. LLMs thrive on it. To perform effective semantic search and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the system must understand the schema, lineage, description, and tags associated with every piece of content. ​ Data Accessibility & Discovery: Your data is only as good as a model's ability to find it. Creating a single, discoverable catalog where your AI agents can find vectorized documents, API schemas, and historical records is crucial. It converts "hidden tribal knowledge" into accessible context. ​ Business Context: This is the bridge. Raw data needs corporate semantics. Is this dynamic pricing based on current market or historical average? Does "customer" mean active or total? Injecting and managing this corporate logic is essential to make AI answers relevant. ​Thinking of your foundation as "just a database" is a critical error. Thinking of it as a governed, high-fidelity knowledge base that provides semantic clarity is the key. How are you ensuring your data foundation is trusted enough to power user-facing AI? ​#GenerativeAI #DataEngineering #DataArchitecture #DataStrategy #DataFoundation #DataGovernance #DataQuality #ContinuousLearning #RAG

content_raw: Architecting the Future: The Architectural Evolution and ROI of Kubernetes 14 years ago, Google open sourced the architectural blueprints of Borg as Kubernetes. It did not just win the container orchestration wars; it fundamentally rewrote the unit economics of enterprise cloud infrastructure. For CTOs and Platform Architects, K8s is no longer an engineering line item. It is the definitive cloud operating system. Understanding its architectural evolution is critical to building resilient, scalable, and cost-efficient platform strategies today. Paradigm 1: Declarative State & Micro-Scheduling (2014–16) · The Architecture: Shifted infrastructure from imperative scripting to a continuous Reconciliation Loop. Introduction of the Pod as the atomic scheduling unit. · The Executive Impact: Mitigated configuration drift. Infrastructure became self-healing by design, significantly reducing operational downtime and manual system administration overhead. Paradigm 2: Extensibility via CRDs & Control Plane Dominance (2017–19) · The Architecture: The standardization of CRD and the Operator Pattern. decoupled the control plane from the core codebase. · The Executive Impact: K8s transformed from a container scheduler into a universal API engine. Platform teams could now manage databases, service meshes and cloud infrastructure natively. Paradigm 3: Multi-Cluster Topology & Ephemeral Autoscaling (2020–23) · The Architecture: The evolution of Cluster API for multi-tenant provisioning, combined with event driven autoscaling and just-in-time node provisioning , replacing legacy Cluster Autoscale limitations. · The Executive Impact: Solved the single blast radius risk. Enabled true multi-cloud, hybrid-cloud, and edge deployment strategies while radically optimizing cloud spend through intelligent, rapid bin-packing. Paradigm 4: Platform Engineering & Dynamic GPU Orchestration (2024–Present) · The Architecture: High-density workload abstraction via Internal Developer Platforms and specialized scheduling frameworks (Kueue, Volcano) designed for non-homogeneous hardware topologies (Nvidia H100s/B200s). · The Executive Impact: Solved developer cognitive overload by abstracting the K8s API into guardrailed developer portals. Simultaneously, it optimized CapEx/OpEx for Generative AI by maximizing expensive GPU utilization through advanced batch scheduling and fractional slicing. Strategy Takeaway Kubernetes did not succeed because it was a flawless product; it succeeded because it is an extensible platform for building enterprise platforms. If your platform engineering team is still exposing raw YAML and kubectl access to product developers, you are accruing massive cognitive debt. The modern K8s strategy requires abstracting the infrastructure layer away from developers while hardening the control plane to drive multi-tenant efficiency and AI workload readiness. #Kubernetes #PlatformEngineering #CloudArchitecture #CTO #DevOps #AIInfrastructure #CloudEconomics … more

content_raw: Since coding is becoming increasingly commoditized with Generative AI and prompt engineering & vibe coding, the center of gravity in Software Engineering and Information Systems life cycle is gradually shifting. Not away from engineering - but toward a discipline that was always foundational, yet often undervalued in practice : Requirements Engineering. We may be witnessing an expansion of Requirements Engineering into a family of specialized disciplines, each addressing a different dimension of modern socio-technical systems: 1- System Requirements Engineering 2- Architecture Requirements Engineering 3- Data Requirements Engineering 4- Data Management Requirements Engineering 5- Data & AI Governance Requirements Engineering 6- UX Requirements Engineering 7- Cybersecurity Requirements Engineering 8- Infrastructure Requirements Engineering 9- AI Requirements Engineering 10- DevOps Requirements Engineering (including CI/CD requirements) 11- Compliance Requirements Engineering 12- Viability / Financial / Economic Requirements Engineering. Rather than a single homogeneous activity, Requirements Engineering increasingly appears as a multi-layered discipline, structured around three complementary planes: I- Structural Layer : Architecture, Data, Infrastructure requirements II- Cross-functional Layer : UX, AI, DevOps requirements III- Control & Governance Layer : Cybersecurity, Ethics/Regulation/Business Compliance, Quality/Risk/Performance/Resources/etc. Governance, Viability requirements In this view, modern systems are no longer “built” in a linear sense - they are specified, constrained, and continuously shaped across multiple interacting requirement domains. This shift has important implications for Software Engineering practice. The role of software engineers is progressively evolving : from primarily writing code and building systems from scratch, toward specifying, designing, architecting, orchestrating, validating, and governing complex, safe, secure, compliant, desirable, and economically viable software & AI systems. In #System #engineering, #Coding is not disappearing, but it is no longer the central bottleneck. content_raw: Developing an application has become an educational exercise in many cases. This is the thought occurred to me after we were introduced the concept of Transformers. Transformers are industrialized, homogenized Large Language Models (LLMs) designed for parallel computing. A transformer model can carry out a wide range of tasks with no fine-tuning. Transformers can perform self- supervised learning on billions of records of raw unlabeled data with billions of parameters. From these billion-parameter models emerged multimodal architectures that can process text, images, audio, and videos. ChatGPT popularized the usage of transformer architectures that have become general-purpose technologies like printing, electricity, and computers. Applications are burgeoning everywhere! Google Cloud AI, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, OpenAI, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Google Colab Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Hugging Face, Meta, and myriad other offers are emerging. The functionality of transformer models has pervaded every aspect of our workspaces with Generative AI for text, Generative AI for images, discriminative AI, task specific-models, unsupervised learning, supervised learning, prompt design, prompt engineering, text-to-code, code-to-text, and more. Sometimes, a GPT-like model will encompass all these concepts! The societal impact is tremendous. A project manager can now go to OpenAI’s cloud platform, sign up, obtain an API key, and get to work in a few minutes. Users can then enter a text, specify the NLP task as Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, and obtain a response created by a Google Vertex AI or a ChatGPT transformer model. Finally, users can go to Google’s Gen App Builder and build applications without programming or machine learning knowledge. The numbers are dizzying. Bommasani et al. (2023) created a Foundation Model ecosystem that lists 128 Foundation Models 70 applications, and 64 datasets. The paper also mentions Hugging Face’s 150,000+ models and 20,000+ datasets! The list is growing weekly and will spread to every activity in society. Where does that leave an AI professional or someone wanting to be one? Should a project manager choose to work locally? Or should the implementation be done directly on Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, or AWS? Should a development team select Hugging Face, Google Trax, OpenAI, or AllenNLP? Should an AI professional use an API with practically no AI development? Should an end-user build a no-code AI application with no ML knowledge with Google’s Gen App Builder? The answer is yes to all of the above! You do not know what a future employer, customer, or user may want or specify. Therefore, you must be ready to adapt to any need that comes up at the dataset, model, and application levels. … more
