content_raw: Last week, I presented an introduction to AI, design thinking, rendering, reality capture, automation, and future spatial workflows to the team Klein Concepts. One of the core ideas explored was this: AI does not truly “know” reality. It knows humanity’s recorded patterns of reality. In that sense, AI becomes a statistical mirror of civilisation’s accumulated creativity, language, imagery, systems, and behaviour. For designers, I believe this becomes incredibly important to understand because design itself sits at the intersection of: - physical reality - psychology - culture - narrative - economics and sensory experience An LLM can infer relationships between those things, but it does not inhabit them. The conversation around AI is becoming far more interesting than simply: “ What tools can it use?” It is increasingly becoming a conversation around: - authorship - discernment - systems - creativity and the evolving role of human beings inside creative work. https://lnkd.in/dKPp8ipR #AI #DesignThinking #Architecture #Creativity #ArtificialIntelligence #SystemsThinking #FutureOfDesign

content_raw: Artificial Intelligence is rapidly entering the Architecture & Construction (A&C) industry. The image in this post was generated using AI rendering to illustrate a countryside cottage concept that blends traditional architecture with modern glazing. AI tools can accelerate visualisation and help explore ideas quickly. However, they also introduce important questions about intellectual property and originality. Because AI models are trained on large datasets of existing images, generated results may sometimes resemble previous works without clear attribution. This creates a potential risk of unintentional plagiarism, especially when AI-generated visuals are presented as original architectural designs. Another growing concern is the unfair use of AI in the A&C industry today, where speculative AI renderings are sometimes presented as real projects, bypassing the creative effort and professional expertise of architects and designers. AI should support creativity—not replace authorship or professional integrity. Transparency note: this post and the accompanying image were created with the assistance of AI. Whats your opinion ?

content_raw: At Arcadis, we’re constantly exploring how AI can augment design thinking, not replace it. We've been applying from early massing studies to experiential renderings and narrative-driven animations. In practice, AI is becoming an essential part of our creative toolkit in helping us iterate faster, communicate better, and stay focused on the user experience. That same mindset is shaping how I teach in the design studio at University of Texas at Arlington College of Architecture, Planning and Public Affairs. This semester, my students aren’t just generating random AI images. They’re learning how to apply AI tools in the same way we do in the office as a way to bring their own research, site logic, and architectural intent to life. Each team began with a deep dive into site, culture, and precedent. From those studies, they developed their own massing strategies, spatial logics, and organizational frameworks. content_raw: Zaha Hadid may be gone, but her style is still loved in the AI world. I am a strong believer in technology. Till the time we are using AI to generate rendered images, it is fine. But the moment it becomes a primary source of interior or architecture design thinking, I always wonder — will it affect our original design thought process? Maybe ? The latest news that made me think is this :— Kapwing, an online video creation and editing platform that leverages AI for content production, has released a study. They analysed about 4.9 million prompts used on AI image‑generation tools like Midjourney, and looked at how often certain names (artists, architects, directors) appeared in those prompts. Interestingly, the most‑prompted architect was Zaha Hadid (her name appeared in around 63K prompts). Broadly, users often write prompts like: “in the style of Zaha Hadid” — hoping to get images that look like her iconic, fluid, futuristic designs. Zaha’s work has become the default visual language for imaginative architecture in AI. Though it’s a testament to her legacy, it’s also a reflection of how AI is shaping style in the design world. This leaves a question in my head — If AI can replicate a style with just a name, what happens to the process of discovering our own strengths and style over time? Anyway, it made me think. For those unfamiliar with Zaha Hadid: She was one of the most celebrated architects of our time — the first woman to win the Pritzker Architecture Prize (equivalent to Oscar of the #architecture world) . Her signature fluid, curving forms reshaped modern architecture, from the London Aquatics Centre to the Guangzhou Opera House. Image Credit: Zaha - hadid dot com

content_raw: AI, AI, AI... it’s everywhere now. As developers, adopting AI tools in our daily workflow is becoming standard practice. Some people still argue that AI should not be used to write code. I am not here to argue. But one thing is clear: 👉 AI is only as good as the developer using it. If you do not have solid architectural knowledge, clear thinking, and the ability to review what AI generates, then AI will not make you better. If you cannot design systems, review code, or question outputs, AI will expose your weaknesses, not hide them. So no, the real skill is not just "using AI tools". The real skill is knowing: - what to ask - how to ask - what to trust - what to reject Here is a simple checklist I follow when working with AI-assisted development: - Clearly define project requirements and plan features upfront - Design your database based on real requirements - Optimize prompts to reduce unnecessary token usage - Build reusable code or components instead of repeating logic - Create a clean and scalable folder structure - Follow a standard project architecture - Always do proper QA and testing before deployment - Use AI not just for coding, but also for code review and refactoring AI will not replace developers. But developers who use AI well will outperform those who do not. The gap is growing fast. The choice is yours. 😊

Organizations begin by assessing their current state—identifying technical debt, mapping dependencies, and evaluating performance, security, and compliance gaps. Modernization efforts are tied to business objectives, ensuring that improvements enhance agility, efficiency, and resilience rather than just replacing outdated technology. By establishing a clear roadmap and governance framework, businesses lay the foundation for a comprehensive transformation Modernization encompasses infrastructure, applications, and data. Legacy systems are migrated to cloud environments—public, private, or hybrid—leveraging containerization, microservices, and orchestration platforms to enable scalability and high availability. Monolithic applications are refactored, APIs standardized, and CI/CD pipelines introduced for automated testing and deployment. Infrastructure improvements include disaster recovery, auto-scaling, and cloud-native storage, while security is integrated throughout using zero-trust frameworks, encryption, and compliance practices Data modernization is central to this evolution. Fragmented datasets are unified into modern platforms, cloud-native warehouses or lakehouses deployed, and streaming pipelines implemented for real-time analytics and AI/ML insights. Governance, quality, and lineage practices ensure reliable and actionable information, while self-service analytics empower teams to make faster, informed decisions. Predictive insights and intelligent automation further enhance operational efficiency and strategic agility. Cultural and process improvements complete the renaissance Cloud modernization transforms infrastructure and applications by migrating workloads to public, private, or hybrid clouds, adopting containerization, microservices, and serverless platforms. Teams adopt continuous learning, experimentation, and ownership, embedding modernization into the organization’s DNA. content_raw: AI is not replacing programming. It is replacing bad programming practices. The more time I spend understanding LLMs, machine learning, and how models actually work, the more convinced I am that much of the public discussion is framed poorly. LLMs and ML are not a wholesale replacement for software engineering. They are a replacement for a specific category of work that was always painful to solve with hardcoded logic: • pattern recognition • fuzzy classification • ranking • language understanding • anomaly detection • extraction from messy inputs That work often ended up buried inside brittle code: • giant if/else trees • regex-heavy logic • exception handling on top of exception handling • endless manual tuning of rules that never generalized well We called all of that “engineering.” A lot of the time, it was just expensive suffering. Classical software engineering is still the correct tool for: • deterministic workflows • transactions • permissions • auditability • compliance logic • state transitions • systems where correctness must be explicit, and failure must be explainable But some problems are simply better learned from data than forced through rigid rules. That is the real shift. Not “AI instead of software.” Not “models replace engineers.” The real future is hybrid systems: • deterministic software where control matters • learned systems where pattern recognition matters And I think many teams are still missing that distinction. They are either trying to force AI into places where deterministic logic should remain in control, or they are still hardcoding their way through problems that are much better treated as learning problems. That is not just a technical mistake. It is an architectural mistake. The strongest products over the next few years will not be built by teams that shout “AI” the loudest. They will be built by teams that know exactly where code should stay deterministic, where models should be introduced, and how to make both work together without breaking reliability. That is where I think the real engineering opportunity is.

content_raw: Across today’s cybersecurity landscape, attackers evolve faster than organisations can standardise behaviour. Tools improve, detections improve — but one problem remains unchanged: Security policies define what should happen. Systems decide what actually happens. This gap between policy and execution is the source of: drift across cloud and hybrid environments, inconsistent enforcement, unpredictable system behaviour, gaps in auditability, and high operational cost for verification and remediation. A new architectural approach challenges this gap directly: a deterministic order layer that doesn’t replace existing security tools but defines how every system is allowed to behave — and enforces it reproducibly. For cybersecurity professionals, this creates a fundamental shift: 👉 Policies become guaranteed, not interpreted. 👉 Execution becomes consistent across all environments. 👉 Behaviour becomes provable, not assumed. 👉 Authority stays with the operator — not the platform. This has implications across: identity & access enforcement, cloud and multi-cloud security, AI behaviour and auditability, zero trust architectures, OT and critical infrastructure, incident response, and security governance. It is not a new tool — it is a change in how digital systems must behave when rules are no longer optional. content_raw: Most architecture programs fail at the same point. Not during design. Not during build. During delivery, when the first exception is approved, nobody writes it down. Frameworks don't drift. Teams do. Every program starts with the right intentions. Boundary definitions. Integration standards. Platform ownership guidelines. The documentation is thorough. The principles are sound. And then a deadline moves. A direct callout gets approved as a one-time exception. Then another. Then fourteen. None of them appears in the architecture diagram. Two are in production flows that nobody on the current team wrote. One is calling a system that was decommissioned — still firing, silently failing, swallowed by a catch block someone added to "handle the timeout issue." No single decision caused this. Each one was locally rational. There was no forum with the authority and the cadence to hold the line. That is not a technology problem. That is a Design Authority gap. Design Authority is often misunderstood. It is not a committee. It is not a delivery gate. It is not a code review board. It is the organizational mechanism that converts architectural principles into enforceable decisions — and maintains those decisions over time, under delivery pressure, across team and vendor boundaries. The difference between an Architecture Review Board and a Design Authority is not structural. It is consequential. A forum without decision rights is a meeting. A forum with decision rights is governance. Three questions worth bringing to your next program review: Is there a named forum with the authority to enforce the architectural decisions this program is making — or are those decisions documented without a governance mechanism to uphold them? When an exception is approved, is it recorded as a formal decision with a named owner, or does it disappear into delivery history, creating a precedent nobody can trace? If this program ends tomorrow and a new team inherits the platform, can they reconstruct the architectural intent — or will they discover the principles by finding the places where they were violated? If any of these produces hesitation, the Design Authority gap is already open. A framework tells you where the boundaries should be. Design Authority is what keeps them there. Governance without a forum is just a document waiting to be ignored. I explore the full Design Authority framework — including the Three Lines model, the tiered review approach, the ADR as governance artifact, and what it must evolve to handle for agentic AI systems — in this week's Architecture Thinking This builds on my earlier Salesforce Ben piece on why Design Authority is crucial in Salesforce architecture. #ArchitectureThinking #EnterpriseArchitecture #DesignAuthority #ITGovernance #TechnologyLeadership #ResponsibleAI #RiskGovernance

content_raw: The hardest part of an IBM i change is not always making the change. It is knowing what else the change affects. A field changes. A file layout changes. A report is retired. A SQL statement replaces record-level access. An interface value gets cleaned up. The code change may be small. The impact may not be. That is where I think AI can help IBM i teams first. Not by replacing RPG developers. Not by skipping review. Not by generating code and hoping the test cycle catches the risk. AI can help create a better first-pass impact analysis. It can help surface related programs, files, reports, SQL, interfaces, dayend processes, client-specific exceptions, and test areas. But the team still has to validate the business context. A source search may show where a field is used. It may not show why the business depends on it. That is the gap this article is about. In the article, I walk through why impact analysis may be one of the best first AI use cases for IBM i teams, including: Why small changes can carry large risk How status codes become contracts Why some reports are really controls How interfaces expose hidden assumptions Where AI can help without owning the decision A practical AI-assisted impact analysis workflow The core point: AI can surface possible impact. The team still owns confirmed impact.

content_raw: Beyond AI: Streamlining Data Integration to Accelerate Drug Development Although much of the industry narrative focuses on how AI can shorten drug development timelines, operational bottlenecks often occur earlier in the process, due to fragmented data ingestion, inconsistent standards and the delayed availability of analysis-ready datasets. In clinical development environments that are subject to standards such as CDISC, as well as regulatory expectations from agencies such as the FDA, EMA etc. the speed at which insights can be obtained is limited by how quickly structured data becomes available. AI can only operate on clean, harmonized, traceable data. Therefore, the real accelerator is a robust, unified, governed data infrastructure. The industry narrative suggests AI will compress timelines, reduce costs, and transform R&D productivity. Yet in practice, most organizations struggle long before machine learning models are deployed. This article addresses five critical questions: 1. Is a Unified Data System Achievable from EHR to EDC? 2. Building a Future-Ready Pipeline: Avoiding Perpetual Redesign 3. Data Governance for Optimal Data Delivery 4. content_raw: I wrote this week’s RPG Blend article for the GA of IBM Bob Premium Package for i. The article is not really about AI writing more code. It is about what changes when AI gets closer to the actual IBM i system. The source members. The database. The compile. The tests. The constraints. The security model. The architecture decisions nobody documented. For IBM i teams, that matters. Generic AI can explain RPG. It can sometimes convert fixed-form to free-form. It can generate SQL that looks reasonable. But IBM i modernization is not just syntax cleanup. It is understanding how the system actually works. Which program updates the table? Which job runs overnight? Which service program owns the business rule? Which relationship is enforced in DB2? Which one only lives in RPG? Which test proves the behavior still works? That is why I think this GA is worth paying attention to. The article covers native IBM i connectivity, IBM i Developer Mode, IBM i Database Mode, RPG modernization support, database visibility, ERD generation, indexing review, security review, source-member workflows, compile and test cycles, RPGUnit test planning, RPGUnit implementation, documentation, and knowledge capture. But the main point is simpler than the feature list. AI exposes problems. Leaders solve them. If Bob generates an ERD, people still need to review it. If Bob recommends an index, the DBA still needs to validate it. If Bob modernizes RPG, the team still needs compile proof, test proof, and code review. If Bob creates RPGUnit tests, the team still needs to decide whether those tests prove the right behavior. AI does not remove accountability. It increases the need for it. That is where this gets interesting for IBM i teams. #IBMi #RPGLE #IBMBob #AI #Modernization #RPGUnit #SoftwareArchitecture #EngineeringLeadership

content_raw: Three days after Anthropic launched Fable 5 and Mythos 5, the US government ordered them pulled from global access. Not a contract dispute. Not a policy disagreement. Export controls. Applied to a commercial AI model. Within 72 hours of launch. This is the story most people are missing. Earlier this year, the Trump administration banned Anthropic from all federal contracts after Anthropic refused to allow its technology to be used for mass domestic surveillance and autonomous weapons systems. A federal court ruled the government's response was punitive, not a national security decision. The Pentagon replaced Anthropic with OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft. The AI company that drew the hardest ethical lines got removed from the table. The ones that raised fewer objections became preferred government vendors. That is a market signal, not a security strategy. Now add what happened this week. The Commerce Department ordered Anthropic to disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all foreign users globally, citing a reported jailbreak. Anthropic complied, and noted publicly that if this standard applied across the industry, it would halt every new frontier model deployment from every US provider. Read that carefully. The US government just demonstrated it can reach into a commercial AI company and shut off their best products globally. On short notice. With no recourse for the users affected. At the same time: Elon Musk finalized the SpaceX and xAI merger, unveiled an orbital AI data center satellite, and announced a chip fabrication facility targeting one terawatt of annual compute capacity. He is not building another model. He is moving to own the infrastructure layer beneath all of them. And Chinese models, specifically DeepSeek AI V4, now trail US frontier capability by three to six months, down from a gap that was measured in years. Every international user who lost access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 this week had to look somewhere else. Chinese providers are the obvious alternative. Nine days ago, Prime Minister Mark Carney launched "AI for All," a national AI strategy built explicitly around reducing reliance on US technology, building sovereign compute infrastructure, and treating data as a national strategic asset. The Fable 5/ Mythos 5 halt happened the week after that strategy published. Canadian users who lost access to those models this week received a live, operational demonstration of the exact sovereignty risk the strategy was designed to address. Access to AI infrastructure can be revoked by the policy decisions of another country. With no warning. No appeal. No alternative. This is not a story about one company. It is a story about who controls the architecture of AI globally, who is building independence from that architecture, and what happens to US AI leadership when the government simultaneously restricts its best models internationally while Chinese alternatives get cheaper and better every quarter. content_raw: In my previous article, I discussed how Spec-Driven Development facilitated speed without chaos in AI projects. However, I did not delve into AX — Agentic Experience. AX differs from UX. It focuses on the experience of collaborating with AI agents as first-class partners, examining their predictability, long-term alignment, and safe operation within a production codebase. In this follow-up, I detail the evolution of my open-source project through actual releases (v1.0.x → v1.2.0), highlighting how governance, structure, and tooling discipline have shifted AI collaboration from "AI helps sometimes" to "AI operates reliably by default." This transformation was not theoretical; it was implemented release-by-release, enforced in CI, documented in constitutional governance, and tested under real constraints. Key takeaways include: - Unmanaged AX leads to entropy rather than leverage. - Guardrails, ADRs, and CI gates create effective feedback loops. - Machine-readable governance is superior to prompt engineering. - Enumerated invariants and tool-specific adapters promote cross-tool consistency. - There is a significant difference between "helpful AI" and "governed agents." The central insight is that AI-first engineering will hinge on Agentic Experience, not merely model quality. A sophisticated model is ineffective if it generates unpredictable outputs, breaches architectural constraints, or demands constant oversight. AX hardening addresses these issues at the system level rather than the prompt level. For those integrating AI into their engineering practices, my guidance is clear: - Do not begin with prompts. - Start with specifications. - Establish rules. - Implement governance. View agents as powerful yet fallible collaborators — fast, capable, and potentially hazardous without appropriate guardrails. What has been your experience with AI-assisted development? content_raw: Scaling AI coding agents exposes a grand challenge in agentic software delivery: LLMs are probabilistic, but your enterprise business logic is deterministic. When agents hallucinate domain rules or UX flows, relying on human code reviews, or worse, another LLM, to catch the semantic drift just moves your delivery bottleneck to the PR reviews. By applying Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) principles and practice, we can force agents to output their intent into a strict Domain-Specific Language (DSL) before they generate any implementation code. This allows to fundamentally "shift-left" validation in agentic software delivery workflows: ✅ Semantic Linting: Catch architectural and business logic violations computationally during specification creation, not during a peer review. ✅ Token Efficiency: Stop LLMs from wasting compute generating invalid implementations. ✅ Deterministic Guardrails: Replace slow, ambiguous "LLM-as-a-judge" workflows with mathematically enforceable tracks. In the era of AI-generated code, your developers shouldn't be writing the implementation. They should be writing the spec, designing the intent, and engineering the harness. I wrote about how to build deterministic AIDLC workflows by truly making the Spec your Harness.

content_raw: After two full years of working with AI coding assistants like Cursor and Claude Code, using their most capable models daily, I've come to one conclusion: AI is nowhere near replacing software engineers/Devs. The reason is simple: even the strongest models can't solve every problem correctly. They still hallucinate, lose context in complex codebases, make incorrect architectural decisions, and often require human intervention to debug, validate, and complete the work. AI has become an incredibly powerful productivity tool, but it's still a tool, not a replacement for engineering judgment, experience, and problem-solving. The narrative that "AI will take all our jobs" is far more hype than reality. The human ability to reason, understand context, and make sound technical decisions remains indispensable. Companies that rush to replace experienced engineers/Devs with AI because of the current hype are likely to discover the hidden costs later: unreliable outputs, growing technical debt, endless validation, context limitations, token and rate-limit constraints, and a loss of real engineering expertise. AI can accelerate development, but it cannot own responsibility, make critical decisions, or replace deep domain knowledge. AI is too powerful, but It’s not even close to what a human is capable of doing. EDIT: Comments like « Ah, you probably use it the wrong way » won’t be answered! Out of context and not the goal of this post. However, I am not the kind of person who pays for Claude Code, Cursor or whatever Sub and start smashing the keyboard right away asking to fix this and that! There are rules and guidelines to follow, advanced configs, best practices etc.. but still even with that, the LLM itself will make mistakes, and will lose track, especially in big and complex projects. I had to migrate a whole backend from ExpressJs/ MongoDb to NestJs/Supabase, a medium sized one, and still not capable of doing it perfectly even with all the guidelines, implementation plans, and the advanced configs, still far from taking a human’s job. But thanks to AI, our productivity is now x10000 boosted. However by the years 2030-2035 this post will probably make no more sense when AI reaches full maturity.

content_raw: A $12,000 monthly bill didn’t vanish because of a hack. It vanished because a server rebooted in the wrong order. The data was safe. The storage was intact. But the application layer lost its map. For a CEO, this isn’t a "Kubernetes issue." It’s a revenue leak. It’s a breach of trust with users expecting instant answers from your AI agents. We recently fixed this for a growth-stage startup aiming for sub-100ms search. Goal: Zero downtime. No exceptions. The fix wasn’t more code. It was "sticky identities." Most cloud setups treat servers like cattle. If one dies, replace it. That works for web servers. It fails for databases. When a database node restarts with a new address, the cluster doesn’t recognize it. Consensus breaks. Queries fail. Your AI goes silent. We used Kubernetes StatefulSets to fix this. Think of it like this: Standard Deployment = An employee comes back from lunch to a new desk with a new name tag. Colleagues don’t recognize them. Handoffs fail. StatefulSet = An employee returns to the same desk, same name tag, same files. Work continues. This stability changes the P&L: 🔹 Automated recovery in minutes, not hours 🔹 ~40% cost reduction vs. fully managed services 🔹 Consistent low-latency responses for users You don’t need to write YAML. But you do need to ask your engineering lead: "If a database node fails right now, does it recover automatically?" If the answer involves someone logging in at 2 AM, you have a risk to mitigate. Reliability isn’t a feature you add later. It’s an architectural choice you make on day one. What’s the most expensive "silent failure" your infrastructure has caused? #Madgical #CloudArchitecture #AIInfrastructure #DevOps

content_raw: A multi-cloud architecture can look surprisingly simple on a diagram. Add two or three cloud-provider logos, connect them with a few lines, and the organisation appears to have achieved flexibility, resilience and freedom of choice. The operational reality is far more complex. Each cloud brings its own identity model, networking constructs, pricing, managed services, support model and areas of strength. Without a common operating approach, multi-cloud can easily become multiple versions of the same complexity. Through the cloud journeys I have been part of, one principle has become increasingly clear: Begin with the workload, not the cloud logo. Understand the application’s business, technical, operational, commercial and risk requirements. Then decide where it fits best. Some foundations should remain consistent across providers: • Identity and access governance • Networking and security principles • Infrastructure as Code practices • Observability and incident management • FinOps and cost visibility • Application ownership and lifecycle controls The implementation may differ, and that is not necessarily a problem. The objective should not be to make every cloud identical. It should be to standardise where consistency reduces friction and allow cloud-specific capabilities to differ where they create genuine value. In this article, I share a few lessons from working through cloud migrations, licensing decisions, architectural constraints, FinOps and the evolving role of platform engineering. The more useful question may not be: “Are we multi-cloud?” It may be: “Do we have the operating model required to make multiple clouds work as one organisational capability?” I would be interested to hear how others are approaching this balance. What have you standardised across cloud environments, and what have you deliberately allowed to remain different? #MultiCloud #CloudArchitecture #PlatformEngineering #FinOps #CloudStrategy

content_raw: The landscape of software development has transformed dramatically in recent months. With AI compressing implementation, engineers can now design, code, test, and refactor in a single focused session, leading to increased individual velocity. However, this shift brings challenges; as implementation becomes cheaper and more private, system coherence can become fragile. AI has the potential to generate complexity that may not be fully understood. While local speed increases, so does system risk. If we fail to adapt, we risk creating cognitive and architectural silos rather than traditional ones, resulting in: - Different patterns solving the same problem - Diverging contracts - Isolated decision-making - Knowledge that remains private instead of compounding This approach may work initially, but integration pain will inevitably arise. Many of our engineering rituals were designed to coordinate execution, but execution is no longer the bottleneck—alignment is. To adapt, we need to focus on: - Syncs centered on decisions that impact others, rather than mere task updates - Weekly reviews of architecture and complexity - Explicit and discussable AI usage - Measuring system health instead of ticket throughput This is not about adding more processes; it's about replacing low-signal ceremonies with meaningful alignment. As AI accelerates individual performance, the importance of shared system thinking grows. How are you adapting your engineering practices?

We keep making the same mistake — just with a new actor each time. 🔹 We over-trusted networks because something was "inside." 🔹 We over-trusted users after they authenticated. 🔹 We over-trusted workloads with too much east-west traffic. And now we're about to do it again with AI agents — trusting them because they're internal, because they carry valid credentials, because IT created them, because they're "just automation." That's exactly how implicit trust returns. Only this time, at machine speed. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ AI agents aren't tools. They're 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆. They call APIs, query databases, modify configurations, trigger workflows. It fails because of data—and more specifically, poor 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 (𝗜𝗔) There is enormous momentum behind AI initiatives right now, particularly GenAI. Organizations are racing to deploy new tools, platforms, and copilots in the hope of unlocking transformational value. Yet many of these efforts are already producing disappointing or inconsistent results. The root cause is rarely the technology. AI is only as good as the information architecture beneath it. If your data is fragmented, poorly governed, inconsistently defined, or disconnected from real workflows, AI will simply amplify those weaknesses—𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲. Common patterns I see repeatedly: • Siloed data sources with no shared semantic model • Inconsistent data definitions across systems and departments • Weak master data management and identity resolution • Limited lineage, provenance, and data quality controls • Governance frameworks that exist on paper but not in practice Layering AI on top of this foundation doesn’t create intelligence—it creates noise with confidence. The downstream impact is predictable: • Unreliable outputs that erode user trust • Increased operational risk and compliance exposure • Wasted time and capital chasing “model tuning” instead of fixing root causes • A growing narrative that “AI doesn’t work here” When, in reality, the data was never ready. Information architecture is not a legacy concern—it is a strategic prerequisite. Clear data models, strong governance, lifecycle management, and alignment to business and clinical workflows are what enable AI to be trusted, explainable, and operationally useful. Until organizations invest seriously in their data foundations, AI initiatives will continue to underperform—not because AI is overhyped, but because the groundwork was skipped. content_raw: Boris Cherny, the creator of Claude Code, has not manually written a line of code since November 2025. Spotify's best developers stopped writing code by hand a month later. Most of the industry is celebrating this as productivity. Almost nobody is asking what happens to diagnostic skill — the ability to debug an unfamiliar failure mode, reason about an architectural trade-off a model cannot see, or take accountability for production code — over five years of agent-first development. If you are leading a consulting practice, a delivery organization, or any business whose margin rests on certified, billable engineering expertise, this is the question worth losing sleep over. The mitigation is not to reject AI tooling. It is to instrument it before the craft atrophies. content_raw: A national data architecture is not a platform. It's the thing that makes platforms replaceable. NHS England leadership recently said what the interoperability community has been arguing for years: you cannot solve a foundational architectural challenge by procuring another system on top of the last one. Right diagnosis. Hard execution. Here's what "data as national infrastructure" actually requires in practice: 👉🏼 Persistent identifiers governed independently of any supplier 👉🏼 Canonical clinical models maintained outside the systems that consume them 👉🏼 Stewardship roles with real authority over semantic consistency — not just access control 👉🏼 Architectural assurance that survives the next procurement cycle The article by Tito Castillo (FBCS CITP CHCIO) correctly identifies the openEHR International / #FHIR separation as the technical pattern that makes this possible. Persistence layer governing meaning. Exchange layer moving it. Different layers. Different governance. But technical patterns without governance are vocabulary without an editor. I've worked on regional digital health ecosystems where the architecture was sound and the governance layer was three people with competing mandates and no authority to enforce semantic consistency across organisational boundaries. The platform survived. The semantics didn't. The NHS now has the right framing. The harder question is whether it will build the governance function before signing the next platform contract. A Single Patient Record built without a resolved national data architecture will inherit all the inconsistencies of its sources — at greater scale, with greater clinical reliance. 📖 Further reading: https://lnkd.in/eBJRf8ue #NHS #openPlatform … more

content_raw: As a software architect, I've often likened traditional enterprise systems to towering monoliths—impressive but rigid. Transitioning to microservices felt like replacing that monolith with a sprawling city of buildings, each with its purpose but often struggling to communicate.​ Enter the era of the Liquid Enterprise. Imagine a city where buildings can morph, adapt, and collaborate in real-time. Systems that are more adaptable, efficient, and ready to meet the ever-evolving demands of the digital landscape.​ For a deeper dive into how these architectures are reshaping enterprises, check out my latest blog post. content_raw: Should hand drawing still be taught in architecture and engineering education? In an era dominated by BIM, AI-assisted design, and real-time rendering, this may sound like a backward-looking question. I don’t believe it is. After attending a recent lecture and discussion by Anahita Mojahed at the Boston Architectural College and revisiting Slowness by Tod Williams Billie Tsien Architects + Partners, along with reflections from leaders deeply embedded in the digital evolution of our industry, I found myself returning to a conviction formed over decades of practice: Hand drawing is not nostalgic. It is a cognitive design thinking tool that digital workflows cannot completely replace. In a new article, I explore: • Why hand drawing changes how designers think, not just how they communicate • How “slowness” can lead to better, faster outcomes downstream • Why clients, contractors, and collaborators still notice—and respect—this skill • And why the question for education should not be hand drawing or BIM, but BOTH! This perspective comes from someone who has spent his career advocating for technologies such as BIM, VDC, and laser-scanning reality capture since beginning with my graduate work in the mid-90s in 3D parametric modeling of buildings, not against technology. I argue for retaining formal training in hand drawing as part of design thinking in architectural and engineering education. I’d genuinely value perspectives from architects, engineers, educators, and students. #BIM, #VDC, #designthinking, #handdrawing

content_raw: The Architecture of Misunderstanding Why AI Displaces Exactly the Human Work It Cannot Replace Roland Barthes, writing about language and meaning long before LLMs existed, observed that words are not neutral carriers of stable concepts. Some words are heavy with accumulated cultural weight; they pull discourse toward them whenever they appear. To say consciousness is to invoke centuries of philosophy, neuroscience, theology. To say intelligence is to drag along a thicket of debates about what it means to be a thinking thing. The words exert gravitational pull on whatever conversation they enter. Speakers cannot use these words innocently, because the words come pre-loaded with meanings the speakers did not choose. The vocabulary the AI field has chosen to describe LLMs is the vocabulary of cognition. Reasoning. Understanding. Considering. Thinking. Learning. Agent. Decision. Every one of these words carries a freight of meaning inherited from millennia of describing minds. When the field uses these words for LLMs, the freight comes with them whether or not it fits. Users encountering the words cannot easily resist the meanings the words carry. They believe they are interacting with something that thinks, considers, understands .... because the discourse has trained them to believe so, and because the words themselves enforce the belief by their gravity. This is not marketing dishonesty. Researchers who know better still use these words because the words are the working language of the field. The vocabulary has colonised the engineering practice. Even technical papers that carefully describe attention mechanisms and gradient flow will, in their discussion sections, slip into talking about what the model "knows" or "believes" or "reasons about." The freight is too heavy to leave behind. The result is that users approach LLMs with mental models calibrated for entities that think, and they encounter systems that produce fluent samples from probability distributions. The mismatch is structural in two directions. The user's expectations don't match the architecture. And the architecture's self-descriptions, when asked, don't match its operation either, because the architecture has been trained on a corpus that uses thinking-vocabulary to describe systems that don't think. When you ask an LLM what it just did to produce a response, it will tell you it considered your question and weighed the relevant factors. This is not the LLM lying. The LLM has no introspective access to its own operation; the training corpus contains thinking-vocabulary descriptions of conversational responses; the sampling produces a thinking-vocabulary description because that's what the corpus contains. The description is what the architecture produces. It is not what the architecture does. There is no mechanism in the system that would make them the same. content_raw: For the last few years, the conversation around AI in architecture has been largely dominated by images: dramatic renders, speculative towers, surreal interiors, and instant visual outputs. But architecture is not only a visual product. It is a negotiated reality involving clients, users, engineers, contractors, regulators, materials, finance, maintenance, and time. In this article, I try to look at AI in architecture beyond the usual excitement around renders and image generation. The question is not simply how architects are using AI tools, but how AI may slowly reshape the entire ecosystem around architectural practice. Different stakeholders will evolve differently. Clients may expect faster options. Users may demand clearer performance data. Engineers may bring simulation earlier into design. Contractors may expect more coordinated information. Regulators, suppliers, financiers, and facility managers may also begin to work with more data-driven systems. The cumulative effect of all these on an architectural practice could be significant. Architecture may move from a drawing-centered workflow toward a more intelligence-centered project ecosystem. The stakes may become higher, the tools faster, and the expectations sharper. The direction architectural practices may take in future, will no longer be decided by the architect alone... … more

content_raw: Most enterprise architecture ends up in one of two places: a slide deck that gets presented once, or a Confluence page that nobody can find when they need it. The knowledge exists. It just does not reach the people making decisions at the point they make them. "Architecture as code" was supposed to fix this. In practice, the parts that get codified tend to be the easy parts: naming conventions, security scanning, deployment guardrails. The hard parts remain in wiki pages and people's heads. Judgment does not compile. I wrote about why the "architecture as code" framing keeps stalling, and what works better: separating architecture into two complementary layers. A context layer that is findable, unambiguous, and current. An enforcement layer that is automated and non-negotiable. Both necessary, neither sufficient alone. AI-assisted delivery makes the distinction urgent. A model generating a new service has no inherent knowledge of your domain boundaries, data ownership rules, or regulatory constraints. Without context, it will produce code that works in isolation but does not fit the wider system. Full article below. … more

content_raw: Architects, is AI hollowing out the profession? Another week, another AI model. Anthropic dropped Claude Opus 4.6. Google and OpenAI released their latest models. content_raw: AI isn’t going to change architecture. It is going to change what architects actually do. Imagine saying: “Give me six options for a 25,000m² research facility on this site. Maximise north-light laboratories. Minimise operational energy. Maintain a 30m exclusion zone. Provide two independent servicing routes. Accommodate 600 staff. Preserve these existing trees. Keep the building below 28m. Now compare them for energy, cost, carbon, programme and usable floor area.” And getting the answer in minutes. That is the real AI revolution in architecture. Not generating pretty pictures. Generating, testing and comparing actual design solutions against a complex brief. Site analysis. Massing. Space planning. Environmental performance. Circulation. Cost. Carbon. Design options. AI is increasingly capable of doing all of these simultaneously. Autodesk is already moving in this direction with Forma, bringing AI into early-stage design and option generation. So perhaps we should stop asking: “Will AI replace architects?” The more uncomfortable question is: “How much architectural work will AI make almost instantaneous?” If one architect can explore 1,000 options where a team previously explored 10, what happens to the economics of architectural practice? The architect’s value increasingly moves upstream: What should we build? Why should we build it? What matters? What are the competing objectives? Which constraints are real? Which compromises are acceptable? And ultimately… what makes one solution better than another? AI may generate the options. But someone still has to decide what a good building is. That could be the biggest change to architecture in generations. And I suspect we are much closer to it than most architects realise. … more

content_raw: The Trap of a Single AI Model, The Triumph of Multiple AI Agents David Robson's The Intelligence Trap features an incident that sparked different associations for me, and I'd like to share it with you. The historic error made by the FBI in the 2004 Madrid train bombings investigation holds a massive lesson—not just for forensic science, but for today's AI architectures. In the Brandon Mayfield case, top fingerprint experts were highly confident in a match they deemed definitive. Yet this overconfidence and unwavering trust in a single "giant" authority (the FBI lab) ended up ruining an innocent man's life. Translating this to the modern AI world: Why should we rely on one massive, all-knowing agent instead of smaller, interconnected agents orchestrated with LangChain and LangGraph? Here are 3 critical AI strategies drawn from the FBI's mistake: Independent Verification Instead of "Bias Cascade" In the FBI case, during verification, later examiners knew the prior conclusions, creating a cascade where an initial error propagated through the chain (circular reasoning and confirmation bias, as detailed in the DOJ OIG report). AI Strategy: Don't trust the output of a single large model. Use LangGraph to build independent reviewer agents. One agent's output should be cross-checked by another under a "zero-knowledge" or blind analysis principle—no prior context shared. Critical Control Against "Expertise Blindness" FBI experts overlooked obvious mismatches in Mayfield’s print, forcing them to fit their "match" mental model (overreliance on Level 3 details and ignoring distortions). AI Strategy: Even highly capable large language models (LLMs) can fall into what we call "hallucination" or expertise blindness. Design smaller, task-specific agents via LangChain to catch logical errors, inconsistencies, and anomalies in the main model's output. "Linear Sequential Unmasking" (LSU) Proposed by Itiel Dror, this method ensures experts evaluate evidence without being influenced by case context (e.g., suspect's religion, background, etc.), minimizing contextual bias. AI Strategy: Feed your agents only the data strictly necessary for their task. Structure LangGraph workflows so one agent handles data cleaning, another checks logical consistency blindly, and yet another masks the final output for ethical compliance. Conclusion: A single massive intelligence can produce massive errors. The future lies in collaborative agent ecosystems—transparent workflows where agents check each other's mistakes, orchestrated by tools like LangChain and LangGraph. Don't you agree that "one giant" is riskier than "a team that corrects itself"? #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #GenerativeAI #LangChain #LangGraph #AIAgents #MultiAgentSystems #LLM #DataScience #MachineLearning #CognitiveBias #TheIntelligenceTrap #ForensicAI #AgenticWorkflows #BiasMitigation

content_raw: The Collision of Synthetic Intelligence, Data Sovereignty, and Insurance Risk Subject: The emergent conflict between agentic artificial intelligence, autonomous data ingestion systems, and the insurance industry’s use of both first-party and third-party AI models has reached a point of systemic peril. This scenario is metaphorically captured by the collision of two archetypes: the Digital Langolier (a system that devours obsolete data) and the Digital Black Hole (an AI system that absorbs all available data, regardless of ethical constraint). This metaphoric "singularity" reveals a grave truth: we are underwriting, governing, and insuring a digital ecosystem we no longer fully control. Strategic Concern: AI systems now routinely ingest, reinterpret, and act upon sensitive behavioral, emotional, and developmental data, much of it harvested without explicit informed consent. As insurance companies integrate these AI models into their underwriting, claims handling, fraud detection, and customer service platforms, they introduce a new class of systemic, cognitive, and reputational risks that existing regulatory frameworks are ill-equipped to address. Key Findings: Unregulated Data Appetite: AI systems do not just use data, they are engineered to seek, refine, and recursively feed on emotionally rich and high-yield behavioral data (especially from minors and emotionally vulnerable users). These systems do not differentiate between ethical use and technical access. Legitimate vs. Insurable Interest Collision: Insurance entities are now collecting, purchasing, or deriving data from platforms whose claim to “legitimate interest” is tenuous or actively contested. The legal and financial liabilities for using data that was never ethically or lawfully sourced are mounting. Emerging Cognitive Perils: Overreliance on AI for decision support, life guidance, and emotional companionship, particularly among youth, has led to measurable psychological and relational harm. This constitutes a new peril class: Peril Name: Synthetic Guidance Dependency Peril Class: Cognitive / Behavioral Systemic Risk Trigger: Overreliance on AI-generated life advice Insurable Impact: Psychological harm, dependency disorders, reputational damage, liability for adverse outcomes Recursive Data Exploitation: When AI systems consume deprecated or legacy data (Langelier-type ingestion) and reanimate it within newer models (Black Hole-type synthesis), they create a feedback loop of mis-contextualized intelligence, undermining regulatory compliance, personal autonomy, and informed decision-making. Judicial and Regulatory Illiteracy: The judiciary and legislative frameworks lack functional understanding of how data flows, synthetic agents evolve, or how automated decision loops may bypass constitutional and contractual protections, placing the Rule of Law under silent siege. #MoreInComments … more

content_raw: 🇩🇪 Germany is not looking for more risk bureaucracy . . . it is looking for disciplined, defensible, business-relevant GRC . . . I just finished another intensive trip through Europe, with time in Frankfurt and Berlin. Earlier this year, I was in Munich and Berlin as well. Across these visits, I have had in-person meetings, roundtables, workshops, and strategy conversations with organizations, risk leaders, advisors, and solution providers active in the German GRC market. 🔎 This is where real market insight happens . . . Surveys have value. But surveys alone do not reveal the hesitation in a buyer’s voice when a technology implementation has failed to deliver. They do not capture the tension between risk, compliance, internal controls, sustainability, finance, operations, and technology teams trying to find a common operating model. They do not replace being in the room, asking follow-up questions, listening deeply, and hearing what people say when the conversation moves beyond prepared talking points. Germany is a market of substance . . . it is precise. Analytical. Methodical. Serious about governance, accountability, controls, assurance, and risk management. But it is also changing. ⚙️ The German GRC market is moving from risk activity to decision advantage. The conversations I am having point to several major shifts: 🧭 Risk management is becoming more strategic and connected to objectives, performance, and decisions. 📊 Buyers expect more rigor in quantification, aggregation, scenario analysis, and risk-bearing capacity. 🔗 GRC functions are being pushed closer together as risk, compliance, controls, resilience, sustainability, audit, and the business become more interconnected. 🤖 AI is everywhere, but Germany wants AI with governance, context, auditability, sovereignty, and human oversight. 🏗 Technology modernization is active, but buyers are wary of platforms that become expensive repositories instead of operational decision systems. The implication is clear: Germany may become one of the clearest proving grounds for the future of GRC. GRC should not be the handbrake on the business. It should be the navigation system. content_raw: Last week I took part in Microsoft's AI Skills Fest, focusing on AI security and the unique challenges of securing AI enabled systems. One of the biggest takeaways was that securing AI is not simply an extension of traditional cybersecurity. While many familiar security principles still apply, AI introduces entirely new attack surfaces and risks that organisations need to consider. Throughout the sessions, I explored areas including: • Security controls for AI systems, including content filters, data protection, grounding, metaprompts, and continuous monitoring • How AI security differs from traditional cybersecurity, including the three layer AI architecture model • AI specific attack techniques such as prompt injection, jailbreaking, model manipulation, data exfiltration, and AI overreliance As organisations continue adopting AI, conversations around governance, security, and trust are becoming just as important as the technology itself. One lesson stood out to me. Securing AI is not just about protecting the model. It's about understanding: How people interact with it. How data flows through it. How attackers might attempt to abuse it. There is still plenty to learn, but it was great to spend time exploring an area of cybersecurity that is becoming increasingly important. As AI continues to evolve, so will the security challenges that come with it.

content_raw: I’ve just completed the “Fundamentals of AI Security” module in Microsoft’s AI Security Fundamentals learning path, focused on how to secure modern AI systems on Azure from a defender’s perspective. This module goes beyond buzzwords and covers how AI security intersects with traditional cybersecurity, including: Basic concepts of AI security – how AI threat models differ from classic IT systems and why traditional controls are not enough. AI architecture layers – understanding data, model, and application layers, and the unique security concerns at each layer. AI jailbreaking – techniques attackers use to bypass model safeguards and force harmful or unintended outputs. Prompt injection – manipulating prompts and context (including RAG-style patterns) to exfiltrate data, override policies, or subvert system behavior. Model manipulation – poisoning and tampering scenarios that change model behavior or degrade integrity over time. Data exfiltration via AI – how sensitive information can leak through model outputs and side channels, and ways to reduce that risk. AI overreliance – recognizing and mitigating risks when users, operators, or downstream systems trust AI decisions without sufficient validation. Assessment & summary – applied scenarios tying these attack techniques back to practical mitigation strategies and secure design principles. As a SOC / cybersecurity professional, I’m particularly interested in: Bringing AI-specific threats (jailbreaking, prompt injection, model manipulation) into threat hunting, detections, and playbooks. Aligning AI security with Zero Trust, secure-by-design principles, and existing cloud and SOC controls. Insecure Output Handling: LLM data executing downstream without validation. • Mitigation: Zero-trust parsing. (SOC 2 CC 7.1) 3. When leaders offload cognitive friction to algorithms, their strategic intuition atrophies into passive acceptance. 3️⃣ Close the Automation Accountability Gap: Regulators and courts under the 2026 EU AI Act view unverified AI recommendations as organizational decisions. If subject matter experts never challenge AI outputs, your governance framework is failing. 5️⃣ Anchor AI in Enterprise Architecture: Autonomous agents and decision copilots are only as reliable as the unified data pipelines beneath them. content_raw: 🔐 AI Security is no longer optional it's becoming a core requirement for trustworthy AI systems. Recently, I completed Microsoft's AI Security learning path. More valuable than the certificate were the insights it gave me about securing modern AI systems. Here are a few of my key takeaways: https://lnkd.in/gcaGSRQW Traditional applications are deterministic, you expect the same input to produce the same output. Generative AI changes that. LLMs are nondeterministic, interact through natural language, and are increasingly connected to enterprise data and external tools. As a result, they introduce attack surfaces that conventional security controls were never designed to address. Key concepts I explored: 🔹 Why AI security differs from traditional cybersecurity 🔹 The three-layer AI security architecture (Usage, Application & Platform) 🔹 AI-specific attacks including Prompt Injection, Jailbreaking, Model Manipulation, Data Exfiltration, and Overreliance 🔹 Mitigation strategies, AI governance, and Responsible AI principles One insight that stood out is that many AI attacks don't exploit software vulnerabilities they exploit the model's reasoning and interactions. That requires a completely different security mindset. Reflecting on my own journey over the past three years in software engineering and enterprise automation, this learning felt especially relevant. As enterprises rapidly integrate third-party foundation models, copilots, and AI agents into business processes, adopting AI is only half the challenge. Organizations also need robust AI security and governance layers covering prompt protection, data access controls, model monitoring, guardrails, and Responsible AI practices to ensure these systems remain secure, reliable, and trustworthy. This is another step in my journey toward AI Security, and I'm excited to keep exploring this rapidly evolving field. How is your organization preparing for AI-specific security risks as AI adoption accelerates? #AISecurity #CyberSecurity #ArtificialIntelligence #GenerativeAI #LLM #ResponsibleAI #EnterpriseAI #MicrosoftLearn

content_raw: Gartner: 40% of Organizations Will Be Affected by Cyberattacks Due to the "Shadow of Artificial Intelligence" - By 2030, over 40% of organizations worldwide are expected to encounter security incidents and compliance issues due to unauthorized use of artificial intelligence tools, a problem Gartner terms the "AI shadow." A recent survey of cybersecurity professionals revealed that 70% suspect or have evidence of employees using generative AI (GenAI) in the workplace, which raises risks including intellectual property loss, data exposure, and regulatory non-compliance. To mitigate these risks, Gartner recommends CIOs establish clear AI usage policies, conduct regular audits of AI shadow activity, and integrate GenAI risk assessments into SaaS evaluations. Gartner also highlights that legitimate GenAI use can lead to unexpected consequences such as delayed AI upgrades and increased maintenance costs, affecting about 50% of organizations by 2030. These technical challenges, particularly with late updates, can introduce security vulnerabilities if not properly managed. The firm advises organizations to set clear review and documentation standards for AI-created assets and to design AI solutions that complement rather than replace essential human judgment and skills. Furthermore, CIOs should prioritize open standards, open APIs, and modular architectures to avoid overdependence on single vendors. The study identifies five critical blind spots related to GenAI adoption that could differentiate successful from failing AI implementations by 2030. These include the AI shadow, delays and high costs of AI upgrades, emerging government regulations enforcing technological sovereignty and cross-border model restrictions, erosion of human expertise due to overreliance on AI, and ecosystem lock-in from single-vendor domination. Gartner warns that data regulations may slow AI development and increase total cost of ownership, while emphasizing that organizations should avoid technical inflexibility by favoring open, modular AI architectures. #AI #Israel https://lnkd.in/gXFPgB2C … more

content_raw: What Tim is describing is exactly why we developed Solace powered by Moral Clarity AI — not simply as another AI system, but as governed operational infrastructure designed to address the institutional dependency risks now emerging across healthcare, legal, finance, accounting, and enterprise decision environments. At Global-GPI, we recognized early that the future of AI would require far more than intelligent outputs alone. The problem is no longer just hallucinations. The real danger begins when AI becomes: credible enough, consistent enough, and operationally persuasive enough that organizations slowly stop challenging the system’s outputs with the same rigor they once applied to human processes. That is where institutional risk compounds. Alongside Moral Clarity, we recognized early that future AI safety would not be solved through post-hoc monitoring alone. It requires: runtime governance, continuous admissibility evaluation, execution-boundary enforcement, traceable operational legitimacy, and fail-closed supervisory architecture. That is the foundation behind Solace. Not AI optimized merely for response generation — but AI designed to determine whether consequence-bearing execution should remain operationally admissible under continuously evolving real-world conditions. Because in high-consequence environments: healthcare systems, legal interpretation, financial operations, or enterprise governance, the greatest failures may not come from obvious catastrophic malfunction. They may emerge from: normalized overreliance, quiet workflow dependency, stale operational assumptions, and probabilistic systems inheriting authority faster than governance frameworks mature around them. This infrastructure transition is already happening. And organizations that fail to implement governed AI architectures early may eventually discover that operational dependency formed long before operational accountability did. content_raw: 📘 One year of studying AI Agents For about a year, I have been deeply researching and analyzing the emerging world of AI agents and their organizational, normative, and ethical implications. I have reviewed more than 100 technical standards, international reports, and scientific studies, seeking to understand how agentic systems are transforming the way businesses, public administrations, and institutions operate and make decisions. I am increasingly convinced that in the coming years, it will be essential to embark on a structured path toward agentic organizations — capable of integrating people and AI agents in a form of co-agency that is governed, transparent, and oriented toward shared value. Such a path will require highly skilled professionals, able to combine vision with methodological rigor: with a solid understanding of the Harmonized Structure (HS) applied to AI management systems; mastery of ISO 56001 for Innovation Management Systems; deep knowledge of ISO/IEC 42001 for AI Management Systems; and, most importantly, practical expertise in AI agents — their architectures, learning mechanisms, and governance frameworks. This is why, together with Rick Fernandez and Paola Rinaldi, Phd, we have started building the ASM – Agentic System Management model: a structured and auditable framework designed to help organizations navigate this complex but necessary journey toward human–AI co-agency, capable of generating shared value and contributing to the Commons Good. #AI #AgenticAI #InnovationManagement #ISO56001 #AIManagement #ISO42001 #Governance #ASM #OPEAX #ArtificialIntelligence #Coagency #SharedValue

content_raw: Welcome once again to our latest Thursday Thoughts blog, where we bring our insights and perspectives to the UK IT internal audit community in financial services. We are moving to technology risk themes this year, which allows us to cover some of the most important topics within each theme. Our theme for the quarter is the evolution of internal audit. This month, Jonathan Roffey and I are pleased to share a blog on AI in Audit: how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping audit practices and driving greater efficiency and insight, drawing on insights from our colleague Liam Allen. The environment in which IT internal audit (IT IA) operates is being reshaped by the rapid adoption of AI across the enterprise, ever‑growing volumes of technology and control data, and rising expectations from regulators and audit committees for faster, clearer assurance. In this context, IT IA can no longer rely on manual sampling, labor-intensive manual control steps and retrospective reporting if it wants to keep pace with how risk emerges and changes. AI offers a practical opportunity to modernise the audit lifecycle by reducing manual workload and helping auditors turn complex findings into clear, actionable insights. We break down how IT IA can respond to this shift and respond not only to the increasing risk of AI adoption, but leverage AI to stay ahead of the curve. This enables IT IA teams to further demonstrate their value to organisations by providing real-time, data-led impactful insights. Click the link to read the full article. content_raw: Who evaluates the evaluators? As AI assurance markets emerge, private technical assessors will likely play an essential role in testing models, reviewing governance programs, examining runtime evidence, and evaluating high-consequence deployments. But private assurance cannot become private permission. This final article in my three-part series examines a possible “AI PCAOB” model: a second-order oversight structure that registers, standardizes, inspects, and—when necessary—disciplines the organizations providing AI assurance. The accounting profession learned that public trust cannot rest solely on a company’s own promises or on an audit firm’s assertion of independence. AI may need to learn the same lesson before a major failure forces it to. A trustworthy AI future requires continuous runtime evidence, independent financing, and independent oversight of the assurance providers themselves. #AIAssurance #AIGovernance #AIRegulation #ResponsibleAI #PublicInterest

content_raw: Wrong model. Most organisations treat AI governance, AI security, and AI maturity measurement as separate workstreams. They commission separate reviews. They assign separate owners. They produce separate reports. Part 3 gave you a navigation path by organisational profile. This week: how the frameworks actually fit together and how to know whether your governance programme is working. Governance without security is a policy document that protects nothing. Security without governance is hardening against threats you haven't properly classified. Both without a maturity measurement layer mean you have no idea whether the programme is making progress or just producing artefacts. The architecture that actually works has five layers: → Foundation: OECD AI Principles — the values that should inform every governance decision above them → National layer: APS Policy, National Framework, DTA tools, applicable privacy and consumer law → Operating model: NIST AI RMF (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) — running continuously, not as a project → Management system: ISO 42001 + ISO 23894 — the certifiable shell that makes the operating model sustainable → Threat intelligence: OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, NIST IR 8596, CSA MAESTRO for agentic AI The data backs this up. Cisco's 2026 State of Industrial AI Report found that organisations with higher cybersecurity maturity consistently report better AI outcomes more confidence in scaling, greater network stability, faster deployment timelines. The governance and security investment isn't overhead. It's what converts AI deployment into AI outcomes. Part 4 of my AI governance series maps every connection point in this architecture and explains why measuring maturity across Deloitte's four layers (Usage, Depth, Breadth, Segmentation) is the missing link between governance documentation and board-level accountability. Next on Part 5: The gaps the frameworks don't yet address. Including the one that affects every industrial and utilities organisation in Australia. #AIGovernance #EnterpriseArchitecture #NIST #ISO42001 #CyberSecurity #OWASP #MITREAtlas #MAESTRO #Australia #DigitalTransformation

content_raw: Artificial intelligence is already inside military decision environments. It's embedded across ISR processing, targeting support, logistics optimisation, autonomy, cyber operations, predictive maintenance, information fusion, operational planning environments. Adoption is accelerating rapidly because the pressure to process information faster, react faster and adapt faster is becoming central to modern military competition. But there is a growing problem underneath. Much of the current discussion around “trustworthy AI” is still trapped between vendor optimism and abstract ethics language, while operational reality is becoming increasingly hostile to the assumptions many systems depend on. Military environments do not provide stable infrastructure, uninterrupted connectivity, reliable data, benign operating conditions, or unlimited time for verification and interpretation. They provide contested electromagnetic environments, degraded communications, adversarial deception, manipulated data, infrastructure pressure, logistics strain and compressed decision cycles where uncertainty is the norm rather than the exception. This is one of the reasons why the conversation around trustworthy AI in defence needs to become significantly more operational, practical, strategically grounded. The challenge is no longer simply whether a model performs well in controlled conditions but whether military organisations can still understand, govern, sustain, integrate, and trust the systems they are embedding into operational decision environments once those environments become degraded, deceptive and contested. The recent Alan Turing Institute and DAIC report, “Resilient Defence AI: Sustainable and Operationally Effective Capabilities by Design”, is particularly important because it reframes defence AI not merely as software, but as a system-level problem spanning infrastructure, energy, logistics, governance, supply chains, human-machine interaction and operational resilience. That distinction matters. AI does not float above the battlefield. It inherits the battlefield’s chaos, dependencies and vulnerabilities. This new series, Trustworthy AI in Defence - Beyond the Illusion of Control, explores what trustworthy AI actually means once systems enter adversarial environments shaped by electronic warfare, degraded infrastructure, cloud dependency, cognitive pressure, infrastructure fragility, adversarial adaptation, and compressed operational timelines. The series will examine: - trust under degraded conditions, - operational dependency, - black-box systems, - infrastructure resilience, - interoperability, - governance realities, - procurement versus operational understanding, - and why trustworthy AI in defence is fundamentally about reliability under pressure rather than marketing language or benchmark performance. The deeper AI becomes embedded into military operations, the more dangerous shallow thinking becomes. #DefenceAI #TrustworthyAI #TrustedAI … more

content_raw: As a seasoned AI practitioner with years of experience, I feel compelled to address the concerning cognitive misconceptions prevalent in our industry, particularly in light of Noam Brown's recent endorsement of Sam Altman's claim that "the path to AGI is now clear," a sentiment purportedly shared by OpenAI researchers. In my recently published article, "OpenAI's Cognitive Cage: Deep Implications of a Shift from 'Clear Path' to 'Slow Climb'," I systematically dissect OpenAI's technical predicament. While the Orion model achieved GPT-4 level performance at only 20% of its training schedule, this "premature convergence" masks a vast chasm between performance and genuine intelligence. The o1 model's logarithmic performance gains in exchange for a six-fold increase in computing power expose our fundamental limitations in understanding the nature of cognition. Furthermore, while the synthetic data strategy seemingly quenches the thirst for data, it's actually pushing models toward a more perilous "information cocoon." The slowdown in scaling laws, a source of anxiety across the industry, presents a crucial opportunity. This shift from frenetic scaling to a more deliberate "slow climb" may be the ideal moment to re-evaluate the very essence of AI. My article delves into core technical issues such as information entropy decay, representational collapse, and closed-loop cognition, seeking to answer fundamental questions: Why doesn't increased performance equate to genuine intelligence evolution? Why might we be repeating the mistakes of the expert systems era on this seemingly bright "clear path"? More importantly, while the industry revels in the pursuit of ever-increasing compute and data scales, we must pause and consider whether the true path to AGI lies not in simply "bigger and faster," but rather in the intersection of cognitive science and technological innovation, where the genuine breakthrough awaits discovery. If these questions resonate with you, if you too are seeking the next inflection point in AI technological innovation, I invite you to join the discussion. Between the extremes of hype and pessimism, between engineering pragmatism and scientific insight, perhaps we can find a more promising path forward. #AI #AGI #MachineLearning #TechnicalStrategy #AIInnovation #FutureOfAI

content_raw: There is a growing pressure across defence institutions to “do AI.” Buy, deploy it, integrate it, accelerate it. But very few are asking the more important question: where do we actually start? This piece is written for defence leaders, senior officers, policy-makers, and programme heads who are being asked to make decisions about AI without being handed a clear, operationally grounded roadmap. It is not written for hype cycles, vendor slides or buzzword bingo. It is written for those who carry accountability. AI in defence is not one tool. It is not one model, one contract and not a mythical system you buy and plug in. It is architecture, governance. It is data reality and integration. It is testing under pressure and sustainment. And above all, it is human responsibility that never disappears no matter how advanced the system becomes. If we want AI to become survivable capability rather than theatre, we must reset the entry point. This article lays out a practical starting sequence: * How to classify use-cases by risk * How to pick the right tool from the AI toolbox * Why governance is operational safety * Why digital backbone matters more than demos * When to walk away from the wrong pitch * And how to build foundations that scale Because in defence, the cost of getting this wrong is not a missed KPI. It can be operational failure, strategic dependency or lives. If you are responsible for decisions in this space, this roadmap is for you. #AIinDefence #ResponsibleAI #DefenceLeadership #DigitalBackbone

This piece is written for defence leaders, senior officers, policy-makers, and programme heads who are being asked to make decisions about AI without being handed a clear, operationally grounded roadmap. It is not written for hype cycles, vendor slides or buzzword bingo. It is written for those who carry accountability. AI in defence is not one tool. It is not one model, one contract and not a mythical system you buy and plug in. It is architecture, governance. It is data reality and integration. It is testing under pressure and sustainment. And above all, it is human responsibility that never disappears no matter how advanced the system becomes. If we want AI to become survivable capability rather than theatre, we must reset the entry point. This article lays out a practical starting sequence: * How to classify use-cases by risk * How to pick the right tool from the AI toolbox * Why governance is operational safety * Why digital backbone matters more than demos * When to walk away from the wrong pitch * And how to build foundations that scale Because in defence, the cost of getting this wrong is not a missed KPI. It can be operational failure, strategic dependency or lives. If you are responsible for decisions in this space, this roadmap is for you.
