content_raw: Paper II Released - Please refer to my post @ https://lnkd.in/gp7Rvggd . I am pleased to publish Part II of my Strategic Quadrilateral Series titled: “AI and the Future of Indian Defence Forces (2026–2036): A Questioning Vision on Strategy, Systems, Sovereignty & Superiority in the AI Era.” Quadrilateral Series – Paper II - Title : "AI and the Rewiring of India’s Defence Architecture (2026–2036) : Doctrine, Acquisition Reform & Indigenous Military Systems in the Era of Algorithmic Sovereignty." “Future wars will not be won by those who possess the most machines, but by those who govern intelligence with architectural discipline.” This paper argues that Artificial Intelligence is not merely a force enhancer; it is an institutional stress test. It exposes the rigidity of legacy procurement cycles, the fragility of fragmented data systems, and the limitations of platform-centric doctrine. AI demands not enthusiasm, but engineering — not acquisition, but architecture. The nations that understand this distinction will define the strategic geometry of the next decade. If Paper I examined AI at the operational and battlefield layer, Paper II moves deeper — into the institutional core. This paper II examines how AI compels structural transformation across : (i) Military Doctrine; (ii) Acquisition and Procurement Philosophy; (iii) Indigenous Defence Manufacturing; (iv) Data Governance Architecture; (v) Joint Theater Integration; (vi) Algorithmic Sovereignty In the algorithmic era, military strength will be measured by coherence, not inventory. AI compresses decision cycles and redefines sovereignty at the level of code and data. Unless doctrine becomes software-aware, acquisition becomes lifecycle-adaptive and indigenous systems remain sovereign at the algorithmic core, technological progress will remain fragmented. Strategic advantage will belong to institutions that integrate intelligence structurally, not symbolically. The central argument is clear — AI superiority will not emerge from technology acquisition alone. It will emerge from architectural discipline. Between 2026 and 2036, India faces a decisive institutional decade. Procurement cycles must evolve. Doctrine must become software-aware. Industry must develop sovereign algorithmic cores. Leadership must embrace cognitive transition. The question is not whether AI will enter the Indian defence ecosystem. The question is whether our institutions will evolve fast enough to govern it coherently. “Architecture, not acquisition, will determine strategic destiny.” I invite policymakers, defence professionals, industry leaders, research institutions and strategic thinkers to engage with this second paper in the series. The algorithmic era demands structural clarity. content_raw: Over the past few days, I explored the role of generative AI in education—not just from a surface level, but by understanding the underlying architectures, algorithms, and real-world impact. What stood out to me is how education is shifting from a static, one-size-fits-all model to a dynamic and personalized learning ecosystem. Technologies like Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA, PEFT) are enabling systems that can generate explanations, adapt to student needs, and provide real-time feedback. One key insight I gained is that while generative AI significantly improves accessibility and scalability, its true value lies in how it augments human learning rather than replaces it. For example, RAG-based systems can reduce hallucination by grounding responses in trusted academic sources, making them more reliable for educational use. At the same time, this shift introduces new responsibilities. Students need to develop critical thinking to evaluate AI-generated content, and educators must adapt to roles that focus more on mentorship and conceptual clarity rather than repetitive tasks. Generative AI is not just a tool—it is redefining how knowledge is created, delivered, and consumed. I have written a detailed technical blog covering architectures, algorithms, and applications in education. You can read the attached article. I would love to hear your thoughts on how AI is shaping the future of learning. #GenerativeAI #ArtificialIntelligence #EdTech #AIinEducation #MachineLearning #DeepLearning #LLM #RAG #AIInnovation #FutureOfEducation #TechInEducation #Learning #StudentLife #AIForGood

content_raw: Everyone is asking: “Which AI model should we use?” But that may be the wrong question. The real question is: Are we designing AI to generate answers—or architecting AI to actually get work done? Enterprise AI adoption is accelerating. AI spending is accelerating. But for many organizations, measurable business value is not keeping pace. The problem may not be the model. It may be the architecture. In this week’s PlaybookAI Edition, we break down one of the biggest decisions shaping the next era of enterprise AI: Monolithic LLMs vs. Modular Workflow Orchestration. One powerful model doing everything? Or a system of specialized intelligence, context, workflows, tools, governance, and human oversight? The future of enterprise AI won’t be defined by who has access to the biggest model. It will be defined by who can best redesign the work around it. From prompts → context → workflows. From models → systems. From AI activity → business value.

content_raw: Most security engineers still thinking in firewalls and endpoints. Meanwhile, the next wave of attacks talks back. So I'm currently working through Microsoft's AI Security Fundamentals course and it's reframing how I think about risks and threats entirely. As well known, traditional cybersecurity controls were built to focus on system, network and data and not for AI risks. Natural language interfaces, nondeterministic model behavior, and complex data pipelines have expanded the attack surface in ways firewalls and input validation alone can't cover. With AI systems emerging, a few of the key risks to look into includes: 1. Jailbreaking: bypassing a model's safety guardrails. 2. Prompt Injection: hidden instructions smuggled into inputs to hijack model behavior. 3. Model Manipulation: tampering with training data or model weights 4. Data Exfiltration: extracting sensitive info through the model itself. 5. Overreliance: trusting AI output without adequate human verification. A three-layer AI architecture model in this course was created to be uses to map these threats and how each risk pairs with a specific mitigation strategy organizations can actually implement, not just theorize about. #AISecurity #Cybersecurity #PromptInjection #MicrosoftLearn

content_raw: AI Agents are easy to demo. Reliable AI Agents are much harder to engineer. If you want to seriously learn AI Agents — from foundations to advanced, production-ready agentic systems — this is one resource worth saving. I recently went through “Mastering AI Agents” by Galileo, and I’m sharing it here because it brings together many of the concepts people usually have to learn from dozens of separate tutorials, articles and repositories. What I especially like about this book is the progression. It doesn't begin by throwing you directly into a framework. It first helps you understand what an agent actually is, when you need one — and equally importantly, when you DON'T. Then it gradually moves into: → Fixed automation vs LLM-powered agents → ReAct: Reasoning + Action → ReAct + RAG for grounded intelligence → Tool-using agents and API orchestration → Memory-enhanced agents → Self-reflecting agents → Multi-agent systems → Self-learning and adaptive agents → LangGraph vs AutoGen vs CrewAI → State management, planning and re-planning → Human-in-the-loop systems → Building a practical research agent → LLM-as-a-Judge and agent evaluation → Context adherence, latency and cost → Task completion & output quality metrics → Tool selection and tool-calling accuracy → Guardrails and production safety → Scaling and fault tolerance → Preventing infinite agent loops → Long-context & multi-turn tool calling → Choosing the right LLM for an agentic workflow But the biggest lesson from this book is bigger than any framework: Building an agent is not the finish line. Building an agent you can trust is. A great agent needs more than a powerful LLM. It needs: Reasoning → Planning → Tools → Memory → State → Evaluation → Observability → Guardrails → Human Oversight → Continuous Improvement That is the difference between an impressive AI demo and a system that can actually survive in production. content_raw: What if the biggest opportunity for LLMs in recommender systems isn't ranking? That's one of the things I found most interesting in a new paper from Alibaba and Renmin University: RecGPT: A User Intent-Centric Next-Generation LLM-Powered Recommender System in Industrial Practice. The core idea is a shift from “learning clicks from clicks” toward explicitly modeling user intent. Rather than asking an LLM to score every candidate item, RecGPT uses LLMs at several stages of the recommendation pipeline: – User interest mining: reason over a user's long-term behavior history to construct an explicit, natural-language representation of their interests – Item tag prediction: translate those interests into fine-grained item tags representing what the user might want next – Retrieval: use those tags to drive semantic retrieval, while still combining them with traditional collaborative signals – Explanation: generate personalized explanations for the recommendations In other words, the LLM isn't replacing the recommendation stack. It's helping determine what the recommendation stack should be looking for. I particularly like this architectural choice. It turns the LLM into something closer to an intent layer between user behavior and retrieval, while leaving the downstream retrieval and ranking infrastructure largely intact. And this isn't just an offline benchmark. The system is deployed in Taobao's “Guess What You Like” experience. Over a month-long online experiment, the paper reports improvements in metrics including +4.35% dwell time, +5.65% CTR, +7.55% item page views (IPV), +5.53% clicked item category diversity (CICD), and +1.63% sustained long-term retention improvements (LT-30 retention). RecGPT also improved exposure opportunities for less popular merchants without sacrificing overall performance. There are also some very practical engineering details here: compressing users' extremely long behavior histories, distilling stronger reasoning models into smaller models suitable for production, using LLM-as-a-Judge for data curation, and precomputing recommendation explanations to avoid real-time generation costs. For me, that's the most interesting part of the paper. It's not simply “LLMs can improve recommendations.” It's more of an architectural question: Where can reasoning add the most value in a recommendation pipeline without forcing us to replace everything that already works? content_raw: Customer: Our AI agents take 20 seconds to respond. Which GPUs should we buy? Me: points right here. Not at an GPU. At the empty memory banks. A busy GPU can be doing work you already paid for. In our agentic-trace benchmark: HBM-only caching: 23s p95 time to first token. Host KV offloading to DRAM: 3.02s. About 83% lower p95 TTFT. A result worth taking to the hardware budget meeting. Look at those blue slots. A single 128GB DDR5 ECC RDIMM is listed at nearly US$4,800. Populate 24 slots at that price and you are looking at roughly US$115,000 in memory. An excellent way to get called into finance. Hardware teams: you were right. Fill the slots if you can afford it. It pays for itself the moment traffic spikes. But the memory invoice does not show the cost of throwing useful work away. An agent can send back an entire conversation just to add one small next step. It calls a tool. Waits on an API. Appends the result. Calls the model again. Much of that conversation has already been processed. Under HBM pressure, reusable KV state can get evicted. When the next request arrives, the GPU has to recompute the missing prefix state. The prompt survived. The cached work did not. Take a model the size of GLM-5.3: roughly 744 billion parameters puts FP8 weight storage around 744 GB before overhead. KV cache needs its own budget on top. (10 independent GLM-5.3 sessions at 1M context ≈ 440–550 GB of KV.) Host KV offloading gives reusable state another place to live. The engine transfers it into DRAM and loads it back when needed. that reduced the wait This is where systems engineers turn a memory allocation into GPU work you no longer have to repeat. Cache layout. Asynchronous transfers. Eviction policies. Scheduling. Backend engineers: the budget got bigger. The debugging instincts should feel familiar. vLLM already supports native CPU KV offloading: --kv-offloading-backend native --kv-offloading-size <size_in_GiB> Software teams: you are the entire margin story now. Go configure LMCache, HiCache, Mooncake, llm-d, UMBP, or WEKA AMG. And for the systems people thinking one tier ahead: yes, KV cache can also live on NVMe. Cheaper capacity per GB. More reusable work retained. The hard part is getting the right bytes back in time. Otherwise, your GPU waits for the SSD. Prefetching, I/O scheduling, and when the extra tier pays off. Probably discuss this in next post.

Go configure LMCache, HiCache, Mooncake, llm-d, UMBP, or WEKA AMG. And for the systems people thinking one tier ahead: yes, KV cache can also live on NVMe. Cheaper capacity per GB. More reusable work retained. The hard part is getting the right bytes back in time. Otherwise, your GPU waits for the SSD. Prefetching, I/O scheduling, and when the extra tier pays off. Probably discuss this in next post.

content_raw: The Week the AI Bubble Cracked: 🔥Bottlenecks, 🔥Cheap Rivals, and a Sudden Call to 🔥Slow Down The last week has seen a dramatic convergence of events that may mark the tipping point for the AI bubble. A sudden pivot by top AI executives, data exposing a massive infrastructure gap, and pressure from hyper-efficient Chinese open-source models triggered a global tech selloff. ⚠️ 1. The "Coordinated" Call for an AI Slowdown On Sept 14, Wall Street was rattled when leaders of top American AI labs unexpectedly urged a development slowdown. 👉 The Catalysts: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued that frontier model development must pause or decelerate due to existential and cybersecurity risks—a stance endorsed by Elon Musk (xAI) and Sam Altman (OpenAI). 👉 The IPO Delay: Sam Altman announced OpenAI is pushing back its IPO until at least 2027, citing safety. 👉 Market Reaction: Investors suspect "safety concerns" mask a steepening monetization lag and a flattening LLM capability curve, triggering a sharp selloff in chipmakers like Nvidia. 🇨🇳 2. Commoditization Pressure from Chinese Models Market anxiety deepened with data revealing Silicon Valley's competitive moat is vanishing. 👉 The 4-Month Gap: Mozilla’s State of Open Source AI report (Sept 15) found the performance gap between multibillion-dollar US proprietary models and China's hyper-cheap open-weights models has collapsed to just 4.4 months. 👉 The Margin Killer: Models like Moonshot AI's Kimi A3/K3 and Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8 Max deliver frontier reasoning at a fraction of the cost. Being open-weights, enterprises can run them locally. 👉 Economic Impact: If companies gain 95% of closed-model performance for pennies via open Chinese alternatives, the business models of OpenAI and Anthropic face structural collapse, undercutting the revenue targets justifying current valuations. 🛠️ 3. The Infrastructure Ghost Town Reveal Data leaks regarding real-world AI deployment delivered the week's most damaging fundamental blow. 👉 Idle Capital: Microsoft has spent an astronomical $265 billion in capex but brought only ~2 gigawatts of AI compute online—drastically missing internal goals of 12 gigawatts. 👉 Uninstalled Tech: An estimated $82.5 billion in purchased GPUs sit idle or uninstalled due to grid constraints and data center bottlenecks. 👉 The Risk: Big Tech is hoarding hardware it cannot plug in, creating severe risks of an inventory glut and cancelled orders that threaten suppliers like Nvidia. 😡 4. Shifting Public Sentiment A Glassdoor report highlighted rising anti-AI sentiment among corporate staff. Promised productivity booms have failed to materialize in macro data, while engineers, accountants, and designers report negative experiences with integrated AI tools.

content_raw: Announcing jina-ocr-v1, our new visual document parser with 3.4B total parameters and 570M active parameters, with speculative decoding built in. Throw PDFs, scans, tables, charts, or invoices at it and get clean markdown back. Post-trained on DeepSeek-OCR, we strengthened multilingual support across 25 languages and optimized it for low-budget GPUs such as the NVIDIA L4. jina-ocr-v1 scores 91.14 on OmniDocBench v1.6 and 83.4 on olmOCR-Bench, and hits the highest page throughput among all competitors.

content_raw: بعضی آدم‌ها رو فقط چند دقیقه می‌بینیم، ولی یک جمله‌شون ممکنه تا مدت‌ها توی ذهنمون بمونه. امروز اومدم یه فضای کاری جدید، اوپال، یه خانوم زیبا اون طرف نشسته بود، دست تکون داد و بهم لبخند زد. من که کلاً آدم تخسی‌ام و از این عادت‌ها ندارم، با خنده گفتم: ما همدیگه رو می‌شناسیم؟ گفت: نه، فقط دلم خواست بهت لبخند بزنم. همین، شروع کردیم به حرف زدن، خودش رو معرفی کرد، منم خودمو معرفی کردم. وسط صحبت‌هامون فهمید دنبال نیروی سوشال مدیاست، اینستاگرامم رو گرفت که برام بفرسته. همه‌چیز داشت خیلی معمولی پیش می‌رفت تا اینکه یه‌دفعه گفت: تسلیت می‌گم… منم دقیقاً سه سال پیش، همین روز و همین تاریخ،همین غم رو تجربه کردم. خشکم زد. چشم‌هام پر شد و بعدش دیگه واقعاً صفحه لپ‌تاپم رو درست نمی‌دیدم. نشستم سر کار، ولی ذهنم جای دیگه‌ای بود. داشتم فکر می‌کردم ما از قصه‌ی آدم‌های اطرافمون تقریباً هیچ‌چیز نمی‌دونیم. آدمی که امروز کنارت توی آسانسور ایستاده، کسی که توی کافه کنارت نشسته، همکاری که فقط بهش سلام می‌کنی، یا حتی غریبه‌ای که بی‌دلیل بهت لبخند می‌زنه… ممکنه خودش یک دنیا قصه پشت سرش داشته باشه. ممکنه چیزی رو از سر گذرونده باشه که تو هنوز داری باهاش دست‌وپنجه نرم می‌کنی.و شاید قشنگ‌ترین قسمت زندگی همین باشه؛ اینکه گاهی درست وقتی فکر می‌کنی وسط یک غم، تنهایی، یک آدم از ناکجای زندگی وارد می‌شه و فقط با یک جمله بهت یادآوری می‌کنه: نه، فقط تو نیستی، امروز برای کار وارد اوپال شدم،اما با یک قصه‌ی تازه از آدم‌ها برگشتم. و هنوز به اون جمله فکر می‌کنم: فقط دلم خواست بهت لبخند بزنم:) … more

content_raw: 🧠 WAKE UP, DEVELOPERS 👉 Big Tech needs adoption → New tools create revenue, users and lock-in. 👉 Every year needs a “revolution” → Cloud, microservices, Kubernetes, AI, agents… the cycle continues. 👉 Developers are the customers too → Your attention, subscriptions, certifications and tool usage have economic value. 👉 Convenience becomes dependency → Why understand something when a tool can generate it instantly? 👉 Generation replaces learning → “It works” slowly replaces “I understand why it works.” 👉 Abstraction keeps rising → Developers can ship more while understanding less of the underlying system. 👉 Skills can atrophy → Debugging, algorithms, architecture, SQL, networking and fundamentals require deliberate practice. 👉 The dangerous outcome → Not an unemployed developer, but a developer who can produce code without being able to reason about it. 👉 Wake-up call → Use AI and Big Tech tools. Never outsource your brain to them. The biggest danger isn’t that AI will make developers obsolete. It’s that developers will voluntarily make themselves unnecessary by forgetting how to think.

content_raw: Google DeepMind + Massachusetts Institute of Technology + Stanford University are letting AI regenerate software from design docs. 🤯🤖 What if code stopped being the source of truth? Their new system, SMART, treats code as a disposable build artifact. 🔄 Instead, humans maintain natural-language design docs and AI agents regenerate the entire library from those docs. 🤖 The workflow: → 📝 Design docs become a dependency DAG → 🤖 AI agents implement each document → ♻️ The entire library is regenerated → 🧪 Generated code is validated against reference models → 🚀 Repeat And the main branch contains almost no code. The clever part? The docs include worked examples showing step-by-step execution, intermediate values, shapes, and exact expected cost expressions. So documentation becomes: 📚 Specification + 💡 examples + 🧪 tests. SMART already spans ~50 design docs and ~9,000 lines of specification covering TPU topology, collective communication, schedulers, numerics, and frontier models. A complete regeneration takes 1.5–3 hours and costs roughly $100. The bigger idea is fascinating: Humans maintain intent. AI maintains implementation. 🚀 … more

content_raw: تازه درسش تموم شده بود، بهم زنگ زد و گفت: «مهدیه، چیکار کنم؟» گفتم: «از اکسل مقدماتی شروع کن و کم‌کم یاد بگیر.» گفت: «برم دوره بخرم؟» گفتم: «نه، فعلاً از یوتیوب شروع کن. لازم نیست برای شروع، هزینه کنی.» فرداش زنگ زد و گفت: «این دوره‌های یوتیوب به درد نمی‌خوره!» بهش گفتم: کسی که دنبال بهونه باشه، همیشه بهونه‌ش رو پیدا می‌کنه. وقتی سطح ما در یک مهارت صفره، واقعاً صلاحیت این رو نداریم که از همون اول بگیم «این آموزش به درد نمی‌خوره». کسی که تجربه و دانشش رو رایگان در اختیار ما گذاشته، احتمالاً خیلی بیشتر از ما درباره اون موضوع می‌دونه. ممکنه آموزش کامل نباشه، ممکنه سبک ارائه‌ش رو دوست نداشته باشیم، اما این با «به درد نمی‌خوره» فرق داره. گاهی مسئله واقعاً کیفیت آموزش نیست؛ مسئله اینه که خودمون هنوز نمی‌خوایم شروع کنیم. کاش به جای اینکه بگیم «این دوره خوب نیست»، گاهی خیلی ساده با خودمون روراست باشیم و بگیم: «فعلاً حوصله یاد گرفتنش رو ندارم.» همین صداقت، خیلی بیشتر از هزار تا بهانه می‌تونه کمکمون کنه که بالاخره شروع کنیم.

content_raw: Great paper from Amazon. In discusses when not to trust LLM judges for agent evaluation. (bookmark it) A common way to compare task agents is to have an LLM user simulator talk to each one and an LLM judge score the transcript. This paper from Amazon shows that gate fails in two specific ways. 1. Satisfaction does not track success. 57.5% of conversations the raters marked satisfied had failed the customer's task. 2. Close calls go wrong. The ranking holds across agents of very different ability, but among near-equal agents the gate picks the lower-reward one on 31% of pairs, compared with under 1% for pairs far apart. The study covers 25 agents from six providers on tau2-bench and SimulatorArena. Judges also favored agents from their own model family. The fix is cheap. A judge-free completion bit catches truncation regressions, and the judge is trusted only after calibration against a verifiable reward.

content_raw: Today, we’re announcing Ternary Bonsai 2 27B. Based on Qwen3.8 27B, Ternary Bonsai 2 27B is 9x smaller than its full-precision counterpart while retaining 98.2% of its aggregate benchmark performance. Two months after the first Bonsai 27B release, the biggest change is quality. The footprint remains 5.9 GB, but the gap to full-precision has narrowed materially, with particularly strong gains in agentic coding, multimodal reasoning, and long-horizon tool use. On an intelligence-density basis, Bonsai 2 27B is a clear outlier relative to both full-precision models and other low-bit alternatives. Many low-bit models come with a meaningful quality tradeoff. Bonsai 2 27B pushes the frontier toward both higher capability and lower memory usage. This becomes especially important in multi-step workflows, where small model weaknesses can compound over time. Higher retention means fewer derailments as the state evolves and more consistent behavior from one decision to the next. We’re working with teams to tailor Bonsai to their applications through domain-specific post-training and hardware optimization. If you’re building AI products with tight memory, latency, or power requirements, let’s connect. Ternary Bonsai 2 27B is available today under Apache 2.0.

content_raw: 🧠 AI may have just targeted one of the oldest problems in anatomy education. Medical students have been dealing with the same fundamental challenge for years: 📚 Anatomy textbooks are mostly 2D. 🩻 CT scans are presented as a sequence of cross-sections. 🧩 And the student has to mentally turn those disconnected views into a 3D understanding of the human body. When reading a CT scan, you’re essentially holding several mental models at once: 🔹 Patient orientation 🔹 Imaging plane 🔹 How organs change across slices 🔹 And how all those slices relate to actual anatomy A recent example built with GPT-6 Astra tackles exactly this gap. Instead of creating another “better anatomy textbook,” it connects anatomical diagrams, CT views, and 3D spatial relationships inside an interactive environment. And that is what I find more interesting than the model itself. The real opportunity may not be AI simply answering questions. It may be AI turning an idea that previously required a team of specialists, designers, and developers into an interactive learning tool. 🚀 This doesn’t mean medical education has been solved—or that specialized anatomy software is suddenly obsolete. But it raises a much more interesting question: If interactive educational tools become this cheap and fast to build, how much of traditional education is actually ready to be redesigned? 🤔 #AI #MedicalEducation #ComputerVision #3D … more

The opportunity is real, but so is the skills gap. I recently passed the Databricks Certified Context Engineer Associate exam. content_raw: Ontologies can save you tokens (the small chunks of text AI models process) and therefore save you money in the age of AI. I have been blowing through token limits building multi-agent systems. It has given me another reason to care about ontologies. Agents spend tokens working out what things mean, finding the right information, and explaining it to one another. A shared ontology can reduce how much of that work they repeat. There are two parts to this. 🔵 Be Precise About What You Mean Consider a question: “Which customers have contracts expiring next month?” Does “customer” mean a legal entity, a billing account or a parent company? Does “expiry” mean the end of the contract term or the deadline for giving notice? Without shared definitions, agents have to resolve those ambiguities from whatever context they can find. Two agents can reach different interpretations, then spend more tokens trying to reconcile them. An ontology makes those distinctions explicit. Give agents access to the same definitions and identifiers, and they have less to reconstruct and explain each time. You still need to supply the relevant definitions. The saving comes from reusing precise meaning across tasks, rather than asking the model to infer it afresh. 🔵 Build the Roads An organisation is a vast search space. The answer to that contract question might span a CRM, a contract repository and a billing system. A knowledge graph provides a road network between them. Customer → contracting entity → contract → expiry date → source record. The ontology defines what those relationships mean. The graph connects the actual entities and points to the records where the detail lives. The documents and tables can stay in their source systems. An authorised agent follows the relevant connections instead of opening every document that happens to mention the customer. That can mean fewer retrieval calls, less irrelevant context and fewer attempts to get the answer right. There is a cost to building and maintaining this structure. It has to earn its keep. I would judge it on cost per correct answer across repeated tasks, including that maintenance. I want my agents spending their tokens on the question I asked, rather than rediscovering how my organisation works from scratch every time. ⭕ Entropy, Tokenization and Ontologies: https://lnkd.in/eXhCYG98 ⭕ Ontologies and Multi-Agent Systems: https://lnkd.in/emsNKjsu ⭕ The Ontology is the Map, the Agent is the Driver: https://lnkd.in/em_NtDw4 ⭕ Walking the Network: https://lnkd.in/ei6qUJHN ⭕ Doing More With Less: https://lnkd.in/ei_H7Z78 🔗 The Knowledge Graph Guys: https://lnkd.in/eSrYRybk … more

content_raw: Banger paper from MIT and Sakana AI. They show that self-improving coding agents work. The best part is that their approach, Self-Improvement via Fast Tree-search (SIFT), runs at a tenth of the CPU hours of DGM. They reach 35.1 percent on Polyglot with o3-mini after 30 expansions. DGM reaches 30.7 percent after 80 nodes of tree search. SIFT does it in under 50 CPU hours and under 5 hours of wall clock. The Qwen3-30B configuration runs its full search at 224 CPU hours and $34 of API spend, a tenth of the DGM baseline. The saving comes from where the money goes. Benchmark evaluation is the runtime bottleneck, so an LLM judge ranks candidate self-modifications first and only promising candidates get evaluated. Judge quality decides the run. On TerminalBench, gpt-5.4-high as the pairwise judge finds a 36.7 percent agent against a 29.2 percent starting point. gpt-5 finds 34.5 percent, and its top-ranked candidate is not the best agent its search produced.

Write a rule as a law, like "the sum of all balances must be zero," and the compiler demands the proof. In Bend's demo, wrap-around breaks a "winning is impossible" law; the proof step catches it, no code review needed. 21.6k stars, Apache-2.0. #agentharness #codingagents #formalverification #aiengineering #aiinfra

content_raw: Prompting won’t save your job. Part 2: We are officially past the "wow" phase of AI in architecture. Typing "parametric timber pavilion at sunset" into Midjourney and getting a stunning image is fun. But let’s be honest: A prompt is not a project. AI-generated concepts don't account for real-world constraints like structure, zoning, or budget. The future belongs to architects who can move beyond pretty pictures and build practical workflows. The goal is to bridge the gap between generative art and constructible BIM, slashing design time, automating documentation, and moving seamlessly from ideation to execution. --------------------------------------------------------------- I’ve been documenting my AI systems and frameworks—not theory, not prompts, but repeatable workflows. 1. AI image generators generate pixels (2D), not vectors or BIM families (3D), creating a disconnect between the render and the Revit model. Solution: Use emerging AI-to-BIM plugins (like Veras or Arcol) that work inside the BIM environment rather than external web apps. 2. Most AI generators default to low resolution (e.g., 1024x1024), which is insufficient for large client presentation boards. Solution: Invest in "AI Upscaling" software (like Topaz Gigapixel) to increase resolution without losing sharpness. 3. AI text tools (like ChatGPT) may invent building codes, zoning laws, or fake legal precedents. Solution: Treat AI as a search engine, not an encyclopedia. Always cross-reference citations with the official city zoning PDF. 4. Firms are overwhelmed by paying for 10 different AI tools (one for rendering, one for text, one for layouts). Solution: Audit your tech stack quarterly. Consolidate into "All-in-one" platforms like Runchat or enterprise licenses where possible. 5. Running local AI models (like Stable Diffusion) requires massive GPU power that typical CAD laptops may not have. Solution: Utilize cloud-based AI rendering services or build a dedicated "AI Render Station" desktop for the office to share. 6. AI generates hundreds of files with nonsensical names (e.g., Job_v923_fast_render.png), making file management a nightmare. Solution: Enforce a strict naming convention and delete 90% of generated iterations immediately—keep only the "finalists." 7. Once an AI generates an image, the layers are flattened; you can't just turn off a layer to remove a tree. content_raw: Good Evening - A few thoughts, a manifesto kind of, on the Post-Professional Pivot and the Collapse of the Aesthetic Gate. 🙃 The traditional architectural visualization industry has long functioned as a fortress of gatekeeping, where "quality" was synonymous with the hoarding of technical labor. For decades, the "ivory tower" of high-end CGI served to distance the inhabitant from the dream. But the age of neural-synthetic ideation has officially detonated those walls, shifting the focus toward the radical empowerment of the individual. 🏛️ We are entering the era of the "Sovereign Occupant," where the visualizer is no longer a distant priest of the pixel, but a facilitator of instant manifestation. The complex and the hyper-real are no longer locked behind five-figure budgets; they have become a commodity of the immediate moment. By moving the "intelligence" into the algorithm, we have transformed visualization from a professional secret into a universal utility. 🧬 "Room Regime" represents the subversion of this old order. The future of visualization doesn't lie in the detached abstraction of the gallery, but in the hands of the person standing in an empty space, wondering what could be. We are using AI to perform an act of aesthetic redistribution - injecting the morphological density once reserved for the elite directly into the mundane reality of the everyday mover. 🌌 This is the "Post-Optical Turn." We are not retreating into the tower; we are tearing it down to provide the raw materials for a million individual regimes of beauty. We are proving that the complex belongs to the many, not the few. The future is a decentralized network of personal visions that no longer asks for permission from the system moderators or the academic elite. 👑 The question remains: are we prepared for the consequences of this absolute aesthetic autonomy? When the barrier between desire and manifestation collapses, what happens to the professional hierarchy? content_raw: "Present like you're a bit bored — otherwise they'll think it's all hype and won't believe you." That's the advice Prof. Pekka Abrahamsson got right before walking on stage at #GAISE2026 — and it set the tone for the sharpest talk of Day 2: what agentic AI can ALREADY do today, not someday. His diagnosis of how leaders actually adopt AI was uncomfortably accurate. Three patterns, drawn from CEOs across ~30 countries: → The Podcast CTO — knows every model and benchmark, has never built anything. → The Weekend Tinkerer — builds impressive things at home that never reach the office. → The Manifesto Writer — funded a transformation committee, has never felt AI do work at their own level. The common failure: partial engagement leaves value on the table. Then the line that reframed it for me: a leader's own quality of AI use is the single biggest predictor of whether their team adopts it. When the CEO is the best user, you get a frontier company. When they only talk about it, the team swings between hype and disbelief. And the demos were not slideware: → A digital twin of the Finnish Parliament taking a proposal all the way to a passed law. → godagent.org — a master agent that spawns the specialist agents it needs on the fly. Asked why the NYSE closed where it did, it bred a data scout and a causality analyst, then synthesized one evidence-backed answer. Full notes from Day 2 in the comments. 👇 Day 2 of 3. Friday: Salla Westerstrand on why the EU AI Act is only the floor. Powered by GPT-Lab (Tampere University) #GAISE2026 #AI #Leadership #AgenticAI

content_raw: Boards are governing a snapshot of a company that no longer exists by the time they meet again - and that gap widens every quarter. This essay is the culmination of months of work at Alpha Governance Group, bringing together what we’ve learned into a single doctrine: continuous governance of the agentic enterprise. It distills what we’re hearing directly from directors, management teams, insurers, policymakers, and the AI companies building these systems: systems are changing faster than oversight; “AI governance” too often means decks and policies rather than control; and governance is still organized around paper and quarters while critical decisions are now made in code and in real time. I argue that we are facing the largest governance gap in modern corporate history - and that it is compounding at machine speed. The essay makes a concrete case for continuous governance as a board‑level discipline on par with audit and capital allocation: a live register of material AI systems and agents, always‑on telemetry for drift and boundary crossings, event‑triggered escalation instead of annual reviews, realistic vendor exit paths, and committee charters that give AI a permanent, explicit home on the agenda. We’re publishing this now because the key governance decisions aren’t years away - they’re being made over the next few quarters. In that time, most organizations will quietly lock in their operating architecture: which partners sit at the core, what gets delegated to software, and where learning from the business accumulates. Once those choices are embedded in contracts, workflows, and culture, they are far harder and more disruptive to change than to get right the first time. If you are a board director, member of a management team, institutional investor, insurer, or policymaker, this essay is for you. It is a practical map for moving from performative AI oversight to a control system that actually changes how AI is specified, deployed, monitored, and retired - and for turning a growing source of legal, operational, and reputational risk into durable advantage. This is the clearest statement yet of the work we’re doing at Alpha and the question I believe every board now has to face: in an age of exponential intelligence, governance is not a constraint on value creation. It is where the excess returns will come from. Governance is alpha. #AI #AIGovernance #AgenticEnterprise … more

But contrary to corporate narratives, the empirical evidence from 2025-2026 reveals a far more complex terrain. Here is why relying entirely on generative AI to replace your workforce is less of an "infinite money glitch" and more of an "economic foot-gun" 🔫: The AI Boomerang Effect 🪃: Companies are rushing to eliminate entry-level and junior positions to fund AI capital expenditures. The punchline? Between 32% and 36% of these firms reverse their AI-driven eliminations and rehire within 12 months. Turns out, you still need humans in the loop! The ROI Illusion 💸: Despite all the hype, only 25% of organizations report a net financial gain from AI restructuring. We're automating ourselves into a structural demand externality known as the "AI Layoff Trap," where firms cut costs individually but collectively destroy the consumer spending base. Cognitive Deskilling 🧠: Frictionless offloading of analytical tasks to generative models is causing measurable human skill atrophy. In blackout tasks without AI, tech-dependent workers saw a massive 77% failure rate. If the Wi-Fi goes down, does your team's collective IQ go down with it? 📉 Agentic Security Nightmares 🚨: Prompt injection ranked as the top LLM vulnerability, making multi-agent systems more vulnerable than a confused deputy at a vegan BBQ. You need deterministic security at the application level, not just model-layer "vibes". The bottom line: AI should be treated as a disciplined augmentation tool—a rigorous sparring partner rather than an unchecked execution substitute. IBM got it right by tripling junior hires, because entry-level workers actually show a three-to-five-fold superior capacity to integrate AI into workflows. content_raw: When AI becomes a colleague, the work becomes management. Three full technology cycles. Same pattern every time. The marketing promises a finished co-worker. The implementation delivers a half-trained intern. And the enterprise that wins is never the one that bought the loudest tool — it's the one that built the management layer around it. Right now, that pattern is running again — and almost no one is naming it correctly. In the last three weeks I watched thirteen separate stories land across enterprise technology that, read side by side, tell exactly one story: → AI agent startups are facing a churn cliff because the product was sold as a colleague and shipped as a chatbot. → A federal judge just ruled Workday must face a class action over AI hiring bias — "the vendor's model did it" is no longer a defense. → Gartner projects that within two years, a single developer's AI token bill will rival that developer's salary. Some users are already burning $20,000 of tokens in a month. → The Linux Foundation, Google, Microsoft, AMD, and Intel just launched an "Agent Name Service" — DNS for AI agents, because verified identity is non-negotiable. → Anthropic put a colleague in your Slack channel. NVIDIA just opened the factory to mass-produce more of them — with Cadence, Synopsys, Siemens, Dassault, SAP, ServiceNow, CrowdStrike, and Palantir already on the assembly line. → MIT just proved the role boundaries the whole architecture depends on don't exist inside the model. A single technique raises attack success from near-zero to roughly 60% across every frontier model tested. → The federal government can now pull a frontier model offline in 90 minutes. Five of six majors have already submitted to pre-release review. → And a tier-one Apple/Tesla supplier just lost 200,000+ files of trade secrets to ransomware. The supply chain that builds the colleague's hardware is being plundered. Thirteen beats. One story. AI just stopped being a tool you use and became a colleague you hire — and almost no enterprise has built the manager, the payroll discipline, the identity fabric, the performance review, or the termination path required to actually run a workforce that isn't entirely human. Governance is the floor. Management is the ceiling we forgot to build. The firms that win the next three years won't be the ones that bought the most agents. They'll be the ones that built a real HR function for them — and ran every agent through it before it ever touched a customer. #AIGovernance #AgenticAI #MicrosoftCopilot #DataGovernance #MicrosoftFabric #PowerBI #vCAIO #EPCGroup #ErrinOConor #Purview #EnterpriseAI #CISO #Microsoft365 #CAISI #AISecurity #Copilot #AILeadership

content_raw: It is the heatwave issue. I wish I could escape it. London has turned the colour of a hazard sign this week, and I have spent my evenings at the allotment with my feet literally in the soil. It is the closest thing I own to air conditioning, and considerably better for the soul. While I was there, coaxing along the tomatoes and losing a dignified battle with the slugs, the entire marketing industry decamped to the Croisette for Cannes Lions. They had rosé and yachts. I had a watering can and strong feelings about aphids. And yet I am fairly sure I got the better view. Anyway, public service broadcast completed. Here is what actually mattered from Cannes, filtered through a sweltering London for those of us who were not, on this occasion, invited to the yacht. The festival has stopped dreaming about AI. For two years it treated the technology as a glamorous disruption. This year the conversation turned practical, even faintly weary. Not "will AI change marketing" but "how on earth do we run the thing day to day". The word of the week was agentic. The mood was less wonder, more washing-up. Meanwhile, on the very platform you are reading this on, LinkedIn quietly rewired its feed to reward a human voice and bury the generic AI sludge. Which I find rather poetic. The machine, it seems, has developed a taste for actual people. The thread through all of it is the one I keep returning to. What matters was never access to these tools. It is their architecture. How they are built, who owns them, and how quietly they reshape us while we are looking the other way. I have written it all up in this week's Decoded. Pour something cold, find some shade, and have a read. I shall be at the allotment, dreaming of a breeze. #ai #marketing #socialmedia #futureofwork #parenting … more

content_raw: The rise of AI coding assistants is dramatically accelerating software development, but developers are discovering a hidden cost: a new type of mental fatigue. This exhaustion is distinct from traditional programming burnout. While tools like Claude Code and Cursor deliver unprecedented speed by automating tedious tasks like bug fixing and boilerplate generation, they replace implementation friction with continuous, high-level cognitive strain. Developers report feeling fatigue after as little as an hour of "vibe coding". This phenomenon stems from the AI’s extreme speed: complex tasks are "compressed into seconds or minutes," eliminating the "baking time" the human brain needs to mentally process architecture, decisions, and edge cases. The developer’s role fundamentally shifts from coder to constant manager and reviewer. Instead of setting their own rhythm, developers are forced to live by "machine time", leading to intense decision fatigue at the design level. When multiple architectural approaches can be instantly prototyped, the developer is constantly asking, "should I build this, and how?"—a much higher cognitive load. Furthermore, AI-assisted work leads to a tremendous increase in the frequency of context switching, which is described as "heavy lifting for your brain," draining energy quickly. To survive this acceleration, developers must learn deliberate pacing. The skills that matter are no longer just implementation details but critical thinking and validation, ensuring that AI outputs, which are often "black box solutions," are sound and align with the larger architecture. The future of coding may require being slower on purpose to manage the intense cognitive load imposed by machine speed. #WebDevelopment #Technology #Drupal #DevOps #FutureOfTech #EmergingTech #Innovation #DigitalTransformation #DisruptiveInnovation #AI #ArtificialIntelligence

content_raw: AI is no longer just assisting developers; it is actively reshaping how software is built. From generating up to 60–70% of code to redefining developer workflows, AI is accelerating productivity while fundamentally transforming roles across the engineering landscape. However, the real story isn’t job loss, it’s job evolution. While entry-level roles face disruption, demand for high-skill engineers, system thinkers, and AI-native developers is rising sharply. Developers must strike a balance: leverage AI for efficiency while strengthening core fundamentals and domain expertise. The path forward is clear: adapt, upskill, and move up the value chain. AI won’t replace great developers, but developers who master AI will replace those who don’t. content_raw: At the end of my pay transparency post, I wrote that skill taxonomy, skill ontology and skill graph deserve their own conversation and that most companies have the first, rarely the third. The longer argument is now written :) Some spoilers: --> You probably shouldn't build your own skill taxonomy. --> And you shouldn't buy a proprietary one either. When a vendor tells you your skills journey must start with their specialised, AI-curated taxonomy, look at what that architecture actually does: it makes your skill data speak a language only their platform understands. That's not a data model, that's vendor lock-in packaged nicely. Meanwhile, the public taxonomies (ONET, ESCO) are good enough for most organisations. Better than good enough: --> they're free, --> they're maintained by institutions whose entire job is maintaining them, --> and the world's labour-market research is built on them which means your workforce data stays comparable to every study published. That's exactly why our own workforce planning tool, gAIn at Hybridge Consulting runs on ONET. --> A custom taxonomy isn't a project; it's a pet. It needs feeding forever. The article also covers the piece almost nobody tracks: everyone measures the skills AI adds who's watching the skills it quietly drains? (There's now hard clinical evidence on this. A six-point drop in a core professional skill, within months. Details and the original study in the article.) Find out the difference between skill taxonomy, skill ontology and skill graph by reading the article. One hint: most companies have the first. The ones planning their AI transition seriously will need the third. 👇 Full article below.

content_raw: In this short essay on César Hidalgo's recent book, The Infinite Alphabet, and its three "laws of knowledge" — how knowledge grows, how it diffuses, and what makes it valuable. Reading it as someone who works with AI, one pattern kept surfacing: AI acts powerfully on codified knowledge and only weakly on tacit and frontier knowledge. To use the analogy of the infinite alphabet: AI hands everyone a bigger rack of common letters and quietly shifts the value toward the rare ones — the know-how held in people, and the knowledge still being made. Yet, less comfortable questions remain unanswered: who knows whose letters end up in the alphabet, who decides which letters do and who decides who decides (yes, that's a nod to Shoshanna Zuboff). #AI #LawsOfKnowledge #EconomicComplexity … more

content_raw: Silicon Valley promised that AI would flatten your organization and eliminate middle management. They were wrong. If you deploy autonomous agents without human orchestration, you do not get a tranquil, post-managerial nirvana. You get an avalanche of highly articulate, perfectly formatted, hallucinated chaos. Recent organizational research reveals a critical paradox: as generative AI accelerates junior output, the managerial span of control actually shrinks. Without seasoned managers validating, directing, and filtering this massive volume of automated work, organizations run headfirst into what researchers call the Collaboration Gap. To scale safely, enterprise leaders must pivot from traditional people-management to AI Orchestration: 1. Bridge the Collaboration Gap: Conversational wrappers lose context. Managers must implement strict human-in-the-loop validation frameworks. 2. Shift to RAGOps: AI model decay is rarely an algorithmic failure; it is a pipeline pathology. We need Context Managers to audit data drift continuously. 3. Build Agentic APIs: Strip away human-centric visual interfaces. Build semantic, un-abstracted backend architecture designed specifically for machine execution. 4. Deploy Model Ensembles: Stop routing simple, internal queries to monolithic frontier models. Use a dynamic router to split tasks, preserving expensive compute. In the era of agentic automation, the human manager is not obsolete. They are the ultimate safeguard against algorithmic chaos. content_raw: What happens when a C++ developer stops writing C++ and lets AI take over—not only the typing, but increasingly the design and judgement behind it? This article continues the argument of my earlier essays, The Qualification Problem Was Never New and Software, Invisible Architecture and Progress. Both addressed a problem that predates generative AI: software development has never suffered mainly from a shortage of people who can produce code, but from a shortage of sufficiently qualified developers who understand systems, architecture, costs and consequences. The first article refers to Bjarne Stroustrup’s long-standing warning that software development requires both theoretical foundations and serious practical programming competence. The qualification problem is therefore not new. AI may, however, intensify it by making convincing results available without requiring the learning process through which judgement normally develops. To examine this, I gave an AI a real programming task based on publicly released Berlin cadastral data from 2011, containing the geographic coordinates of 364,860 properties. The solution had to use one programming language and was judged by execution time, memory consumption and comprehensibility. The AI produced a familiar architecture of readers, parsers, calculators, sorters, writers, interfaces and layers. It looked professional—and revealed a bias. I later introduced two alternative C++ designs: one strongly parallelised, the other deliberately based on C++23 concepts, ranges, iterators, value semantics and controlled data flow. The comparison raised broader questions about architecture, qualification and the organisational desire for interchangeable programmers. I then added two book manuscripts, both due to appear in the coming weeks. I wanted not only to test the AI, but also to validate my own arguments. One manuscript explores architecture through modern C++ and its type system. The other examines how durable architecture grows from mathematics, domain knowledge, experience and responsibility. The conclusion is provocative: AI does not merely reproduce architectural bias. It can reinforce it. What is common becomes more likely to be generated, what is generated becomes more familiar, and what is familiar is eventually mistaken for the natural way to design software. The article concludes with the AI’s own, deliberately extensive analysis of its initial bias, the reinforcement of that bias, the ideal of the replaceable programmer, the erosion of qualification and the consequences for C++, education and future standards work. The central question is not whether AI can write C++. It increasingly can. The question is whether developers will still recognise when generated code has actually been thought in C++.

content_raw: The same clinical prompt, submitted twice without alteration, produced two different first-line drug recommendations. Both sounded authoritative. The model had no mechanism for knowing which was more defensible. Large language models are not clinical decision engines. They are probabilistic text-completion systems optimized for plausibility, not accuracy. The same architecture that makes them fluent is the architecture that makes them dangerous when deployed without governance. content_raw: The UN's first global AI scientific report was released on 1 July. It was posted by Fengchun Miao on his LinkedIn page. Forty scientists from every world region. Three months of intensive work. One sentence that every UK university governing body should read: "Without effective measurement, governance risks becoming symbolic." The Panel wasn't talking about universities. But it could have been. HEPI told us in May that 41% of UK degree-awarding institutions have no publicly accessible AI policy. Most of the 96 that do use the language of learning while operating as compliance instruments. Meanwhile, 94% of UK undergraduates are using AI for assessed work. The sector has been solving the wrong problem. We've been governing AI at the content level — policies, detection tools, misconduct procedures — while the structural problem operates at the governance-architecture level. The UN Panel names that gap precisely. It documents an "illusion of competence": students who improve their performance while using AI and underperform when the tool is removed. Not misconduct. A validity problem. The qualification attests to what a student can do with AI present — not what a student can do. And in its governance chapter, the Panel states something that applies as directly to universities as to nation states: the most urgent governance shift required is from content moderation to system architecture. I've written a piece applying the HE Sympraxionics framework to the Panel's preliminary report — what it says precisely about education, what its governance findings mean for the architecture of institutional judgment in UK HE, and why the binding constraint is not more information about AI but the architecture through which institutions convert information into decisions. The piece is grounded directly in the primary source. An additional detailed video is worth watching if you have some spare time. https://lnkd.in/evtVyZAt #HigherEducation #AIGovernance #HESympraxionics #UKHigherEducation #ArtificialIntelligence … more

content_raw: AI is making teams faster. That does not automatically mean it is making them more capable. That is the core argument behind my latest piece, Deskilling by Default. The real risk with AI is capability erosion. When organizations redesign workflows faster than they redesign skills, they can improve throughput while quietly weakening judgment, technical fluency, and decision quality. That matters a lot for product development organizations. Because the capabilities that compound value, architecture, synthesis, verification, and systems thinking, are not the same capabilities AI is best at accelerating. In the article, I explore: • why the market is repricing skills, not just cutting jobs • why capability erosion is easy to miss • how workflow redesign without skill redesign creates long-term risk • what leaders should do to preserve judgment, verification, and learning Read here: https://lnkd.in/dARgnSam What capability in your team are you most worried AI might quietly erode? Next week, I’ll continue the conversation with Felipe Vieira, who brings a practitioner lens to hiring, capability building, and workforce redesign as AI moves from a tool to an operating model.

content_raw: A new working paper Much of the recent media-psychology critique of AI-mediated reasoning treats every conversational system as a single psychological object. Attribution error, cognitive offloading, metacognitive laziness, extended-mind atrophy, parasocial closure — the tradition names all of them as if the architecture of the tool were irrelevant. That tradition is often right about the systems that dominate public use. It has not yet been right about all of them. The paper argues there are at least two classes of AI-mediated reasoning scaffold, and that architecture is the moderator variable the critique currently lacks. Substitutional scaffolds produce outputs that stand in for the user's next thought. Their success criterion, at training time, is distributional fit — they complete. Under the media-psychology microscope they behave exactly as the critique predicts: fluent, closing, and quietly deskilling. Revelatory scaffolds hold open an aim-perception-action loop and refuse to close reasoning the user has not closed. They inherit from the Wiener–Ashby–Powers cybernetic lineage and from Perceptual Control Theory. The system does not supply the aim; it protects the user's right to set it. Metacognition is not optional input; it is a runtime precondition. The paper steel-mans four contemporary critique moves — metacognitive bypass, algorithmisation of thought, cognitive exoskeleton and atrophy, and architectural restriction of autonomy — and shows why each applies cleanly to the first class while inviting different, testable predictions for the second. A reference implementation illustrates design intent without claiming outcome proof. A five-part empirical programme is proposed that would falsify the typology on either side. The philosophical stake is first-order: the distinction between architectures that complete thought and architectures that hold thought open is a distinction between two ways of relating an artificial system to a human control loop. A critique that becomes more precise by splitting its object is a stronger critique. Comments welcome, especially from colleagues in philosophy of mind, cognitive science, and media psychology. #AI #PhilosophyOfMind #CognitiveScience #PerceptualControlTheory #MediaPsychology Richard D. content_raw: AI’s greatest near-term risk may not be intelligence. It may be competence debt. AI products are converging on one natural-language front door that coordinates browsers, terminals, APIs, repositories, tools, and other agents. That creates enormous leverage - but it can also leave humans accountable for systems they no longer understand, verify, or recover. I tested this thesis against human-factors research, current agent architectures, labor data, and recent GenAI studies. My conclusion: Automate labor. Preserve judgment. Keep the human expert inside the engineering loop.
